UN3658.stem: A 55-year-old man is seen in a sleep clinic with loud snoring, witnessed pauses in his breathing, unrefreshing sleep and daytime sleepiness. His Epworth Sleepiness Scale score is 14 and his BMI is 36 kg/m². He has no heart failure or chronic lung disease, and all sleep diagnostic services are available locally. Which is the most appropriate first diagnostic test?
A 55-year-old man has reduced libido, erectile dysfunction, fatigue and loss of muscle mass. His morning testosterone is low, with a raised LH and FSH. Where is the defect?

UN3658.presentation: Moderate obstructive sleep apnoea syndrome — DVLA advice
UN3658.stem: A 49-year-old man who holds a car licence only has a sleep study showing moderate obstructive sleep apnoea, with an apnoea–hypopnoea index of 22 events per hour. He has excessive daytime sleepiness and recently nearly fell asleep while waiting at traffic lights. Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) treatment is being arranged. He asks what this means for his driving. What is the most appropriate advice?
UN3658.correct_answer: He must stop driving now and must notify the DVLA himself

UN3658.presentation: Suspected arrhythmic syncope — choosing ambulatory ECG
UN3658.stem: A 66-year-old man is seen in the cardiology clinic after two episodes of sudden loss of consciousness without warning while seated, 5 months apart, each with full recovery within a minute. Examination, 12-lead ECG (no conduction abnormality) and echocardiogram are normal. The cardiologist suspects an arrhythmic cause. Which investigation is most appropriate next?

A 52-year-old man presents with recurrent episodes of chest pain occurring at rest. During an episode, ECG demonstrates transient ST-segment elevation. Coronary angiography later reveals normal coronary arteries. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN3661.stem: A 55-year-old woman with pernicious anaemia stopped attending for her vitamin B12 injections two years ago. She now reports tingling in both feet and feeling unsteady when walking in the dark. On examination, vibration sense and joint position sense are reduced in both feet, ankle reflexes are absent and both plantar responses are extensor. Romberg's test is positive. Which condition is most likely?
UN3661.correct_answer: Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord

UN3661.presentation: Subacute combined degeneration of the cord
UN3661.stem: A 58-year-old woman with vitiligo and hypothyroidism has had numb feet for several months and now falls when walking in the dark. She has reduced vibration and joint position sense in the feet, a positive Romberg test, absent ankle reflexes and extensor plantar responses. Her full blood count shows a macrocytic anaemia, her serum B12 is low and her folate is also low. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
UN3661.correct_answer: Intramuscular hydroxocobalamin first, adding folic acid once B12 replacement has started

UN3661.presentation: Suspected B12 deficiency with neurological signs — timing of treatment
UN3661.stem: A 68-year-old man is seen on the acute medical unit with 2 months of numbness in both feet, unsteadiness in the dark and falls. Vibration and joint position sense are impaired in the feet and Romberg's test is positive. Haemoglobin is 92 g/L with mean cell volume 118 fL. Vitamin B12 deficiency with spinal cord involvement is suspected. What is the most appropriate management?
UN3661.correct_answer: Send a B12 level, then start intramuscular B12 now

UN3661.presentation: Nitrous oxide-related vitamin B12 deficiency — initial test
UN3661.stem: A 20-year-old student presents to his GP with 3 weeks of numbness in both feet and an unsteady gait. He says he has inhaled large amounts of nitrous oxide from canisters most weekends for the past year. Romberg test is positive and vibration sense is reduced at the ankles. Vitamin B12 deficiency caused by nitrous oxide use is suspected. Which test should be used as the initial test for vitamin B12 deficiency?

A 20-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her flatmate. She has felt flu-like since last night and now has a severe generalised headache, has vomited twice and keeps her eyes closed because the room lights hurt. She is febrile. Passive flexion of her neck is painful and restricted, and she cannot fully straighten her knee when her hip is flexed. There is no rash. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN3661.presentation: Extradural haemorrhage — scoring the Glasgow Coma Scale
UN3661.stem: A 24-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after being struck on the side of the head with a cricket ball. He was talking at the scene, but in the department he has become drowsy. His eyes open only when pressure is applied to his fingernail bed. He utters random, inappropriate words but no conversation. When pressure is applied above the eye, his arms bend slowly at the elbows and wrists with the arms drawn towards the chest, rather than moving away from or towards the stimulus. CT head shows a right temporal extradural haematoma. What is his Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score?

UN3661.presentation: Subacute Combined Degeneration of the Cord
UN3661.stem: A patient with low vitamin B12 develops a progressive unsteady gait, loss of vibration sense and proprioception in the feet, and weakness. Examination shows ABSENT ankle jerks but EXTENSOR (upgoing) plantar responses. What is the most likely diagnosis?
UN3661.correct_answer: Subacute combined degeneration of the cord

UN3661.presentation: Infantile haemangioma — drug treatment of a high-risk lesion
UN3661.stem: A 10-week-old boy has a rapidly growing infantile haemangioma on the upper eyelid. It now partially covers the pupil when his eyes are open. He is otherwise well, with normal heart rate and blood glucose. He is seen urgently by the paediatric dermatology team, who plan to start drug treatment. Which drug is most appropriate?

UN3662.stem: A patient with type 2 diabetes has painful, burning, symmetrical numbness and tingling in both feet (a glove-and-stocking distribution) that disturbs sleep. Glycaemic control has been optimised. He also has coexisting low mood. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment for the neuropathic pain?

A 60-year-old man with long-standing type 2 diabetes has burning, painful paraesthesiae in both feet in a 'stocking' distribution, worse at night. What is the most appropriate first-line drug for the neuropathic pain?

A 61-year-old woman who lives alone and drinks heavily is assessed on a medical ward. Over several months she has developed burning feet, numbness in a stocking distribution and weakness climbing stairs. There is mild ankle oedema. She has been eating very little.

Deficiency of which vitamin is most likely responsible?
A patient who has had type 1 diabetes for over 15 years is found on repeated testing to have persistently raised urinary albumin excretion. What complication is most likely developing?

UN3662.presentation: Avoiding serotonin syndrome — neuropathic pain in a patient on citalopram
UN3662.stem: A 61-year-old man with type 2 diabetes sees his GP with burning pain in both feet that disturbs his sleep. Painful diabetic neuropathy is diagnosed. He has taken citalopram for depression for 3 years and his mood is stable on it. His renal function is normal. He would like a drug for the pain and wishes to stay on citalopram. Which drug is most appropriate to start?

A 59-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes for 15 years attends her annual diabetes foot check. She says both feet tingle and feel numb, as though she is walking on cotton wool, and are worse at night. Ankle reflexes are absent on both sides and she cannot feel the monofilament on either sole. Muscle power in her legs is normal. Which pattern of nerve damage best fits?

A patient has burning, shooting pain with tingling in a distribution consistent with nerve damage (for example, painful diabetic neuropathy). Standard analgesics have not helped. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

A 64-year-old man has slowly worsening numbness and tingling that began in his feet and has spread upward, with diminished ankle reflexes. Which pattern is most consistent with a peripheral neuropathy?

UN3668.presentation: Nerve Root Causing Weak Ankle Dorsiflexion
UN3668.stem: A 50-year-old man has lower back pain radiating down the outer side of his leg to the top of his foot. On examination, he has weakness when trying to pull his foot upward (dorsiflexion). Which nerve root is most likely affected?

UN3668.presentation: Nerve Root in L5/S1 Disc Prolapse
UN3668.stem: A 41-year-old man develops sudden severe lower back pain after lifting a heavy box at work. The pain radiates down the back of his leg and into his foot. Which nerve root is most likely affected?

UN3668.presentation: Foot drop: L5 root versus peroneal nerve
UN3668.stem: A 52-year-old woman has had 3 weeks of right-sided low back pain radiating down the leg, and her right foot now 'slaps' on the floor when she walks. Examination shows weakness of ankle dorsiflexion and great toe extension, and also weakness of ankle inversion and hip abduction. Sensation is reduced over the dorsum of the foot. Knee and ankle reflexes are preserved. There is no history of leg crossing, recent weight loss or a tight cast. What is the most likely site of the lesion?

A 12-year-old girl who trains in gymnastics four times a week has had 3 months of pain just below her right kneecap. It is worse when kneeling, climbing stairs and landing jumps, and settles with rest. She has no night pain and is otherwise well and afebrile. On examination there is a firm, tender swelling over the tibial tuberosity, and her pain is reproduced by resisted knee extension. There is no effusion, the knee has a full range of movement and examination of the hip is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN3668.presentation: Foot drop — L5 radiculopathy vs common peroneal palsy
UN3668.stem:
A 58-year-old man has had three weeks of his left foot slapping on the ground when he walks. He has lost a lot of weight since weight-loss surgery six months ago and often sits with his legs crossed at his desk. He has also had intermittent aching in his lower back. Examination shows weak left ankle dorsiflexion and big toe extension, with reduced sensation over the dorsum of the left foot. The examining doctor wants to decide whether this is an L5 root lesion or a common peroneal nerve palsy at the fibular head.

Which additional examination finding would most strongly favour an L5 root lesion?

A 68-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and hypertension presents with 2 days of double vision. The two images lie side by side and move further apart when he looks at the television across the room or looks to his right. His right eye cannot move outwards beyond the midline, but all other eye movements, the eyelids and the pupils are normal. The rest of the neurological examination is normal. Which cranial nerve is most likely affected?

A 46-year-old delivery driver has had 2 weeks of pain shooting from his right buttock down the back of his thigh and calf into the sole of his foot, which began after he lifted a heavy parcel. He has no bladder or bowel symptoms and perianal sensation is normal. Straight leg raising is limited to 40 degrees on the right by pain in the leg. An MRI scan shows a posterolateral L5/S1 disc protrusion compressing the right S1 nerve root. Which additional examination finding is most likely?

A 22-year-old army recruit develops severe pain and swelling in both thighs the day after an intensive first week of training that included repeated squats in hot weather. He has noticed his urine is dark brown. Temperature is 37.3°C and blood pressure 128/78 mmHg. Both quadriceps are tender and he has pain-limited weakness of knee extension with normal reflexes and sensation. Urine dipstick is strongly positive for blood but microscopy shows no red cells. Creatine kinase is 48,000 U/L and creatinine is 156 micromol/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN3669.presentation: Nerve Root Causing Weak Ankle Dorsiflexion
UN3669.stem: A 50-year-old man has lower back pain radiating down the outer side of his leg to the top of his foot. On examination, he has weakness when trying to pull his foot upward (dorsiflexion). Which nerve root is most likely affected?

UN3669.presentation: Sciatica with progressive foot weakness — referral urgency
UN3669.stem: A 45-year-old man has had right-sided sciatica from a lumbar disc prolapse for 4 weeks. When his GP saw him a week ago he had mild weakness of right ankle dorsiflexion. He returns because he is now catching his right foot when walking, and ankle dorsiflexion and big-toe extension are clearly weaker than last week. He has no bladder, bowel or sexual symptoms, his perianal sensation is normal, his left leg is unaffected and he has no history of cancer, fever or weight loss. What is the most appropriate management?
UN3669.correct_answer: Urgent discussion with the on-call spinal surgical team

UN3669.stem: A patient develops a foot drop after a period of prolonged leg crossing (or a tight plaster cast). There is weakness of ankle dorsiflexion and foot eversion with sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot, but ankle inversion, plantarflexion and the ankle jerk are preserved. Where is the lesion?
UN3669.correct_answer: The common peroneal (fibular) nerve at the fibular neck

UN3669.presentation: Foot drop: L5 root versus peroneal nerve
UN3669.stem: A 52-year-old woman has had 3 weeks of right-sided low back pain radiating down the leg, and her right foot now 'slaps' on the floor when she walks. Examination shows weakness of ankle dorsiflexion and great toe extension, and also weakness of ankle inversion and hip abduction. Sensation is reduced over the dorsum of the foot. Knee and ankle reflexes are preserved. There is no history of leg crossing, recent weight loss or a tight cast. What is the most likely site of the lesion?

UN3669.presentation: New Unilateral Tremor in an Older Man
UN3669.stem: A 68-year-old man presents with a new tremor affecting one hand at rest, slowness of movement and reduced arm swing while walking. Which diagnosis best fits this presentation?

An elderly man has a triad of gait disturbance (a broad-based, shuffling 'magnetic' gait), urinary incontinence and cognitive decline. Imaging shows enlarged ventricles out of proportion to any atrophy. What is the diagnosis, and why does it matter?
UN3669.correct_answer: Normal pressure hydrocephalus — potentially reversible with shunting

UN3669.presentation: Foot drop — L5 radiculopathy vs common peroneal palsy
UN3669.stem:
A 58-year-old man has had three weeks of his left foot slapping on the ground when he walks. He has lost a lot of weight since weight-loss surgery six months ago and often sits with his legs crossed at his desk. He has also had intermittent aching in his lower back. Examination shows weak left ankle dorsiflexion and big toe extension, with reduced sensation over the dorsum of the left foot. The examining doctor wants to decide whether this is an L5 root lesion or a common peroneal nerve palsy at the fibular head.

Which additional examination finding would most strongly favour an L5 root lesion?

A 74-year-old woman has insidious, gradually progressive memory loss over 2 years. She forgets recent conversations, repeats questions, misplaces items and has word-finding difficulty. There is no stepwise deterioration, no early visual hallucinations or parkinsonism, no prominent early personality change, and no gait disturbance. Neurological examination is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN3671.stem: A patient has slowly progressive limb weakness, visible muscle wasting and spontaneous twitching of the affected muscles, with reduced reflexes in those muscle groups. What type of lesion best fits these findings?

UN3671.presentation: Mixed Upper And Lower Motor Neurone Signs
UN3671.stem: Visible wasting, fasciculations and brisk reflexes accompany progressively worsening weakness in both legs of a 64-year-old woman. Which diagnosis is most likely?

UN3671.presentation: Features Of An Upper Motor Neurone Lesion
UN3671.stem: A patient suddenly becomes weak down one side of the body. Of the options given, which examination sign best fits an upper motor neurone cause?

A patient presents with sudden right-sided weakness and is found on examination to have increased muscle tone and exaggerated, brisk reflexes on the affected side. What type of lesion does this suggest?

A 60-year-old man has progressive weakness with a mix of wasting and fasciculations (lower motor neuron) alongside brisk reflexes and up-going plantars (upper motor neuron), with no sensory loss and no eye-movement or sphincter involvement. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A 60-year-old man has confirmed motor neurone disease with mixed upper and lower motor neuron signs and no sensory loss. Which drug is most likely to modestly prolong survival?

UN3671.presentation: Facial Weakness That Spares the Forehead
UN3671.stem: A patient has weakness affecting only the lower part of the left side of the face, with normal, symmetrical forehead wrinkling on both sides. Which lesion best explains this finding?

A 60-year-old man has progressive weakness, wasting and visible fasciculations of both hands over several months. On examination his reflexes are brisk and the plantar responses are extensor. His speech is slurred and the jaw jerk is brisk. Sensation is entirely normal, and there are no eye-movement or sphincter problems. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN3675.stem: A 52-year-old man with Guillain-Barré syndrome has weakness that is now extending to his arms. He is admitted for close monitoring. Which parameter best predicts impending respiratory failure?

A 26-year-old woman develops progressive difficulty walking upstairs over several days, two weeks after an episode of diarrhoea. On examination she has symmetrical weakness in both legs with absent reflexes. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 76-year-old man taking furosemide and bendroflumethiazide for heart failure is admitted with profound generalised weakness. His serum potassium is severely reduced, and his ECG shows prominent U waves. He is also on digoxin. Which complication is the greatest immediate threat to his life?

A 30-year-old man develops progressive, symmetrical ascending leg weakness over 5 days, 2 weeks after a diarrhoeal illness. Reflexes are absent. CSF shows raised protein with a normal cell count. What is the most appropriate treatment, alongside monitoring of respiratory function?
Breathing becomes increasingly laboured in a patient already diagnosed with Guillain-Barre syndrome. Which complication is most critical to watch for?

A 25-year-old man develops ascending weakness over a week, starting in his legs, with loss of reflexes and mild distal numbness. He had diarrhoea three weeks ago. What is the most important investigation to monitor in the acute phase?
A patient admitted with severe community-acquired pneumonia has an arterial blood gas showing marked hypoxaemia with a PaCO2 that is normal. What type of respiratory failure does this represent?

UN3675.presentation: Deep Neck-Space Infection With Airway Risk
UN3675.stem: A patient being treated for acute tonsillitis develops worsening neck swelling over 24 hours, along with increasing difficulty swallowing and a new stridor. What is the most important immediate concern?
UN3675.correct_answer: Airway compromise from deep neck infection

UN3677.stem: A patient with a long history of alcohol misuse, following an episode of untreated confusion, is left with a profound inability to form NEW memories (anterograde amnesia) and fills gaps in memory with fabricated accounts (confabulation), while other cognitive functions are relatively preserved. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN3677.presentation: Progressive memory loss in an older adult
UN3677.stem: A 78-year-old woman is brought to her GP by her daughter. Over the past 18 months she has increasingly repeated the same questions, misplaced belongings and recently got lost driving to a shop she has used for years. She is alert, her symptoms do not fluctuate, and there are no hallucinations, falls or stroke history. Blood tests are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN3677.presentation: Transient Neurological Symptoms With Atrial Fibrillation
UN3677.stem: A 64-year-old woman with known atrial fibrillation has a brief episode of left arm weakness and slurred speech that resolves within an hour. What is an important underlying mechanism to consider?

UN3677.presentation: Delirium in a previously well older adult
UN3677.stem: A district nurse visiting a 79-year-old retired teacher finds him muddled about where he is and talking about events that did not happen. His wife says that yesterday he was doing the crossword, managing his own tablets and driving to the shops. Since this morning he keeps losing the thread of conversation and drifts off mid-sentence. Which diagnosis should be considered first?

A 45-year-old woman presents with a sudden, severe “thunderclap” headache that peaked within seconds, associated with vomiting, neck stiffness and a brief collapse. A non-contrast CT head, performed 8 hours after onset, is reported as normal. She is now neurologically intact. What is the most appropriate next investigation?

UN3677.presentation: Influenza Complication in an Older Adult
UN3677.stem: During a winter flu outbreak in her area, the family of an 81-year-old woman bring her in because she has suddenly spiked a temperature, developed a cough, and become muddled, which is completely out of character for her. Which complication is particularly important to consider in an older adult?

A man with alcohol dependence had an episode of confusion, nystagmus and ataxia that was not treated with thiamine. Weeks later he has profound short-term memory loss and confabulates to fill the gaps, but is otherwise alert. What is the most likely diagnosis?

An 81-year-old man is brought to his GP by his son. Over three years he has increasingly forgotten appointments, asks the same questions repeatedly and recently got lost driving to a familiar supermarket. His son says he is much the same from day to day. In the consultation he is alert, maintains attention throughout and has no signs of infection. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN3684.stem: A 23-year-old woman develops sudden weakness of her right leg the day after a distressing argument. Examination shows give-way weakness, a positive Hoover's sign, and normal reflexes and tone. MRI of the brain and spine is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 30-year-old woman presents with sudden weakness of the left leg. On examination the power is variable and ‘gives way’, and Hoover's sign is positive (hip extension is weak on direct testing but normal when she flexes the opposite hip against resistance). Reflexes are normal, there is no sensory level, and imaging is normal. She describes a recent significant psychological stressor. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 32-year-old man is assessed on the stroke unit after waking with weakness of his right leg following a very stressful week at work. When asked to push his right heel down into the bed he produces no movement, yet when he lifts his left leg against resistance, firm downward pressure is felt under the right heel. His reflexes and plantar responses are normal and MRI of the brain and spine is normal. He is distressed and keen to get better. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A patient has slowly progressive limb weakness, visible muscle wasting and spontaneous twitching of the affected muscles, with reduced reflexes in those muscle groups. What type of lesion best fits these findings?

UN3684.presentation: Crossed Cranial Nerve And Limb Signs
UN3684.stem: A 59-year-old woman suddenly develops double vision, difficulty swallowing and weakness of her right arm and leg together. Which anatomical site could explain this combination of cranial nerve and limb findings?

A 38-year-old man develops sudden severe spinning vertigo with nausea after a recent cold. It has lasted two days. He also reports muffled hearing and ringing in his left ear since the onset, and has never had a similar episode. He has no vascular risk factors, limb weakness, speech disturbance or double vision, and examination shows horizontal nystagmus.

Which diagnosis is most likely?

UN3684.presentation: Sudden Vertigo With Inability to Stand
UN3684.stem: A 59-year-old man develops sudden severe vertigo, is unable to stand or walk unsupported, and is found to have limb incoordination and nystagmus on examination. Which neurological structure should be particularly suspected?

UN3684.presentation: Facial Weakness Affecting the Whole Side of the Face
UN3684.stem: A patient develops sudden weakness of the entire left side of the face, including the inability to raise the left eyebrow or fully close the left eye. What type of facial nerve lesion does this represent?
UN3684.correct_answer: Lower motor neurone facial nerve palsy

UN3686.stem: A 71-year-old woman has sudden left-sided weakness together with an upper motor neurone pattern of facial weakness on the right. Which cranial nerve is responsible for producing the facial weakness itself?

UN3686.presentation: Facial Weakness Affecting the Whole Side of the Face
UN3686.stem: A patient develops sudden weakness of the entire left side of the face, including the inability to raise the left eyebrow or fully close the left eye. What type of facial nerve lesion does this represent?
UN3686.correct_answer: Lower motor neurone facial nerve palsy

UN3686.presentation: Facial Weakness That Spares the Forehead
UN3686.stem: A patient has weakness affecting only the lower part of the left side of the face, with normal, symmetrical forehead wrinkling on both sides. Which lesion best explains this finding?

A 38-year-old woman develops weakness affecting the entire left side of her face, including being unable to close her left eye and losing movement of her forehead on that side. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN3686.presentation: Unilateral Facial Weakness Including the Forehead
UN3686.stem: A patient wakes with weakness of the left side of the face, unable to raise the left eyebrow or fully close the left eye, while the rest of their neurological examination is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN3686.presentation: Acute Confusion in Sickle Cell Disease
UN3686.stem: A 9-year-old boy with known sickle cell disease becomes suddenly confused and develops weakness down one side of his body. What complication should be urgently considered?

After a penetrating stab injury to one side of the back, a patient has, below the level of the lesion: ipsilateral leg weakness and ipsilateral loss of vibration/proprioception, with CONTRALATERAL loss of pain and temperature sensation. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A patient develops a foot drop after a period of prolonged leg crossing (or a tight plaster cast). There is weakness of ankle dorsiflexion and foot eversion with sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot, but ankle inversion, plantarflexion and the ankle jerk are preserved. Where is the lesion?
UN3686.correct_answer: The common peroneal (fibular) nerve at the fibular neck

UN3687.presentation: Sudden Vertigo With Inability to Stand
UN3687.stem: A 59-year-old man develops sudden severe vertigo, is unable to stand or walk unsupported, and is found to have limb incoordination and nystagmus on examination. Which neurological structure should be particularly suspected?

UN3687.presentation: Posterior Circulation Stroke vs Vestibular Neuritis
UN3687.stem: A 65-year-old man with hypertension and diabetes has sudden vertigo, vomiting and left-sided limb ataxia. He cannot sit unsupported. Head-impulse testing is normal and he has direction-changing nystagmus. What is the most appropriate next step?
UN3687.correct_answer: Urgent MRI brain with diffusion-weighted imaging

UN3687.stem: For several days, a 44-year-old woman has severe vertigo that came on suddenly; there is no accompanying hearing loss or tinnitus. Which diagnosis fits best?

A 38-year-old man develops sudden severe spinning vertigo with nausea after a recent cold. It has lasted two days. He also reports muffled hearing and ringing in his left ear since the onset, and has never had a similar episode. He has no vascular risk factors, limb weakness, speech disturbance or double vision, and examination shows horizontal nystagmus.

Which diagnosis is most likely?

A 52-year-old woman develops an extremely sudden, severe headache that she describes as the worst she has ever experienced, accompanied by vomiting and sensitivity to light. Which diagnosis must be urgently considered?

UN3687.presentation: Sudden Severe Testicular Pain in a Teenager
UN3687.stem: A 15-year-old boy develops sudden, severe pain in his right testicle with associated nausea and vomiting. Why is this presentation treated as a surgical emergency requiring immediate exploration?
UN3687.correct_answer: Testicular viability can be lost if torsion persists

UN3687.stem: A 58-year-old woman develops a painful, swollen calf in one leg several days after major surgery. Which diagnosis must be considered?

A 58-year-old man develops sudden severe pain in his left leg, which becomes cold, pale and loses sensation. Which investigation should be arranged urgently to define the arterial anatomy, provided his condition permits imaging?

UN3688.presentation: Transient Neurological Symptoms With Atrial Fibrillation
UN3688.stem: A 64-year-old woman with known atrial fibrillation has a brief episode of left arm weakness and slurred speech that resolves within an hour. What is an important underlying mechanism to consider?

A 52-year-old man presents with recurrent episodes of chest pain occurring at rest. During an episode, ECG demonstrates transient ST-segment elevation. Coronary angiography later reveals normal coronary arteries. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 32-year-old woman describes recurrent episodes that begin with zigzag lines and flashing lights in her vision lasting about 20 minutes. These are followed within an hour by a throbbing right-sided headache with nausea and sensitivity to light, lasting 4 to 6 hours. Between episodes she is well, and neurological examination is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A patient with Wilson disease develops worsening neurological symptoms after starting penicillamine. What is the most appropriate alternative treatment?
Out of nowhere, a 73-year-old man becomes severely dizzy, starts vomiting, loses his coordination and his speech turns slurred. What is the critical diagnosis that must not be missed?
A 22-year-old man has recurrent episodes of visible haematuria that occur within 1 to 2 days of an upper respiratory tract infection. Complement levels are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 65-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of severe, brief, electric shock-like pain over her right cheek and jaw, each lasting a few seconds. The pain is triggered by brushing her teeth, eating and cold air. Neurological examination is normal. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

A 64-year-old man presents with recurrent episodes of chest pain occurring exclusively at rest, usually in the early hours of the morning. Coronary angiography later demonstrates no significant coronary artery stenosis. Which medication is most appropriate for long-term prevention of these episodes?

UN3828.presentation: Brain abscess — first imaging and avoiding lumbar puncture
UN3828.stem: A 46-year-old man is admitted with 5 days of worsening headache, fever and new right-sided weakness. Two weeks ago he was treated for a dental abscess. His temperature is 38.4°C, Glasgow Coma Scale score is 14 and there is mild right arm and leg weakness. A brain abscess is suspected and blood cultures have been taken. Which investigation should be performed next?
UN3828.correct_answer: Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI of the brain

UN3828.stem: A man with advanced HIV (CD4 count 50 cells/µL) and poor treatment adherence presents with headache, fever and a focal neurological deficit. Contrast CT of the brain shows multiple RING-ENHANCING lesions. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 55-year-old has several weeks of headaches that are worse in the early morning and on lying down, coughing or straining, with associated vomiting. Fundoscopy reveals papilloedema, and there is a new subtle focal neurological deficit. What is the most appropriate next investigation?

A 52-year-old woman has a 1-week history of headache, fever and confusion following a severe sinus infection. Contrast-enhanced MRI shows a single 2 cm ring-enhancing lesion in the left frontal lobe with surrounding oedema. Blood cultures have been taken and the neurosurgical team will review her today. She has no drug allergies. Which empirical antibiotic regimen is most appropriate?
Which patient carries the highest risk of infective endocarditis?
UN3828.correct_answer: A patient with a prosthetic heart valve

UN3828.stem: A 50-year-old man with infective endocarditis on appropriate IV antibiotics develops worsening breathlessness with new severe mitral regurgitation and signs of heart failure. Echocardiography shows a large vegetation and valve destruction. What is the most appropriate next step?
A patient on a statin develops severe, generalised muscle pain along with noticeably dark-coloured urine. Which serious complication should be considered?

A 50-year-old man with a native aortic valve has definite infective endocarditis. Blood cultures grow Streptococcus viridans (penicillin-sensitive). He is haemodynamically stable with no complications. What is the most appropriate antibiotic regimen?
UN3828.correct_answer: IV benzylpenicillin or IV amoxicillin for 4 weeks

UN3879.stem: A 30-year-old man complains that after gripping objects he struggles to let go (his hand 'locks'). He has distal muscle weakness and wasting, frontal balding, bilateral ptosis and early cataracts. There is a family history of a similar condition. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A neurologist is assessing a 30-year-old woman with myotonic dystrophy type 1, whose grip is slow to release and who has bilateral ptosis. Her mother was only diagnosed in her sixties after cataract surgery, while her own newborn son was floppy at birth and needed help with breathing. Genetic testing shows a larger CTG repeat in each successive generation. Which genetic phenomenon is illustrated?

A 55-year-old woman has bone pain and proximal muscle weakness, with difficulty climbing stairs and a waddling gait. Investigations show a low vitamin D, a low-normal calcium and phosphate, and a raised ALP and PTH. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 55-year-old woman with limited sun exposure and a poor diet has diffuse bone pain and proximal muscle weakness (difficulty climbing stairs and rising from a chair). Bloods show low calcium, low phosphate and a RAISED alkaline phosphatase, with a low vitamin D level. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Which of these symptoms most specifically points to involvement of the dominant cerebral hemisphere, in a patient with sudden facial weakness, arm weakness and difficulty speaking?
Breathing becomes increasingly laboured in a patient already diagnosed with Guillain-Barre syndrome. Which complication is most critical to watch for?

A 51-year-old man has been vomiting repeatedly for four days with a gastrointestinal illness. His potassium returns at 2.7 mmol/L. Which of the following is a recognised consequence of this electrolyte abnormality?

A 4-year-old boy has delayed walking, frequent falls and difficulty climbing stairs. He uses his hands to 'walk up' his own legs when rising from the floor (Gower's sign), and has enlarged, firm calves. Serum creatine kinase is markedly elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN3880.stem: A 35-year-old woman with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis develops acute weakness and numbness of both legs over 2 days, impairing her walking. MRI shows a new gadolinium-enhancing lesion in the spinal cord. She is afebrile with no evidence of infection. What is the most appropriate treatment for this relapse?

UN3880.presentation: Multiple sclerosis — worsening symptoms, exclude infection before diagnosing relapse
UN3880.stem: A 34-year-old woman with relapsing–remitting multiple sclerosis is seen in the neurology clinic because her legs have felt weaker and stiffer for 2 days. She has also noticed new urinary frequency and urgency over the same 2 days. She is afebrile and otherwise well. Her last relapse was 18 months ago and her symptoms had been stable since. Which investigation should be done first?

UN3880.presentation: Optic neuritis — investigation for multiple sclerosis risk
UN3880.stem: A 27-year-old woman is seen in eye casualty with 5 days of blurred vision in her left eye and pain on eye movement. The ophthalmologist confirms optic neuritis: reduced acuity and colour vision, a left relative afferent pupillary defect and a normal-looking optic disc. She has no other neurological symptoms. Which investigation gives the most information about her future risk of multiple sclerosis?
A patient with Wilson disease develops worsening neurological symptoms after starting penicillamine. What is the most appropriate alternative treatment?

UN3880.presentation: Recurrent Neurological Episodes In A Young Woman
UN3880.stem: A 27-year-old woman experiences an episode of painful visual loss in one eye, worse on eye movement, and recalls a previous episode of leg numbness that fully resolved. Which diagnosis should be considered?

A 28-year-old woman has had separate episodes over two years: painful loss of vision in one eye (optic neuritis) that recovered, and later a band of numbness ascending from the legs. MRI shows white-matter lesions disseminated in time and space. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN3880.presentation: Neurological Episodes Separated in Time and Location
UN3880.stem: A 27-year-old woman had an episode of blurred vision in one eye six months ago that fully resolved, and now presents with new tingling and weakness in her right leg. Which diagnosis is most consistent?

UN3880.presentation: Multiple sclerosis — driving and the DVLA
UN3880.stem: A 36-year-old man is diagnosed with relapsing–remitting multiple sclerosis in the neurology clinic. Since his latest relapse he has stiffness and weakness of his right leg that makes it hard to move his foot quickly between the pedals. He drives a car to work and has a standard car licence. He asks whether he needs to tell anyone about the diagnosis. What is the most appropriate advice about driving?
UN3880.correct_answer: He must tell the DVLA himself about his diagnosis

UN3882.stem: A 72-year-old man reports progressive slowness of movement over a year. He has an asymmetric resting tremor of the right hand and increasing stiffness, and his handwriting has become smaller. On examination there is cogwheel rigidity, bradykinesia, and a resting tremor that decreases when he reaches for an object. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A 75-year-old man is found to have a tremor at rest, slowness of movement and increased muscle tone. Which diagnosis is most likely?

UN3882.presentation: Asymmetric Resting Tremor With Slowness and Stiffness
UN3882.stem: A 70-year-old man's wife reports that his right hand shakes when it is resting in his lap but settles when he reaches for a cup. He has become noticeably slower getting out of a chair, and his right arm feels stiff on examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?

An older man has a slowly progressive, asymmetrical resting tremor ('pill-rolling'), rigidity (cogwheel) and bradykinesia, with a shuffling gait. He has no early falls and no eye-movement abnormality. What is the most likely diagnosis and most effective symptomatic treatment?
UN3882.correct_answer: Idiopathic Parkinson's disease — levodopa (with a dopa-decarboxylase inhibitor)

UN3882.presentation: New Unilateral Tremor in an Older Man
UN3882.stem: A 68-year-old man presents with a new tremor affecting one hand at rest, slowness of movement and reduced arm swing while walking. Which diagnosis best fits this presentation?

A 58-year-old woman develops a tremor, generalised slowness of movement and difficulty starting to walk; her symptoms began predominantly on one side. Which feature is most characteristic of Parkinson's disease?

UN3882.presentation: Tremor That Appears Only With Action
UN3882.stem: A 60-year-old retired teacher notices both her hands shake noticeably when she holds a cup of tea or tries to write, but the shaking disappears completely when her hands are resting in her lap. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN3882.presentation: Intention Tremor and an Unsteady Gait
UN3882.stem: A patient has a tremor that worsens as the hand approaches a target, overshoots when reaching for objects, and a wide-based, unsteady gait. Which neurological structure is most likely affected?

UN3883.stem: A 58-year-old woman develops a tremor, generalised slowness of movement and difficulty starting to walk; her symptoms began predominantly on one side. Which feature is most characteristic of Parkinson's disease?
An elderly woman on long-term metoclopramide develops symmetrical bradykinesia and rigidity with a mild tremor over a few weeks. What is the most likely cause, and the appropriate first action?
UN3883.correct_answer: Drug-induced parkinsonism — review and stop the offending drug

UN3883.presentation: Tremor not clinically separable from parkinsonism — imaging
UN3883.stem: A 68-year-old man is seen in the neurology clinic with a two-year history of tremor in both hands when holding objects. On examination there is also a slight tremor of the right hand at rest, and arm swing may be mildly reduced on the right, but there is no clear bradykinesia or rigidity. The neurologist cannot confidently distinguish essential tremor from early parkinsonism on clinical grounds. Which investigation should be considered?

A young adult has a movement disorder (tremor and dystonia), personality change and deranged liver function. Slit-lamp examination shows brown rings at the corneal margin. What is the most appropriate diagnostic test?

A 60-year-old man has progressive weakness with a mix of wasting and fasciculations (lower motor neuron) alongside brisk reflexes and up-going plantars (upper motor neuron), with no sensory loss and no eye-movement or sphincter involvement. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 72-year-old man has progressive cognitive decline with marked day-to-day fluctuation in attention and alertness, recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations (he frequently sees animals), and spontaneous parkinsonism with rigidity and bradykinesia. The cognitive and motor features developed around the same time. He had a severe adverse reaction after being given an antipsychotic for the hallucinations. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 70-year-old man who still volunteers at a charity shop has, over three years, become unable to remember the names of new colleagues or what he did the day before, and he now gets muddled when giving change at the till. Neurological examination shows no tremor, rigidity, involuntary movements or focal deficit. Which is the most likely diagnosis?

A 68-year-old man with known Parkinson's disease finds it hard to get going when he starts walking, and his stride length shortens progressively as he continues. Which cardinal motor sign does this describe?

UN3884.stem: A 19-year-old man has recurring wheeze and cough, along with eczema and hay fever. Which condition commonly occurs together with this pattern?
Which of the following urinary symptoms is classified as a 'voiding' lower urinary tract symptom, commonly associated with bladder outlet obstruction?

A 58-year-old woman develops a tremor, generalised slowness of movement and difficulty starting to walk; her symptoms began predominantly on one side. Which feature is most characteristic of Parkinson's disease?
A 75-year-old man is found to have a tremor at rest, slowness of movement and increased muscle tone. Which diagnosis is most likely?

A 72-year-old man reports progressive slowness of movement over a year. He has an asymmetric resting tremor of the right hand and increasing stiffness, and his handwriting has become smaller. On examination there is cogwheel rigidity, bradykinesia, and a resting tremor that decreases when he reaches for an object. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A 70-year-old man with known Parkinson's disease struggles to start walking and repeatedly freezes when approaching doorways. What term describes this symptom?

An older man has a slowly progressive, asymmetrical resting tremor ('pill-rolling'), rigidity (cogwheel) and bradykinesia, with a shuffling gait. He has no early falls and no eye-movement abnormality. What is the most likely diagnosis and most effective symptomatic treatment?
UN3884.correct_answer: Idiopathic Parkinson's disease — levodopa (with a dopa-decarboxylase inhibitor)

UN3884.presentation: New Unilateral Tremor in an Older Man
UN3884.stem: A 68-year-old man presents with a new tremor affecting one hand at rest, slowness of movement and reduced arm swing while walking. Which diagnosis best fits this presentation?

UN3886.presentation: Intention Tremor and an Unsteady Gait
UN3886.stem: A patient has a tremor that worsens as the hand approaches a target, overshoots when reaching for objects, and a wide-based, unsteady gait. Which neurological structure is most likely affected?
A 55-year-old man presents with an unsteady, broad-based gait and a tremor that worsens as his finger approaches his nose on examination. Which part of the nervous system is most likely affected?

A patient has an unsteady, broad-based gait with slurred ('scanning') speech, nystagmus, an intention tremor, past-pointing and difficulty with rapid alternating movements (dysdiadochokinesia). Where does this localise?
Writing or holding a cup of tea makes a 49-year-old man's tremor most apparent, and the rest of his neurological exam is unremarkable. Which diagnosis is most likely?
A 75-year-old man is found to have a tremor at rest, slowness of movement and increased muscle tone. Which diagnosis is most likely?

UN3886.presentation: Confusion with Flapping Tremor in Cirrhosis
UN3886.stem: A patient with decompensated cirrhosis becomes increasingly confused and is noted to have a coarse flapping tremor when his wrists are extended. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN3886.presentation: Essential tremor — first investigation in primary care
UN3886.stem: A 45-year-old man sees his GP with a 6-month history of a bilateral tremor of the hands that is worse when holding a cup or writing. His father had a similar tremor. He has no rigidity or bradykinesia and no other neurological signs. He drinks within recommended limits and takes no regular medicines. Which investigation is most appropriate to request first?

A patient has a bilateral, symmetrical tremor of the hands that is present on maintaining a posture and on action (e.g. holding a cup or writing), improves after a small amount of alcohol, and there is a family history. There is no bradykinesia or rigidity. What is the most likely diagnosis and first-line treatment?

UN3888.presentation: Myasthenia gravis — next test when acetylcholine receptor antibodies are negative
UN3888.stem: A 34-year-old woman is seen in the neurology clinic with a 3-month history of drooping eyelids, double vision and difficulty swallowing, all worse towards the end of the day. She also has fatigable neck weakness. Pupils, reflexes and sensation are normal. Serum acetylcholine receptor antibodies are negative. Which blood test should be requested next?

A 35-year-old woman has drooping eyelids and double vision that are worse at the end of the day and after sustained upgaze, with proximal limb fatigability. There is no sensory loss. What is the most specific confirmatory test?

A 35-year-old woman has intermittent drooping of the left eyelid that worsens through the day and with sustained upgaze, along with intermittent double vision. Her symptoms improve after a period of rest. The pupils are normal and the rest of the neurological examination is unremarkable. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 52-year-old man has noticed over four months that he struggles to lift his arms to shave and to get up from a low sofa. His thigh and upper arm muscles ache slightly. There is no rash, double vision or drooping of the eyelids, and sensation and reflexes are normal. He takes no regular medicines. His creatine kinase is markedly raised. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 16-year-old boy sees his GP about a dragging ache in the left side of his scrotum that is worse after football and towards the end of the day. Standing, there is a soft, irregular swelling above the left testis that feels like a collection of worm-like strands; it becomes much less obvious when he lies flat. It does not transilluminate, and both testes feel normal. Which diagnosis is most likely?

A 25-year-old man has months of low back pain and stiffness that are worse in the morning and after rest, and improve with exercise. He has reduced lumbar flexion and chest expansion, and is HLA-B27 positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN3888.presentation: Ocular myasthenia gravis — first immunosuppressant when pyridostigmine is not enough
UN3888.stem: A 58-year-old man has ocular myasthenia gravis with fluctuating ptosis and double vision. He is positive for acetylcholine receptor antibodies and CT of the thorax shows no thymoma. After 6 weeks on the highest dose of pyridostigmine he can tolerate, the double vision still stops him reading and driving. He has no bulbar, limb or breathing symptoms. Which medicine should be added?

Nursing notes for a 78-year-old woman with an exacerbation of bronchiectasis record that she was muddled on Tuesday night, chatty and orientated on Wednesday morning, and drowsy again by Wednesday evening. Her family are unsure what she is like normally. Which aspect of her history would most point towards delirium rather than a long-standing condition?
UN3888.correct_answer: A level of attention that comes and goes over the day

UN3889.presentation: Newly diagnosed myasthenia gravis — thymus imaging
UN3889.stem: A 34-year-old woman is newly diagnosed with generalised myasthenia gravis. Her acetylcholine receptor antibodies are positive and she has started pyridostigmine in the neurology clinic. Which imaging should be arranged next?

A 47-year-old woman with generalised myasthenia gravis, controlled on pyridostigmine, is admitted with acute pyelonephritis. She has no drug allergies and her kidney function is normal. Before choosing an intravenous antibiotic, the FY1 doctor checks for interactions with her myasthenia. Which antibiotic is contraindicated in her?

UN3889.presentation: Ocular myasthenia gravis — first immunosuppressant when pyridostigmine is not enough
UN3889.stem: A 58-year-old man has ocular myasthenia gravis with fluctuating ptosis and double vision. He is positive for acetylcholine receptor antibodies and CT of the thorax shows no thymoma. After 6 weeks on the highest dose of pyridostigmine he can tolerate, the double vision still stops him reading and driving. He has no bulbar, limb or breathing symptoms. Which medicine should be added?

A 35-year-old woman has intermittent drooping of the left eyelid that worsens through the day and with sustained upgaze, along with intermittent double vision. Her symptoms improve after a period of rest. The pupils are normal and the rest of the neurological examination is unremarkable. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 31-year-old man is referred to the emergency department by his optometrist. For a month his eyelids have drooped more as each day goes on, and by the evening he sees double while watching television. His jaw tires when he chews tough food. He feels much better on waking. His pupils are normal and his tendon reflexes are preserved. What is the likeliest diagnosis?
A patient is being investigated for a suspected malignancy. Which tumour marker is MOST classically associated with PANCREATIC cancer?

A 29-year-old man notices that his right eyelid droops by the evening and he sees double when watching television late at night. Chewing tough meat tires his jaw, and his symptoms are minimal on waking. Reflexes and sensation are normal. Acetylcholine receptor antibodies are positive and CT of the chest shows no thymoma. His breathing and swallowing are unaffected. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

A 35-year-old woman has drooping eyelids and double vision that are worse at the end of the day and after sustained upgaze, with proximal limb fatigability. There is no sensory loss. What is the most specific confirmatory test?

UN3890.stem: An older man with a smoking history has proximal leg weakness, a dry mouth, and absent reflexes that briefly return after a few seconds of sustained muscle contraction. What is the most likely diagnosis and important association?
UN3890.correct_answer: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome — often paraneoplastic (small-cell lung cancer)

UN3890.stem: A 62-year-old man who smokes heavily has several months of proximal leg weakness and difficulty rising from a chair, with a dry mouth. His strength transiently improves after sustained effort, and his depressed knee reflexes become brisker immediately after exercise. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN3890.presentation: Proximal Weakness That Improves With Repeated Effort
UN3890.stem: A long-term smoker in his 60s reports difficulty climbing stairs and rising from low chairs. Examination shows reduced knee reflexes that become more brisk after he repeatedly contracts the quadriceps. What diagnosis is most likely?

A 63-year-old man develops worsening swallowing difficulty, nasal-sounding speech and proximal limb weakness, with notably reduced tendon reflexes that increase slightly after sustained muscle contraction. Which condition should be considered, particularly given its association with small-cell lung cancer?

UN3890.presentation: Mechanism of Erectile Dysfunction with Vascular Risk Factors
UN3890.stem: A 55-year-old man with long-standing type 2 diabetes and hypertension develops persistent erectile dysfunction. Which underlying mechanism is most commonly implicated in this setting?

UN3890.presentation: Significance of Erectile Dysfunction as a Vascular Marker
UN3890.stem: A 58-year-old man with multiple cardiovascular risk factors is found to have erectile dysfunction. Why might this symptom be clinically important beyond its effect on sexual function?
UN3890.correct_answer: It may reflect underlying vascular disease

UN3890.stem: A 23-year-old woman develops sudden weakness of her right leg the day after a distressing argument. Examination shows give-way weakness, a positive Hoover's sign, and normal reflexes and tone. MRI of the brain and spine is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 30-year-old woman presents with sudden weakness of the left leg. On examination the power is variable and ‘gives way’, and Hoover's sign is positive (hip extension is weak on direct testing but normal when she flexes the opposite hip against resistance). Reflexes are normal, there is no sensory level, and imaging is normal. She describes a recent significant psychological stressor. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN3892.stem: A 52-year-old man with Guillain-Barré syndrome has weakness that is now extending to his arms. He is admitted for close monitoring. Which parameter best predicts impending respiratory failure?

A 26-year-old woman develops progressive difficulty walking upstairs over several days, two weeks after an episode of diarrhoea. On examination she has symmetrical weakness in both legs with absent reflexes. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 25-year-old man develops ascending weakness over a week, starting in his legs, with loss of reflexes and mild distal numbness. He had diarrhoea three weeks ago. What is the most important investigation to monitor in the acute phase?

A 30-year-old man develops progressive, symmetrical ascending leg weakness over 5 days, 2 weeks after a diarrhoeal illness. Reflexes are absent. CSF shows raised protein with a normal cell count. What is the most appropriate treatment, alongside monitoring of respiratory function?

A 45-year-old man presents with progressive ascending weakness of both legs over 4 days, now reaching the lower trunk. There is areflexia, and he had a diarrhoeal illness 2 weeks ago. Sensation is intact. Which investigation will best confirm the diagnosis?

UN3892.presentation: Sudden Breathlessness in a Patient With a Known DVT
UN3892.stem: A woman recently diagnosed with a proximal DVT in her left leg suddenly develops severe breathlessness, pleuritic chest pain and a fast heart rate. What complication should be suspected?

A 46-year-old woman is admitted with 5 days of tingling in her feet and increasing weakness, first in her legs and now in her arms. She had a flu-like illness 10 days ago. She now needs a walking frame. Reflexes are absent in all four limbs and she has mild bilateral facial weakness. Forced vital capacity is being monitored and is currently stable. Lumbar puncture shows a raised protein with a normal white cell count. What is the most appropriate treatment?

A 52-year-old woman develops an itchy raised rash within 30 minutes of starting a blood transfusion. Her oxygen saturations, blood pressure and heart rate remain normal throughout. What is the most likely reaction?

UN3893.presentation: Facial Weakness Affecting the Whole Side of the Face
UN3893.stem: A patient develops sudden weakness of the entire left side of the face, including the inability to raise the left eyebrow or fully close the left eye. What type of facial nerve lesion does this represent?
UN3893.correct_answer: Lower motor neurone facial nerve palsy

UN3893.stem: A 71-year-old woman has sudden left-sided weakness together with an upper motor neurone pattern of facial weakness on the right. Which cranial nerve is responsible for producing the facial weakness itself?

UN3893.presentation: Facial Weakness That Spares the Forehead
UN3893.stem: A patient has weakness affecting only the lower part of the left side of the face, with normal, symmetrical forehead wrinkling on both sides. Which lesion best explains this finding?

A 67-year-old man develops sudden left-sided facial droop. On examination he can wrinkle his forehead symmetrically, but the lower half of the left face is weak. He also has mild left arm weakness. What is the most appropriate immediate action?

A 38-year-old woman develops weakness affecting the entire left side of her face, including being unable to close her left eye and losing movement of her forehead on that side. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN3893.presentation: Mixed Upper And Lower Motor Neurone Signs
UN3893.stem: Visible wasting, fasciculations and brisk reflexes accompany progressively worsening weakness in both legs of a 64-year-old woman. Which diagnosis is most likely?

UN3893.presentation: Contralateral Upper Motor Neurone Facial Palsy (Stroke)
UN3893.stem: A 66-year-old man wakes with the right corner of his mouth drooping. When asked, he can wrinkle both sides of his forehead and close both eyes tightly. His right hand is clumsy and grip on that side is weak. Hearing and facial sensation are normal. Where is the lesion most likely to be?

UN3893.presentation: Unilateral Facial Weakness Including the Forehead
UN3893.stem: A patient wakes with weakness of the left side of the face, unable to raise the left eyebrow or fully close the left eye, while the rest of their neurological examination is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN3898.stem: Which of the following urinary symptoms is classified as a 'voiding' lower urinary tract symptom, commonly associated with bladder outlet obstruction?

UN3898.presentation: Headache in late pregnancy in a woman with migraine — first check
UN3898.stem: A 33-year-old woman who is 35 weeks pregnant phones and is seen the same day by her GP. She has a history of migraine with aura and says she has had a headache for 6 hours with flashing lights, which feels like her usual migraine. She has not had a migraine during this pregnancy until now. She has no limb weakness. Her antenatal care has been uncomplicated. Which investigation should be done first?

UN3898.presentation: Known migraine with a thunderclap headache — next step
UN3898.stem: A 34-year-old woman with a 10-year history of migraine without aura telephones her GP. Two hours ago, while lifting a heavy box, she developed a sudden, severe occipital headache that reached its worst within a minute. She says it is 'completely different' from her usual migraines and the worst headache she has ever had. She has vomited once. She is alert and has no weakness. What is the most appropriate next step?
UN3898.correct_answer: Send her to the emergency department immediately

UN3898.stem: A patient describes a bilateral, pressing, 'band-like' tightening headache of mild-to-moderate intensity. There is no nausea, no vomiting, no photophobia and no aura, and it is not made worse by routine activity. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 45-year-old man suddenly develops the worst headache of his life, reaching maximum intensity within seconds, followed by neck stiffness and photophobia. Which feature most strongly supports a diagnosis of subarachnoid haemorrhage?
UN3898.correct_answer: Meningism developing after a thunderclap-onset headache

UN3898.stem: A patient complains of a burning sensation when passing urine. What is this symptom termed?

A 32-year-old woman describes recurrent episodes that begin with zigzag lines and flashing lights in her vision lasting about 20 minutes. These are followed within an hour by a throbbing right-sided headache with nausea and sensitivity to light, lasting 4 to 6 hours. Between episodes she is well, and neurological examination is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A patient describes shimmering zig-zag lines across their vision lasting about 25 minutes, which resolve just before a throbbing one-sided headache develops with associated nausea. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN3901.stem: A 3-year-9-month-old girl cannot yet combine more than two words together and strangers struggle to understand what she is saying, despite a normal hearing test. What should happen next?
UN3901.correct_answer: Arrange formal assessment of her speech and language development

UN3901.stem: An 84-year-old becomes unable to keep fluids down for four days and is found to be clinically dehydrated, with a new rise in creatinine on admission bloods. What is the most likely mechanism?

Paramedics bring a 79-year-old man with type 2 diabetes treated with gliclazide into the emergency department after his daughter found him with left-sided weakness and slurred speech. He has been off his food with a chest infection. On arrival his capillary glucose is very low. Within ten minutes of intravenous glucose, his speech and arm strength return completely to normal. What is the most likely explanation?
UN3901.correct_answer: Focal neurological deficit due to hypoglycaemia

UN3901.stem: Paramedics attend a 66-year-old woman with long-standing poorly controlled hypertension who felt a sudden tearing pain between her shoulder blades. While they are with her she develops slurred speech and weakness of her left arm and leg. Her right radial pulse is clearly weaker than her left. Which single diagnosis best explains all of these findings?

On the fourth day after major abdominal surgery, a patient suddenly becomes breathless with pleuritic chest pain, a tachycardia and mild hypoxia. The chest is clear and there are no new infective features. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A man with advanced HIV (CD4 count 50 cells/µL) and poor treatment adherence presents with headache, fever and a focal neurological deficit. Contrast CT of the brain shows multiple RING-ENHANCING lesions. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN3901.presentation: Features Of An Upper Motor Neurone Lesion
UN3901.stem: A patient suddenly becomes weak down one side of the body. Of the options given, which examination sign best fits an upper motor neurone cause?

UN3901.presentation: Sudden Breathlessness and Shock After Trauma
UN3901.stem: After a road traffic collision, a patient suddenly becomes severely breathless and hypotensive, with markedly reduced breath sounds on one side of the chest consistent with obstructive shock. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN3902.stem: Out of nowhere, a 73-year-old man becomes severely dizzy, starts vomiting, loses his coordination and his speech turns slurred. What is the critical diagnosis that must not be missed?

A 16-year-old boy who has type 1 diabetes is found sitting on the touchline after a school football match. He is pale and clammy, his hands are trembling, his speech is slurred and he is irritable and uncooperative. He had his usual morning insulin but skipped lunch. Capillary ketones are negative. Which diagnosis best fits this picture?

A 60-year-old man has progressive weakness, wasting and visible fasciculations of both hands over several months. On examination his reflexes are brisk and the plantar responses are extensor. His speech is slurred and the jaw jerk is brisk. Sensation is entirely normal, and there are no eye-movement or sphincter problems. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 41-year-old woman on a diving holiday has a regulator failure at depth and makes a rapid, breath-held ascent. Within a few minutes of being pulled onto the boat she becomes confused, her speech is slurred and she cannot lift her left arm. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 38-year-old man is on the infectious diseases ward receiving intravenous antibiotics for Staphylococcus aureus endocarditis of the mitral valve. On the fourth day a nurse finds that the left side of his face is drooping, his speech is slurred and he cannot lift his left arm. These signs were not present an hour earlier. Which complication is most likely?
UN3902.correct_answer: Ischaemic stroke from a septic embolus

UN3902.stem: Following a stroke, a 68-year-old man can follow commands and clearly understands what is said to him, but his own speech is slow, laboured and reduced to short, fragmented phrases. What type of language disorder does this represent?

A 72-year-old man suddenly develops right facial droop, right arm and leg weakness, and slurred speech while at home. His wife calls an ambulance and he arrives 70 minutes after symptom onset. On examination he has a right hemiparesis and dysarthria. Blood pressure is 180/95 mmHg and capillary glucose is normal. He takes no anticoagulants. What is the most appropriate immediate next step?

A patient on long-term lithium presents with coarse tremor, ataxia, vomiting, slurred speech and confusion after starting a new medication. The lithium level is high. What is the most appropriate management?
UN3902.correct_answer: Stop lithium, give IV fluids and consider dialysis if severe

UN3903.presentation: Coughing on Swallowing After a Stroke
UN3903.stem: Two days after an ischaemic stroke, a patient coughs repeatedly every time they are given water to drink. What complication should be suspected?

An 82-year-old woman is on a stroke ward four days after a left hemisphere infarct. The nurse reports that she coughs immediately whenever she takes sips of water, food collects in her right cheek, and some fluid comes back through her nose. After drinking, her voice sounds gurgly. She does not report food sticking behind the breastbone. What type of swallowing problem is most likely?
An adult is choking on food. He is conscious, able to cough but distressed. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
A choking adult becomes unconscious and unresponsive while you are attempting to relieve the obstruction. What should you do next?
UN3903.correct_answer: Start CPR, beginning with chest compressions, and call for help

UN3903.stem: An adult is choking, unable to speak, and coughing ineffectively but is still conscious. What is the most appropriate next action?
UN3903.correct_answer: Up to five back blows, then up to five abdominal thrusts

UN3903.stem: A 57-year-old woman with dermatomyositis diagnosed 3 weeks ago is waiting for her rheumatology follow-up. She already has weakness of her shoulders and hips and a rash on her eyelids and knuckles. She calls her GP practice to report a new symptom. Which new symptom most needs urgent same-day medical assessment?
UN3903.correct_answer: Coughing and choking when she drinks

UN3903.stem:
A 64-year-old man with dysphagia after a stroke has a fine-bore nasogastric tube placed by a trained nurse on the stroke unit so that enteral feeding can begin. The insertion was straightforward and he is not coughing. The dietitian's feed is ready to start.

What must be done before any feed is given?
UN3903.correct_answer: Test aspirate pH, using a chest X-ray if this cannot confirm position

UN3903.stem: A 6-month-old infant is choking with an ineffective cough but is still conscious. What is the correct sequence of intervention?
UN3903.correct_answer: Five back blows, then five chest thrusts, repeating and reassessing

UN3906.presentation: Acute Ischaemic Stroke in Atrial Fibrillation
UN3906.stem: A 79-year-old woman with known atrial fibrillation stopped her apixaban a month ago because of bruising. Her daughter brings her to the emergency department because, an hour earlier, the left side of her face drooped, her left arm became weak and her speech became slurred. Her capillary glucose is normal and she has not had a fit. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN3906.presentation: Transient Neurological Symptoms With Atrial Fibrillation
UN3906.stem: A 64-year-old woman with known atrial fibrillation has a brief episode of left arm weakness and slurred speech that resolves within an hour. What is an important underlying mechanism to consider?
What pulse pattern typifies atrial fibrillation?

A 72-year-old man with atrial fibrillation develops sudden severe pain in his right leg. The leg is pale, cold and mottled, with absent pulses below the femoral artery, reduced sensation and early weakness of the foot. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
UN3906.correct_answer: Immediate referral to vascular surgery as an emergency

UN3906.stem: A 70-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation needs anticoagulation. She has moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis with a mechanical mitral valve. Which anticoagulant is appropriate?

A 74-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation develops sudden, severe pain in her right foot over one hour. The foot looks pale and feels cold to touch.

Which examination finding would most strongly support an acute arterial occlusion?
UN3906.correct_answer: Absent pulses in the foot with delayed capillary refill

UN3906.stem: A 74-year-old man with atrial fibrillation develops sudden, severe, central abdominal pain. The pain is far more dramatic than the examination findings, which show a soft, only mildly tender abdomen. Blood tests reveal a metabolic acidosis with a markedly raised lactate. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN3906.presentation: Pathophysiology of stroke in atrial fibrillation
UN3906.stem:
A 70-year-old woman with long-standing atrial fibrillation has stopped her apixaban because she dislikes taking tablets. Her pharmacist explains that this leaves her more likely to have a stroke, and she asks how an irregular heartbeat can lead to a blocked artery in the brain.

Which explanation is correct?
UN3906.correct_answer: Poorly contracting atria allow blood to pool, so clots form and travel to the brain

UN3910.stem: A 50-year-old man with a known brain tumour reports headache and vomiting, and fundoscopy shows swollen, blurred optic discs bilaterally. What does this finding, papilloedema, indicate in this context?

UN3910.presentation: Child with headache, vomiting and double vision
UN3910.stem:
An 8-year-old girl has had headaches for three weeks. They are worst on waking and she has been vomiting before breakfast. Her mother has now noticed that she sees double and tilts her head when reading. She has no fever, no neck stiffness and no history of head injury.

What is the most appropriate approach?
UN3910.correct_answer: Urgent paediatric assessment for possible raised intracranial pressure

UN3910.stem: A 34-year-old man with a confirmed diagnosis of raised intracranial pressure undergoes fundoscopy as part of his assessment. Which finding would most specifically confirm papilloedema?
UN3910.correct_answer: Bilateral disc swelling with blurred margins

UN3910.stem: A 55-year-old has several weeks of headaches that are worse in the early morning and on lying down, coughing or straining, with associated vomiting. Fundoscopy reveals papilloedema, and there is a new subtle focal neurological deficit. What is the most appropriate next investigation?

UN3910.presentation: Cholesteatoma — red flags for intracranial and facial nerve complications
UN3910.stem: A 34-year-old woman with a known left cholesteatoma is on the waiting list for surgery. She sees her GP with 3 days of worsening left ear pain and discharge, a severe headache and vomiting. Her temperature is 38.6°C. She is alert but there is new weakness of the whole left side of her face, including her forehead. What is the most appropriate action?
UN3910.correct_answer: Arrange emergency same-day hospital assessment by ENT

UN3910.stem: A 58-year-old woman develops sudden severe breathlessness, pleuritic chest pain, a rapid heart rate and a low blood pressure shortly after a long-haul flight. Which complication of pulmonary embolism is particularly concerning in this presentation?

UN3910.presentation: ITP with intracranial haemorrhage — emergency treatment
UN3910.stem: A 41-year-old woman with known immune thrombocytopenia attends the emergency department with a sudden severe headache and vomiting. Her Glasgow Coma Scale score is 13. Her platelet count is 3 × 10⁹/L. CT head shows an intracerebral haemorrhage. A platelet transfusion has been requested and the neurosurgical team has been contacted. Which treatment should be given alongside the platelet transfusion?

A 19-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his flatmate with a few hours of fever, headache, vomiting and aching legs. He is drowsy but rousable. Which examination finding would most strongly suggest meningococcal septicaemia?
UN3910.correct_answer: Non-blanching petechiae on the trunk and legs

UN3912.stem: A 70-year-old man with known Parkinson's disease struggles to start walking and repeatedly freezes when approaching doorways. What term describes this symptom?

A 68-year-old man with known Parkinson's disease finds it hard to get going when he starts walking, and his stride length shortens progressively as he continues. Which cardinal motor sign does this describe?

A 58-year-old woman develops a tremor, generalised slowness of movement and difficulty starting to walk; her symptoms began predominantly on one side. Which feature is most characteristic of Parkinson's disease?

An older man has a slowly progressive, asymmetrical resting tremor ('pill-rolling'), rigidity (cogwheel) and bradykinesia, with a shuffling gait. He has no early falls and no eye-movement abnormality. What is the most likely diagnosis and most effective symptomatic treatment?
UN3912.correct_answer: Idiopathic Parkinson's disease — levodopa (with a dopa-decarboxylase inhibitor)

UN3912.presentation: New Unilateral Tremor in an Older Man
UN3912.stem: A 68-year-old man presents with a new tremor affecting one hand at rest, slowness of movement and reduced arm swing while walking. Which diagnosis best fits this presentation?
A 75-year-old man is found to have a tremor at rest, slowness of movement and increased muscle tone. Which diagnosis is most likely?

A 72-year-old man reports progressive slowness of movement over a year. He has an asymmetric resting tremor of the right hand and increasing stiffness, and his handwriting has become smaller. On examination there is cogwheel rigidity, bradykinesia, and a resting tremor that decreases when he reaches for an object. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A 47-year-old man with chronic alcohol dependence has ongoing memory gaps that he unknowingly fills with invented stories, without any intention to deceive. What is this phenomenon called?

UN3913.stem: A 40-year-old develops involuntary, jerky, dance-like movements (chorea), alongside progressive cognitive decline and behavioural/psychiatric changes. His father had a similar illness that began at a slightly older age. What is the most likely diagnosis and inheritance pattern?

UN3913.presentation: Huntington disease — drug for troublesome chorea
UN3913.stem: A 46-year-old man with genetically confirmed Huntington disease is seen in the neurology clinic. Over the past year his involuntary movements have become worse, and he now spills drinks and has fallen twice. His mood is good, he has no history of depression and he has no suicidal thoughts. Liver function is normal. The team decides to start medication for his chorea. Which drug is most appropriate?

UN3913.presentation: Jerky movements after a sore throat
UN3913.stem:
A 9-year-old girl is brought to her GP because over a fortnight she has become clumsy, drops her pencil and spills drinks. Her teacher has noticed grimacing and brief, irregular jerky movements of her hands and face that disappear when she sleeps, and she has been unusually tearful. Five weeks ago she had a sore throat that was not treated. She has no fever, joint pain or rash.

Which is the most likely cause of her movements?

A 38-year-old man sees his GP. His father, now 58, was recently diagnosed with Huntington disease after developing involuntary jerky movements and personality change. The man has two young children and wants to understand how the condition is passed on in families. Which statement about its inheritance is accurate?
UN3913.correct_answer: It is autosomal dominant, so a child of an affected parent has a 1 in 2 chance of inheriting it

UN3913.stem: A 29-year-old woman at her 12-week antenatal appointment says her husband, aged 38, has just been diagnosed with Huntington disease by the neurology team after developing jerky movements and irritability. She is not affected and has no family history. She asks the midwife what the chance is that the baby has inherited the faulty gene from him. What is the approximate risk?
A 41-year-old man whose mother has Huntington disease asks about how the condition is inherited. What type of inheritance does Huntington disease typically follow?

A 70-year-old man who still volunteers at a charity shop has, over three years, become unable to remember the names of new colleagues or what he did the day before, and he now gets muddled when giving change at the till. Neurological examination shows no tremor, rigidity, involuntary movements or focal deficit. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
On examination, a patient is noted to have involuntary, rhythmic back-and-forth movement of both eyes. What is this finding called?
