UN3915.stem: A 35-year-old woman has intermittent drooping of the left eyelid that worsens through the day and with sustained upgaze, along with intermittent double vision. Her symptoms improve after a period of rest. The pupils are normal and the rest of the neurological examination is unremarkable. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN3915.presentation: Ocular myasthenia gravis — first immunosuppressant when pyridostigmine is not enough
UN3915.stem: A 58-year-old man has ocular myasthenia gravis with fluctuating ptosis and double vision. He is positive for acetylcholine receptor antibodies and CT of the thorax shows no thymoma. After 6 weeks on the highest dose of pyridostigmine he can tolerate, the double vision still stops him reading and driving. He has no bulbar, limb or breathing symptoms. Which medicine should be added?

UN3915.presentation: Newly diagnosed myasthenia gravis — thymus imaging
UN3915.stem: A 34-year-old woman is newly diagnosed with generalised myasthenia gravis. Her acetylcholine receptor antibodies are positive and she has started pyridostigmine in the neurology clinic. Which imaging should be arranged next?

A 47-year-old woman with generalised myasthenia gravis, controlled on pyridostigmine, is admitted with acute pyelonephritis. She has no drug allergies and her kidney function is normal. Before choosing an intravenous antibiotic, the FY1 doctor checks for interactions with her myasthenia. Which antibiotic is contraindicated in her?

A 31-year-old man is referred to the emergency department by his optometrist. For a month his eyelids have drooped more as each day goes on, and by the evening he sees double while watching television. His jaw tires when he chews tough food. He feels much better on waking. His pupils are normal and his tendon reflexes are preserved. What is the likeliest diagnosis?

UN3915.presentation: Myasthenia gravis — next test when acetylcholine receptor antibodies are negative
UN3915.stem: A 34-year-old woman is seen in the neurology clinic with a 3-month history of drooping eyelids, double vision and difficulty swallowing, all worse towards the end of the day. She also has fatigable neck weakness. Pupils, reflexes and sensation are normal. Serum acetylcholine receptor antibodies are negative. Which blood test should be requested next?

A 35-year-old woman has drooping eyelids and double vision that are worse at the end of the day and after sustained upgaze, with proximal limb fatigability. There is no sensory loss. What is the most specific confirmatory test?

UN3915.presentation: Eyelid Drooping That Worsens Through the Day
UN3915.stem: A 34-year-old woman notices her right eyelid droops more and more as the day goes on, and by evening she also sees double. Her limb strength is essentially normal on examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN3916.stem: A 71-year-old woman has sudden left-sided weakness together with an upper motor neurone pattern of facial weakness on the right. Which cranial nerve is responsible for producing the facial weakness itself?

UN3916.presentation: Facial Weakness Affecting the Whole Side of the Face
UN3916.stem: A patient develops sudden weakness of the entire left side of the face, including the inability to raise the left eyebrow or fully close the left eye. What type of facial nerve lesion does this represent?
UN3916.correct_answer: Lower motor neurone facial nerve palsy

UN3916.stem: A 68-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and hypertension presents with 2 days of double vision. The two images lie side by side and move further apart when he looks at the television across the room or looks to his right. His right eye cannot move outwards beyond the midline, but all other eye movements, the eyelids and the pupils are normal. The rest of the neurological examination is normal. Which cranial nerve is most likely affected?

UN3916.presentation: Crossed Cranial Nerve And Limb Signs
UN3916.stem: A 59-year-old woman suddenly develops double vision, difficulty swallowing and weakness of her right arm and leg together. Which anatomical site could explain this combination of cranial nerve and limb findings?

After undergoing pelvic surgery, a 61-year-old woman notices weakness when trying to straighten her knee and reduced sensation over the inner part of her lower leg. Which nerve is most likely affected?

A patient awakens with a 'wrist drop' (inability to extend the wrist and fingers) after falling asleep with their arm draped over a chair. Sensation is reduced over the dorsum of the hand near the base of the thumb. Which nerve is affected?
UN3916.correct_answer: The radial nerve (at the spiral groove of the humerus)

UN3916.presentation: Facial nerve palsy — feature that needs urgent specialist referral
UN3916.stem:
A 52-year-old man sees his GP with weakness of the right side of his face, including his forehead. He cannot fully close his right eye. There are no limb symptoms, the ear canal and eardrum look normal, and there is no rash. The GP is considering a diagnosis of Bell palsy.

Which additional feature should most prompt specialist referral rather than treatment as Bell palsy in primary care?
UN3916.correct_answer: Weakness worsening slowly over three weeks

UN3916.stem: A patient has weakness of the small muscles of the hand with a 'claw' appearance of the ring and little fingers, weak finger abduction/adduction, and sensory loss over the little finger and medial half of the ring finger. There is a positive Froment's sign. Which nerve is affected?
UN3916.correct_answer: The ulnar nerve (commonly at the elbow)

UN4439.stem: A 60-year-old man has progressive weakness, wasting and visible fasciculations of both hands over several months. On examination his reflexes are brisk and the plantar responses are extensor. His speech is slurred and the jaw jerk is brisk. Sensation is entirely normal, and there are no eye-movement or sphincter problems. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 60-year-old man has progressive weakness with a mix of wasting and fasciculations (lower motor neuron) alongside brisk reflexes and up-going plantars (upper motor neuron), with no sensory loss and no eye-movement or sphincter involvement. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A 60-year-old man has confirmed motor neurone disease with mixed upper and lower motor neuron signs and no sensory loss. Which drug is most likely to modestly prolong survival?

UN4439.presentation: Mixed Upper And Lower Motor Neurone Signs
UN4439.stem: Visible wasting, fasciculations and brisk reflexes accompany progressively worsening weakness in both legs of a 64-year-old woman. Which diagnosis is most likely?

A 66-year-old woman sees a neurologist with nine months of worsening clumsiness of her right hand and tripping over her left foot. She has wasting of the small muscles of the hand and visible twitching in both thighs, yet her knee reflexes are brisk and her plantar responses are extensor. Her speech has become slightly slurred. Sensation is normal throughout and she has no bladder symptoms. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 61-year-old man has just been diagnosed with the amyotrophic lateral sclerosis form of motor neurone disease by a neurologist with expertise in the condition. He has limb weakness and fasciculations but can still walk and swallow safely. He asks whether any medicine can slow the disease. Which drug is recommended in the UK for this purpose?

A 69-year-old man with motor neurone disease attends the neurology clinic with his wife. She says that over recent weeks he splutters when drinking tea and that his voice becomes gurgly afterwards. His speech has also become slurred. He has no limb swelling, ear pain, loin pain or headache. Which complication is he most at risk of?

UN4439.presentation: Motor neurone disease — monitoring respiratory muscle function
UN4439.stem: A 66-year-old woman with motor neurone disease attends the multidisciplinary clinic. She reports needing three pillows to sleep, waking unrefreshed and feeling sleepy during the day. Her oxygen saturation at rest on room air is normal. The team wants to assess whether respiratory muscle weakness is developing. Which test is most appropriate to measure this?

UN4441.presentation: Intention Tremor and an Unsteady Gait
UN4441.stem: A patient has a tremor that worsens as the hand approaches a target, overshoots when reaching for objects, and a wide-based, unsteady gait. Which neurological structure is most likely affected?
A 55-year-old man presents with an unsteady, broad-based gait and a tremor that worsens as his finger approaches his nose on examination. Which part of the nervous system is most likely affected?

UN4441.presentation: Subacute Combined Degeneration of the Cord
UN4441.stem: A patient with low vitamin B12 develops a progressive unsteady gait, loss of vibration sense and proprioception in the feet, and weakness. Examination shows ABSENT ankle jerks but EXTENSOR (upgoing) plantar responses. What is the most likely diagnosis?
UN4441.correct_answer: Subacute combined degeneration of the cord

UN4441.stem: A 52-year-old woman with long-standing heavy alcohol use is admitted with acute pancreatitis. On her second day on the ward she becomes disorientated, walks with a wide-based unsteady gait and has nystagmus with weakness of lateral gaze in both eyes. Deficiency of which vitamin should be suspected?

A 50-year-old man with chronic alcohol dependence is brought in confused, with unsteady gait and abnormal eye movements (ophthalmoplegia and nystagmus). What is the most appropriate immediate management?

An elderly man has a triad of gait disturbance (a broad-based, shuffling 'magnetic' gait), urinary incontinence and cognitive decline. Imaging shows enlarged ventricles out of proportion to any atrophy. What is the diagnosis, and why does it matter?
UN4441.correct_answer: Normal pressure hydrocephalus — potentially reversible with shunting

UN4441.stem: A 74-year-old woman has insidious, gradually progressive memory loss over 2 years. She forgets recent conversations, repeats questions, misplaces items and has word-finding difficulty. There is no stepwise deterioration, no early visual hallucinations or parkinsonism, no prominent early personality change, and no gait disturbance. Neurological examination is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 79-year-old woman living alone is admitted after a fall at home. She takes several regular medicines and has noticeably unsteady gait. Which intervention is most likely to reduce her future risk of falls?
UN4441.correct_answer: Multifactorial falls assessment with medication review

UN4451.stem: A 58-year-old woman develops a tremor, generalised slowness of movement and difficulty starting to walk; her symptoms began predominantly on one side. Which feature is most characteristic of Parkinson's disease?
A 75-year-old man is found to have a tremor at rest, slowness of movement and increased muscle tone. Which diagnosis is most likely?

A 72-year-old man reports progressive slowness of movement over a year. He has an asymmetric resting tremor of the right hand and increasing stiffness, and his handwriting has become smaller. On examination there is cogwheel rigidity, bradykinesia, and a resting tremor that decreases when he reaches for an object. What is the most likely diagnosis?

An older man has a slowly progressive, asymmetrical resting tremor ('pill-rolling'), rigidity (cogwheel) and bradykinesia, with a shuffling gait. He has no early falls and no eye-movement abnormality. What is the most likely diagnosis and most effective symptomatic treatment?
UN4451.correct_answer: Idiopathic Parkinson's disease — levodopa (with a dopa-decarboxylase inhibitor)

UN4451.stem: A 72-year-old woman with Parkinson's disease has had several unexplained falls because she cannot correct her balance quickly enough when she is pushed off-centre. Which feature best explains this?

A 68-year-old man with known Parkinson's disease finds it hard to get going when he starts walking, and his stride length shortens progressively as he continues. Which cardinal motor sign does this describe?

UN4451.presentation: New Unilateral Tremor in an Older Man
UN4451.stem: A 68-year-old man presents with a new tremor affecting one hand at rest, slowness of movement and reduced arm swing while walking. Which diagnosis best fits this presentation?

A 60-year-old man has progressive weakness with a mix of wasting and fasciculations (lower motor neuron) alongside brisk reflexes and up-going plantars (upper motor neuron), with no sensory loss and no eye-movement or sphincter involvement. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN4454.stem: A factory worker receives an electric shock and is left with only a small burn mark on his hand; he otherwise appears well. Despite the apparently minor external injury, what serious complication must still be considered?

A 60-year-old woman has recurrent attacks of sudden, severe, electric-shock-like facial pain lasting seconds, triggered by touching her cheek, brushing teeth or cold wind, in a trigeminal distribution. Examination is normal. What is the first-line treatment?

A 65-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of severe, brief, electric shock-like pain over her right cheek and jaw, each lasting a few seconds. The pain is triggered by brushing her teeth, eating and cold air. Neurological examination is normal. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

A 66-year-old man was started on a new drug by his GP three weeks ago for stabbing, electric-shock pains in his cheek triggered by shaving. A 69-year-old man suddenly cannot get his words out and has weakness in his right arm, with a normal blood glucose. Which finding most strongly points to a cortical rather than peripheral lesion?

A 16-year-old boy attends the emergency department with a nosebleed from his left nostril that started 20 minutes ago after picking his nose. His pulse and blood pressure are normal and he has no history of bleeding problems. His father has been holding a tissue against the bridge of the nose with the boy's head tipped back. What should he be advised to do first?
UN5472.correct_answer: Sit up, lean forward and firmly pinch the soft part of the nose for 10–15 minutes

UN5472.stem: A GP receives a telephone call from a 70-year-old woman. Thirty minutes ago, while they were having breakfast, her husband suddenly could not lift his right arm and his speech became slurred and muddled. He is awake and breathing normally. She asks whether she should bring him to the surgery this afternoon. What is the most appropriate advice?
UN5472.correct_answer: Call 999 now for immediate transfer to a hyperacute stroke unit

UN5472.presentation: Acute Confusion in Sickle Cell Disease
UN5472.stem: A 9-year-old boy with known sickle cell disease becomes suddenly confused and develops weakness down one side of his body. What complication should be urgently considered?

UN5485.stem: A 66-year-old woman suddenly cannot find her words and develops weakness of her right arm, though she remains alert. Which cerebral hemisphere is most likely affected?
Sudden weakness and numbness affecting the right arm and leg, with right facial droop, develop in a 69-year-old woman. Which side of the brain is most likely affected?
A 69-year-old man develops sudden left-sided weakness and appears completely unaware of objects placed on his left side. Which cerebral hemisphere is most likely involved?
Which of these symptoms most specifically points to involvement of the dominant cerebral hemisphere, in a patient with sudden facial weakness, arm weakness and difficulty speaking?

A 63-year-old right-handed man is brought to the emergency department by his wife, who noticed at breakfast that the right side of his face had dropped. He understands what is said to him but his speech is halting and effortful, and he cannot find the words he wants. His right arm is markedly weak, while his right leg is only mildly affected. He has no double vision, vertigo or difficulty swallowing. Which arterial territory is most likely to be involved?

UN5485.presentation: Acute Confusion in Sickle Cell Disease
UN5485.stem: A 9-year-old boy with known sickle cell disease becomes suddenly confused and develops weakness down one side of his body. What complication should be urgently considered?

A 38-year-old woman develops weakness affecting the entire left side of her face, including being unable to close her left eye and losing movement of her forehead on that side. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 71-year-old woman has sudden left-sided weakness together with an upper motor neurone pattern of facial weakness on the right. Which cranial nerve is responsible for producing the facial weakness itself?

UN5489.stem: A 60-year-old woman has recurrent attacks of sudden, severe, electric-shock-like facial pain lasting seconds, triggered by touching her cheek, brushing teeth or cold wind, in a trigeminal distribution. Examination is normal. What is the first-line treatment?

A 65-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of severe, brief, electric shock-like pain over her right cheek and jaw, each lasting a few seconds. The pain is triggered by brushing her teeth, eating and cold air. Neurological examination is normal. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

A 61-year-old man tells his GP he gets stabbing pains like an electric jolt across his right cheek and lower jaw. Each lasts a second or two but they come in volleys many times a day, set off by shaving, a cold breeze or chewing. Between attacks he is pain-free. His dentist found no dental problem, and cranial nerve examination is normal. Which condition is he describing?

A 39-year-old woman has trigeminal neuralgia confirmed clinically and started on carbamazepine. Her pain is only partially controlled, and she has also developed mild facial numbness and a subtle left corneal reflex reduction. What is the most appropriate next step?
UN5489.correct_answer: MRI brain to exclude a secondary cause

UN5489.stem: A 58-year-old man sees his GP with stabbing pains in his left cheek and upper jaw that last a few seconds and come in bursts many times a day. Brushing his teeth or a cold breeze sets them off, and he has stopped shaving that side of his face. Between attacks he is pain free. Cranial nerve examination, including facial sensation and corneal reflexes, is normal. His dentist has found no dental cause. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

UN5489.presentation: Worsening Facial Pain After a Cold
UN5489.stem: A 36-year-old man had a mild cold for five days that seemed to be settling, but now develops severe one-sided facial pain, thick yellow nasal discharge and a fever of 38.4°C. Which diagnosis is most likely?

UN5489.presentation: Recurrent Facial Pain With Nasal Discharge
UN5489.stem: A 39-year-old woman has recurring bouts of facial pain, a blocked nose and thick nasal discharge lasting several days whenever she catches a cold. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A 28-year-old otherwise healthy woman develops facial pressure, nasal blockage and thick nasal discharge for three days, along with mild fatigue. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN5493.presentation: Unilateral Facial Weakness Including the Forehead
UN5493.stem: A patient wakes with weakness of the left side of the face, unable to raise the left eyebrow or fully close the left eye, while the rest of their neurological examination is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN5493.presentation: Facial Weakness Affecting the Whole Side of the Face
UN5493.stem: A patient develops sudden weakness of the entire left side of the face, including the inability to raise the left eyebrow or fully close the left eye. What type of facial nerve lesion does this represent?
UN5493.correct_answer: Lower motor neurone facial nerve palsy

UN5493.presentation: Facial nerve palsy — feature that needs urgent specialist referral
UN5493.stem:
A 52-year-old man sees his GP with weakness of the right side of his face, including his forehead. He cannot fully close his right eye. There are no limb symptoms, the ear canal and eardrum look normal, and there is no rash. The GP is considering a diagnosis of Bell palsy.

Which additional feature should most prompt specialist referral rather than treatment as Bell palsy in primary care?
UN5493.correct_answer: Weakness worsening slowly over three weeks

UN5493.stem: A 71-year-old woman has sudden left-sided weakness together with an upper motor neurone pattern of facial weakness on the right. Which cranial nerve is responsible for producing the facial weakness itself?

A 38-year-old woman develops weakness affecting the entire left side of her face, including being unable to close her left eye and losing movement of her forehead on that side. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 30-year-old woman develops, over a day, drooping of the right side of her face. She cannot raise the right eyebrow or close the right eye fully, and the right side of her forehead is involved. There are no other neurological signs. She presents within 72 hours of onset. What is the most appropriate management?

UN5493.presentation: Facial Weakness That Spares the Forehead
UN5493.stem: A patient has weakness affecting only the lower part of the left side of the face, with normal, symmetrical forehead wrinkling on both sides. Which lesion best explains this finding?

A 67-year-old man develops sudden left-sided facial droop. On examination he can wrinkle his forehead symmetrically, but the lower half of the left face is weak. He also has mild left arm weakness. What is the most appropriate immediate action?

UN5574.stem: A 63-year-old right-handed man is brought to the emergency department by his wife, who noticed at breakfast that the right side of his face had dropped. He understands what is said to him but his speech is halting and effortful, and he cannot find the words he wants. His right arm is markedly weak, while his right leg is only mildly affected. He has no double vision, vertigo or difficulty swallowing. Which arterial territory is most likely to be involved?

A 71-year-old woman with long-standing hypertension and type 2 diabetes wakes with weakness of the left side of her face, her left arm and her left leg, all affected to a similar degree. Her speech content and understanding are normal, her visual fields are full and she has no neglect of the left side. Sensation is intact. Which type of stroke is most likely?
Sudden weakness and numbness affecting the right arm and leg, with right facial droop, develop in a 69-year-old woman. Which side of the brain is most likely affected?

A 67-year-old man develops sudden left-sided facial droop. On examination he can wrinkle his forehead symmetrically, but the lower half of the left face is weak. He also has mild left arm weakness. What is the most appropriate immediate action?

UN5574.presentation: Neck pain, headache and focal deficit in a young adult — carotid dissection
UN5574.stem:
A 41-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after her left arm and the left side of her face suddenly became weak, and she started bumping into things on her left. For 3 days she has had a constant pain in the right side of her neck spreading to her right forehead, which began after a roller-coaster ride. She has never had migraines. On examination she has weakness of the left face and arm, ignores objects on her left side, and has a slightly drooping right upper eyelid with a smaller right pupil. She is afebrile, and her blood pressure and capillary glucose are normal.

Which diagnosis best explains her presentation?
A 69-year-old man develops sudden left-sided weakness and appears completely unaware of objects placed on his left side. Which cerebral hemisphere is most likely involved?

UN5574.presentation: Facial Weakness Affecting the Whole Side of the Face
UN5574.stem: A patient develops sudden weakness of the entire left side of the face, including the inability to raise the left eyebrow or fully close the left eye. What type of facial nerve lesion does this represent?
UN5574.correct_answer: Lower motor neurone facial nerve palsy

UN5574.stem: A 66-year-old woman suddenly cannot find her words and develops weakness of her right arm, though she remains alert. Which cerebral hemisphere is most likely affected?

UN5577.stem: Following a stroke, a 68-year-old man can follow commands and clearly understands what is said to him, but his own speech is slow, laboured and reduced to short, fragmented phrases. What type of language disorder does this represent?

UN5577.presentation: Suspected brain tumour in primary care — investigation
UN5577.stem: A 59-year-old man sees his GP with 6 weeks of gradually increasing weakness of his right hand and difficulty finding words. His wife says it has slowly worsened week by week; there was no sudden onset. Examination shows mild right-sided pyramidal weakness. He is otherwise well. Which investigation is most appropriate?
UN5577.correct_answer: Urgent direct access MRI of the brain

UN5577.presentation: Suspected viral encephalitis — key CSF test
UN5577.stem: A 46-year-old woman is admitted to the acute medical unit with 3 days of fever and headache. Today she has become confused, with odd behaviour and difficulty finding words. There is no rash and no neck stiffness. Intravenous aciclovir has been started. CT head is normal, there are no contraindications to lumbar puncture, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) has been obtained. Which CSF test is most important for identifying the cause of her illness?

A 77-year-old woman with no prior psychiatric history is brought to the GP by her daughter. Over the past 3 weeks she has become increasingly confused, has difficulty finding words, and has had one episode of visual hallucination. She was recently started on two new medications: oxybutynin (for urinary incontinence) and amitriptyline (for neuropathic pain). Her MMSE is 21/30. What is the single most likely cause of her symptoms and the most appropriate immediate action?
UN5577.correct_answer: Drug-induced delirium — review and stop anticholinergic drugs

UN5577.presentation: Neck pain, Horner syndrome and TIA — confirming carotid dissection
UN5577.stem: A 42-year-old man attends the emergency department with left-sided neck pain and headache that started after a chiropractic neck manipulation two days ago. His wife noticed that his left eyelid is drooping. This morning he had 20 minutes of right-hand weakness and difficulty finding words, which has fully resolved. On examination he has mild left ptosis and a small left pupil that reacts to light. A non-contrast CT head is normal. Which investigation will best confirm the suspected cause?
UN5577.correct_answer: CT angiography of the head and neck

UN5577.presentation: New behaviour that challenges in a non-speaking autistic child — first step
UN5577.stem: A 9-year-old autistic boy who does not use spoken language is brought to his GP by his mother. Over the past 2 weeks he has started hitting the right side of his face and banging his head. He is eating less and is waking at night. There have been no changes at home or school. What is the most appropriate next step?
UN5577.correct_answer: Look for a physical cause such as dental pain

UN5577.stem: A 66-year-old woman suddenly cannot find her words and develops weakness of her right arm, though she remains alert. Which cerebral hemisphere is most likely affected?
A 3-year-9-month-old girl cannot yet combine more than two words together and strangers struggle to understand what she is saying, despite a normal hearing test. What should happen next?
UN5577.correct_answer: Arrange formal assessment of her speech and language development

UN5578.stem: Hearing tests are normal for a 3-year-old girl, and she clearly follows instructions and responds appropriately to what people say to her, yet strangers can barely make out a word when she talks. Which area of her development is mainly affected?
A 3-year-9-month-old girl cannot yet combine more than two words together and strangers struggle to understand what she is saying, despite a normal hearing test. What should happen next?
UN5578.correct_answer: Arrange formal assessment of her speech and language development

UN5578.presentation: Language difficulty in a school starter
UN5578.stem:
A 5-year-old girl in her first year at primary school struggles to follow instructions such as 'put your book away, then line up at the door'. She speaks in short, muddled sentences and often uses the wrong word. She is sociable, makes good eye contact, shares her toys and enjoys pretend play. Her hearing test is normal, and her puzzles and drawing are at the level expected for her age.

Which problem best explains her difficulties?

To estimate how much alcohol adults in a town drink, a team surveys patients on the hospital's medical wards. The results suggest much higher alcohol intake than national figures. What is the main problem with this study?

A 74-year-old woman has insidious, gradually progressive memory loss over 2 years. She forgets recent conversations, repeats questions, misplaces items and has word-finding difficulty. There is no stepwise deterioration, no early visual hallucinations or parkinsonism, no prominent early personality change, and no gait disturbance. Neurological examination is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 38-year-old man develops sudden severe spinning vertigo with nausea after a recent cold. It has lasted two days. He also reports muffled hearing and ringing in his left ear since the onset, and has never had a similar episode. He has no vascular risk factors, limb weakness, speech disturbance or double vision, and examination shows horizontal nystagmus.

Which diagnosis is most likely?

Following a stroke, a 68-year-old man can follow commands and clearly understands what is said to him, but his own speech is slow, laboured and reduced to short, fragmented phrases. What type of language disorder does this represent?

A 72-year-old man suddenly develops right facial droop, right arm and leg weakness, and slurred speech while at home. His wife calls an ambulance and he arrives 70 minutes after symptom onset. On examination he has a right hemiparesis and dysarthria. Blood pressure is 180/95 mmHg and capillary glucose is normal. He takes no anticoagulants. What is the most appropriate immediate next step?

UN5590.stem: A 63-year-old man speaks to his GP by telephone. For a week, every time he looks up to reach a high shelf or lies back on his pillow, the room spins violently for less than a minute and then settles. Between attacks he feels completely normal. He has no hearing loss, tinnitus, headache, weakness or difficulty speaking. At a face-to-face review the following day, the Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre to the right reproduces his vertigo with a burst of torsional nystagmus after a short delay. Which condition is responsible?

UN5590.presentation: BPPV — persistent despite repeated Epley manoeuvres
UN5590.stem: A 58-year-old man has had positional vertigo for 8 weeks. His GP diagnosed right posterior-canal benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) and has carried out a correctly performed Epley manoeuvre on three separate occasions over this time. Today the Dix–Hallpike test is still positive on the right, with brief fatiguing torsional nystagmus. He has no hearing loss, no headache and a normal neurological examination. What is the most appropriate next step?
UN5590.correct_answer: Refer to an ENT or specialist vestibular service

UN5590.stem: A 60-year-old woman has brief episodes of rotational vertigo lasting under a minute, triggered by rolling over in bed or looking up. The Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre reproduces transient vertigo with rotatory nystagmus. What is the most appropriate treatment?

A 79-year-old woman attends her GP after a fall at home. Six months ago she was diagnosed with right posterior-canal benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) and she has taken prochlorperazine regularly ever since. Today the Dix–Hallpike test on the right again provokes brief vertigo with upbeating torsional nystagmus. She has no hearing loss and the neurological examination is otherwise normal. An Epley manoeuvre is planned for today, and she asks for a stronger tablet to stop the dizziness. Which is the most appropriate change to her medication?

A 69-year-old woman presents with progressive exertional chest pain, dizziness and breathlessness. Examination reveals an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN5590.presentation: Suspected carotid sinus syncope — first-line investigation
UN5590.stem: A 74-year-old man has had two brief episodes of loss of consciousness in 3 months: one while turning his head sharply to look over his shoulder, and one while shaving his neck. He recovered fully within seconds each time. Examination, including lying and standing blood pressure, is normal and there are no carotid bruits. He has no history of stroke, transient ischaemic attack or myocardial infarction. His 12-lead ECG and echocardiogram are normal. Which investigation should be offered first?

A 66-year-old man describes several weeks of sudden spinning lasting under a minute whenever he lies back in bed or tilts his head up to reach a high shelf. He feels nauseated during attacks but is well between them. His hearing is normal and neurological examination is unremarkable. Which bedside test should be used to confirm the most likely diagnosis?

A 62-year-old woman describes several months of intermittent cramping pain in the left lower abdomen along with occasional loose stools alternating with constipation. She has no fever, feels systemically well, and examination reveals no peritonism. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN5856.stem: A 38-year-old woman with known myasthenia gravis develops increasing breathlessness and difficulty swallowing over 24 hours following a chest infection. Her forced vital capacity is falling on serial measurement. What is the most important immediate assessment?
UN5856.correct_answer: Serial FVC with airway and ventilation support on standby

UN5856.stem: A 45-year-old woman with myasthenia gravis has a sudden deterioration with difficulty swallowing and shortness of breath. She cannot sustain a head-lift, and her forced vital capacity has fallen from 30 to 18 mL/kg over 6 hours, and she has a weak cough with pooled secretions. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

A 63-year-old man with myasthenia gravis attends the emergency department two days after starting a course of clarithromycin for a chest infection. He has increasing weakness, double vision and difficulty clearing his secretions, and he is now breathless when lying flat. His speech is becoming nasal. What is the best interpretation of his deterioration?
UN5856.correct_answer: Myasthenic crisis needing urgent assessment of respiratory function

UN5856.stem: A 62-year-old woman with generalised myasthenia gravis is admitted with a chest infection. Over the next 24 hours her voice becomes nasal, she struggles to swallow her saliva, she cannot lift her head off the pillow and her breathing becomes shallow. Her pyridostigmine dose has not been changed, and she has no excess sweating, salivation, diarrhoea or small pupils. Which complication is most likely?

UN5856.presentation: Deep Neck-Space Infection With Airway Risk
UN5856.stem: A patient being treated for acute tonsillitis develops worsening neck swelling over 24 hours, along with increasing difficulty swallowing and a new stridor. What is the most important immediate concern?
UN5856.correct_answer: Airway compromise from deep neck infection

UN5856.stem: A patient with a known dental infection develops rapidly worsening swelling under the chin and tongue, increasing difficulty swallowing saliva and a change in his voice. What should be prioritised immediately?
UN5856.correct_answer: Assessment and protection of the airway

UN5856.presentation: Newly diagnosed myasthenia gravis — thymus imaging
UN5856.stem: A 34-year-old woman is newly diagnosed with generalised myasthenia gravis. Her acetylcholine receptor antibodies are positive and she has started pyridostigmine in the neurology clinic. Which imaging should be arranged next?

A 47-year-old woman with generalised myasthenia gravis, controlled on pyridostigmine, is admitted with acute pyelonephritis. She has no drug allergies and her kidney function is normal. Before choosing an intravenous antibiotic, the FY1 doctor checks for interactions with her myasthenia. Which antibiotic is contraindicated in her?

UN5858.stem: A 28-year-old woman reports double vision. On testing horizontal gaze to the left, her RIGHT eye fails to adduct (move towards the nose), while the LEFT (abducting) eye develops nystagmus. Convergence is preserved. She has had a previous episode of optic neuritis. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
UN5858.correct_answer: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia due to multiple sclerosis

UN5858.stem: A 29-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis reports double vision. On examination, when she looks to the right, her left eye fails to fully adduct while the right eye shows nystagmus. Which structure is classically implicated in this pattern?

UN5858.presentation: Optic neuritis — investigation for multiple sclerosis risk
UN5858.stem: A 27-year-old woman is seen in eye casualty with 5 days of blurred vision in her left eye and pain on eye movement. The ophthalmologist confirms optic neuritis: reduced acuity and colour vision, a left relative afferent pupillary defect and a normal-looking optic disc. She has no other neurological symptoms. Which investigation gives the most information about her future risk of multiple sclerosis?

A 27-year-old man is seen in the neurology clinic with 5 days of numbness spreading up from his feet to his waist and new urinary urgency. Last year he had 3 weeks of double vision that recovered completely without treatment. Examination shows brisk reflexes in the legs and upgoing plantars. MRI shows several periventricular and juxtacortical white matter lesions and a short lesion in the cervical spinal cord. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN5858.presentation: Crossed Cranial Nerve And Limb Signs
UN5858.stem: A 59-year-old woman suddenly develops double vision, difficulty swallowing and weakness of her right arm and leg together. Which anatomical site could explain this combination of cranial nerve and limb findings?

A 68-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and hypertension presents with 2 days of double vision. The two images lie side by side and move further apart when he looks at the television across the room or looks to his right. His right eye cannot move outwards beyond the midline, but all other eye movements, the eyelids and the pupils are normal. The rest of the neurological examination is normal. Which cranial nerve is most likely affected?

A patient with a known pituitary adenoma develops a sudden severe headache, visual disturbance with a bitemporal field defect, and double vision (ophthalmoplegia). They become hypotensive and unwell. What is the most important immediate hormonal treatment?
UN5858.correct_answer: IV hydrocortisone for acute cortisol deficiency

UN5858.stem: A 28-year-old woman has had separate episodes over two years: painful loss of vision in one eye (optic neuritis) that recovered, and later a band of numbness ascending from the legs. MRI shows white-matter lesions disseminated in time and space. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN5859.stem: A 75-year-old man is found to have a tremor at rest, slowness of movement and increased muscle tone. Which diagnosis is most likely?

A 72-year-old man reports progressive slowness of movement over a year. He has an asymmetric resting tremor of the right hand and increasing stiffness, and his handwriting has become smaller. On examination there is cogwheel rigidity, bradykinesia, and a resting tremor that decreases when he reaches for an object. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 58-year-old woman develops a tremor, generalised slowness of movement and difficulty starting to walk; her symptoms began predominantly on one side. Which feature is most characteristic of Parkinson's disease?

An older man has a slowly progressive, asymmetrical resting tremor ('pill-rolling'), rigidity (cogwheel) and bradykinesia, with a shuffling gait. He has no early falls and no eye-movement abnormality. What is the most likely diagnosis and most effective symptomatic treatment?
UN5859.correct_answer: Idiopathic Parkinson's disease — levodopa (with a dopa-decarboxylase inhibitor)

UN5859.presentation: Asymmetric Resting Tremor With Slowness and Stiffness
UN5859.stem: A 70-year-old man's wife reports that his right hand shakes when it is resting in his lap but settles when he reaches for a cup. He has become noticeably slower getting out of a chair, and his right arm feels stiff on examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 68-year-old man with known Parkinson's disease finds it hard to get going when he starts walking, and his stride length shortens progressively as he continues. Which cardinal motor sign does this describe?

A 74-year-old woman has been diagnosed with Parkinson's disease by a specialist. Over the past year her handwriting has become small, she has a tremor of her left hand at rest, and she now takes a long time to dress and has difficulty turning over in bed. Examination shows asymmetrical rigidity and slow, small movements. She lives alone and wants treatment to stay independent. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
UN5859.correct_answer: Levodopa combined with a dopa-decarboxylase inhibitor

UN5859.stem: A patient has a bilateral, symmetrical tremor of the hands that is present on maintaining a posture and on action (e.g. holding a cup or writing), improves after a small amount of alcohol, and there is a family history. There is no bradykinesia or rigidity. What is the most likely diagnosis and first-line treatment?

UN5860.stem: A 58-year-old woman develops a tremor, generalised slowness of movement and difficulty starting to walk; her symptoms began predominantly on one side. Which feature is most characteristic of Parkinson's disease?

A 40-year-old woman has had nasal blockage, facial pressure and a reduced sense of smell continuously for the past four months, with no clear improvement. Which diagnosis is most consistent with this presentation?

A 72-year-old man reports progressive slowness of movement over a year. He has an asymmetric resting tremor of the right hand and increasing stiffness, and his handwriting has become smaller. On examination there is cogwheel rigidity, bradykinesia, and a resting tremor that decreases when he reaches for an object. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A 75-year-old man is found to have a tremor at rest, slowness of movement and increased muscle tone. Which diagnosis is most likely?

An older man has a slowly progressive, asymmetrical resting tremor ('pill-rolling'), rigidity (cogwheel) and bradykinesia, with a shuffling gait. He has no early falls and no eye-movement abnormality. What is the most likely diagnosis and most effective symptomatic treatment?
UN5860.correct_answer: Idiopathic Parkinson's disease — levodopa (with a dopa-decarboxylase inhibitor)

UN5860.stem: A 68-year-old man with known Parkinson's disease finds it hard to get going when he starts walking, and his stride length shortens progressively as he continues. Which cardinal motor sign does this describe?

UN5860.presentation: New Unilateral Tremor in an Older Man
UN5860.stem: A 68-year-old man presents with a new tremor affecting one hand at rest, slowness of movement and reduced arm swing while walking. Which diagnosis best fits this presentation?

A 72-year-old retired teacher is brought to his GP by his wife, who says his handwriting has become tiny and he now takes a long time to get dressed. He takes no regular medication. On examination his right hand shakes while resting in his lap but settles when he reaches for a pen. He has a reduced arm swing on the right when walking, and there is cogwheel stiffness at the right wrist. What is the likeliest diagnosis?

UN6164.stem: A 73-year-old man has recently been diagnosed with dementia. He still drives regularly and asks what he should do next regarding his driving licence. What is the most appropriate advice?
UN6164.correct_answer: Inform the DVLA and follow advice regarding fitness to drive

UN6164.stem:
A 35-year-old man with a car driving licence has been treated on an acute psychiatric ward for his first manic episode. He is now settled, has insight and is due to be discharged next week. He tells you he plans to drive himself home.

What is the most appropriate advice about driving?
UN6164.correct_answer: He must not drive and must notify the DVLA himself

UN6164.stem: A 55-year-old bus driver has had two unprovoked generalised tonic-clonic seizures a month apart. A neurologist diagnoses epilepsy and starts lamotrigine. He asks what this means for his car and bus licences. What is the correct advice?
UN6164.correct_answer: He must tell the DVLA; he cannot drive a car until seizure-free for 1 year, and must be seizure-free for 10 years without medication before driving a bus

UN6164.stem: A 28-year-old man has his first generalised tonic-clonic seizure. He holds an ordinary (Group 1) driving licence. What is the correct advice regarding driving?
UN6164.correct_answer: He must stop driving and notify the DVLA, with a minimum 6-month ban

UN6164.stem: A 70-year-old man has a permanent pacemaker fitted for symptomatic complete heart block, which had caused tiredness and breathlessness but no blackouts. The procedure is uncomplicated and he is to be discharged home today. He drives a car but holds no bus or lorry licence. He asks the FY1 doctor what he must do about driving. Which advice is correct?
UN6164.correct_answer: Do not drive for one week and notify the DVLA

UN6164.presentation: Homonymous hemianopia after stroke — driving advice
UN6164.stem: A 63-year-old man is reviewed in the stroke clinic 6 weeks after an occipital infarct. His limb function and speech are normal, but he has a persistent left homonymous hemianopia on confrontation testing. He drives a car and wants to start driving again because it has been more than a month since the stroke. What is the most appropriate advice?
UN6164.correct_answer: He must stop driving and notify the DVLA himself

UN6164.presentation: Moderate obstructive sleep apnoea syndrome — DVLA advice
UN6164.stem: A 49-year-old man who holds a car licence only has a sleep study showing moderate obstructive sleep apnoea, with an apnoea–hypopnoea index of 22 events per hour. He has excessive daytime sleepiness and recently nearly fell asleep while waiting at traffic lights. Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) treatment is being arranged. He asks what this means for his driving. What is the most appropriate advice?
UN6164.correct_answer: He must stop driving now and must notify the DVLA himself

UN6164.stem: A patient with epilepsy continues to drive against advice and has not informed the DVLA, despite you explaining the legal duty. What is the most appropriate action?
UN6164.correct_answer: Advise them again; if they still drive, inform the DVLA

UN6165.stem: A 58-year-old man who has taken an antipsychotic for many years develops involuntary, repetitive movements of the mouth, tongue and face — lip-smacking and tongue protrusion. He is otherwise mentally stable. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 35-year-old man started on an antipsychotic two weeks ago complains of an unbearable inner restlessness and a compulsion to keep moving. He paces constantly and cannot sit still, and finds it deeply distressing. There are no abnormal involuntary movements at rest. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 68-year-old woman has had Parkinson disease for nine years and takes co-careldopa. Her daughter brings her to the neurology clinic because she now has restless, twisting, flowing movements of her trunk and arms, which are worst about an hour after each dose. Her tremor and stiffness are well controlled at those times. She does not take any antipsychotic. What is the most likely explanation?

A 40-year-old develops involuntary, jerky, dance-like movements (chorea), alongside progressive cognitive decline and behavioural/psychiatric changes. His father had a similar illness that began at a slightly older age. What is the most likely diagnosis and inheritance pattern?
On examination, a patient is noted to have involuntary, rhythmic back-and-forth movement of both eyes. What is this finding called?

A 74-year-old woman has been diagnosed with Parkinson's disease by a specialist. Over the past year her handwriting has become small, she has a tremor of her left hand at rest, and she now takes a long time to dress and has difficulty turning over in bed. Examination shows asymmetrical rigidity and slow, small movements. She lives alone and wants treatment to stay independent. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
UN6165.correct_answer: Levodopa combined with a dopa-decarboxylase inhibitor

UN6165.stem: A 70-year-old man who still volunteers at a charity shop has, over three years, become unable to remember the names of new colleagues or what he did the day before, and he now gets muddled when giving change at the till. Neurological examination shows no tremor, rigidity, involuntary movements or focal deficit. Which is the most likely diagnosis?

UN6165.presentation: Huntington disease — drug for troublesome chorea
UN6165.stem: A 46-year-old man with genetically confirmed Huntington disease is seen in the neurology clinic. Over the past year his involuntary movements have become worse, and he now spills drinks and has fallen twice. His mood is good, he has no history of depression and he has no suicidal thoughts. Liver function is normal. The team decides to start medication for his chorea. Which drug is most appropriate?

UN6167.presentation: Facial Weakness Affecting the Whole Side of the Face
UN6167.stem: A patient develops sudden weakness of the entire left side of the face, including the inability to raise the left eyebrow or fully close the left eye. What type of facial nerve lesion does this represent?
UN6167.correct_answer: Lower motor neurone facial nerve palsy

UN6167.stem: A 71-year-old woman has sudden left-sided weakness together with an upper motor neurone pattern of facial weakness on the right. Which cranial nerve is responsible for producing the facial weakness itself?

UN6167.presentation: Facial Weakness That Spares the Forehead
UN6167.stem: A patient has weakness affecting only the lower part of the left side of the face, with normal, symmetrical forehead wrinkling on both sides. Which lesion best explains this finding?

UN6167.presentation: Unilateral Facial Weakness Including the Forehead
UN6167.stem: A patient wakes with weakness of the left side of the face, unable to raise the left eyebrow or fully close the left eye, while the rest of their neurological examination is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 38-year-old woman develops weakness affecting the entire left side of her face, including being unable to close her left eye and losing movement of her forehead on that side. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN6167.presentation: Lyme disease facial palsy — antibiotic choice
UN6167.stem: A 38-year-old man has a left lower motor neurone facial palsy that developed 5 weeks after a tick bite in the New Forest. Lyme ELISA and immunoblot are both positive. He has no headache, neck stiffness, confusion, limb weakness or palpitations, and his ECG is normal. He is not allergic to any medicines. Which antibiotic treatment is most appropriate?

UN6167.presentation: Mixed Upper And Lower Motor Neurone Signs
UN6167.stem: Visible wasting, fasciculations and brisk reflexes accompany progressively worsening weakness in both legs of a 64-year-old woman. Which diagnosis is most likely?
A 60-year-old man has confirmed motor neurone disease with mixed upper and lower motor neuron signs and no sensory loss. Which drug is most likely to modestly prolong survival?

UN6168.stem: A 35-year-old man wakes with sudden unilateral facial droop. He cannot wrinkle his forehead on the affected side or fully close that eye, and there is no limb weakness or other deficit. What is the diagnosis and key treatment?
UN6168.correct_answer: Bell's palsy — give oral corticosteroids and protect the eye

UN6168.stem: A 38-year-old woman develops weakness affecting the entire left side of her face, including being unable to close her left eye and losing movement of her forehead on that side. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN6168.presentation: Unilateral Facial Weakness Including the Forehead
UN6168.stem: A patient wakes with weakness of the left side of the face, unable to raise the left eyebrow or fully close the left eye, while the rest of their neurological examination is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN6168.presentation: Bell palsy with painful red eye — escalation
UN6168.stem:
A 45-year-old woman was diagnosed with Bell palsy 6 days ago and is taking oral prednisolone. She cannot fully close her left eye and has been using lubricating eye drops by day. She returns to her GP with a painful, red, watering left eye, and her vision in that eye has become blurred. Fluorescein staining shows an area of corneal damage on the lower part of the cornea.

What is the most appropriate management?
UN6168.correct_answer: Same-day referral to the eye department

UN6168.presentation: Facial nerve palsy — feature that needs urgent specialist referral
UN6168.stem:
A 52-year-old man sees his GP with weakness of the right side of his face, including his forehead. He cannot fully close his right eye. There are no limb symptoms, the ear canal and eardrum look normal, and there is no rash. The GP is considering a diagnosis of Bell palsy.

Which additional feature should most prompt specialist referral rather than treatment as Bell palsy in primary care?
UN6168.correct_answer: Weakness worsening slowly over three weeks

UN6168.stem: A 34-year-old woman attends the emergency department after noticing in the mirror that the left side of her mouth droops and she dribbles when drinking. The day before she had an ache behind her left ear. Food tastes odd. On examination she cannot wrinkle the left side of her forehead or fully close her left eye. There are no vesicles in or around the ear, and limb power, sensation and speech are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 30-year-old woman develops, over a day, drooping of the right side of her face. She cannot raise the right eyebrow or close the right eye fully, and the right side of her forehead is involved. There are no other neurological signs. She presents within 72 hours of onset. What is the most appropriate management?

UN6168.presentation: Facial Weakness Affecting the Whole Side of the Face
UN6168.stem: A patient develops sudden weakness of the entire left side of the face, including the inability to raise the left eyebrow or fully close the left eye. What type of facial nerve lesion does this represent?
UN6168.correct_answer: Lower motor neurone facial nerve palsy

UN6482.presentation: Crossed Cranial Nerve And Limb Signs
UN6482.stem: A 59-year-old woman suddenly develops double vision, difficulty swallowing and weakness of her right arm and leg together. Which anatomical site could explain this combination of cranial nerve and limb findings?

A 68-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and hypertension presents with 2 days of double vision. The two images lie side by side and move further apart when he looks at the television across the room or looks to his right. His right eye cannot move outwards beyond the midline, but all other eye movements, the eyelids and the pupils are normal. The rest of the neurological examination is normal. Which cranial nerve is most likely affected?

A 64-year-old woman with long-standing type 2 diabetes attends the emergency department with horizontal double vision that began yesterday and is worst when she looks to her left at the television across the room. Her left eye does not move outward beyond the midline. Her eyelids are not drooping and her pupils are equal and reactive. Damage to which nerve best explains these findings?

A 71-year-old woman has sudden left-sided weakness together with an upper motor neurone pattern of facial weakness on the right. Which cranial nerve is responsible for producing the facial weakness itself?

After undergoing pelvic surgery, a 61-year-old woman notices weakness when trying to straighten her knee and reduced sensation over the inner part of her lower leg. Which nerve is most likely affected?

UN6482.presentation: Third Nerve Palsy — Surgical versus Medical
UN6482.stem: A patient has a droopy eyelid (ptosis) and an eye that is deviated 'down and out'. Crucially, the pupil on that side is DILATED and poorly reactive, and there is pain. What is the most appropriate concern and action?
UN6482.correct_answer: A compressive third nerve palsy — urgent imaging for a posterior communicating artery aneurysm

UN6482.presentation: Nerve Root in L5/S1 Disc Prolapse
UN6482.stem: A 41-year-old man develops sudden severe lower back pain after lifting a heavy box at work. The pain radiates down the back of his leg and into his foot. Which nerve root is most likely affected?

A patient awakens with a 'wrist drop' (inability to extend the wrist and fingers) after falling asleep with their arm draped over a chair. Sensation is reduced over the dorsum of the hand near the base of the thumb. Which nerve is affected?
UN6482.correct_answer: The radial nerve (at the spiral groove of the humerus)

UN6556.stem: A 52-year-old man with Guillain-Barré syndrome has weakness that is now extending to his arms. He is admitted for close monitoring. Which parameter best predicts impending respiratory failure?

A 26-year-old woman develops progressive difficulty walking upstairs over several days, two weeks after an episode of diarrhoea. On examination she has symmetrical weakness in both legs with absent reflexes. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 76-year-old man taking furosemide and bendroflumethiazide for heart failure is admitted with profound generalised weakness. His serum potassium is severely reduced, and his ECG shows prominent U waves. He is also on digoxin. Which complication is the greatest immediate threat to his life?

A 30-year-old man develops progressive, symmetrical ascending leg weakness over 5 days, 2 weeks after a diarrhoeal illness. Reflexes are absent. CSF shows raised protein with a normal cell count. What is the most appropriate treatment, alongside monitoring of respiratory function?
Breathing becomes increasingly laboured in a patient already diagnosed with Guillain-Barre syndrome. Which complication is most critical to watch for?

A 25-year-old man develops ascending weakness over a week, starting in his legs, with loss of reflexes and mild distal numbness. He had diarrhoea three weeks ago. What is the most important investigation to monitor in the acute phase?

A 14-year-old boy was pulled out of a river by friends after going under for a short time. He seemed fine at first, but a few hours later in the emergency department he has a persistent cough, increasing shortness of breath and crackles at both lung bases. Which complication is the main immediate concern?
UN6556.correct_answer: Respiratory compromise from aspiration-related lung injury

UN6556.stem: A patient admitted with severe community-acquired pneumonia has an arterial blood gas showing marked hypoxaemia with a PaCO2 that is normal. What type of respiratory failure does this represent?

UN6634.presentation: Facial Weakness Affecting the Whole Side of the Face
UN6634.stem: A patient develops sudden weakness of the entire left side of the face, including the inability to raise the left eyebrow or fully close the left eye. What type of facial nerve lesion does this represent?
UN6634.correct_answer: Lower motor neurone facial nerve palsy

He has no headache, neck stiffness, confusion, limb weakness or palpitations, and his ECG is normal. He is not allergic to any medicines. Which antibiotic treatment is most appropriate?

A 71-year-old woman has sudden left-sided weakness together with an upper motor neurone pattern of facial weakness on the right. Which cranial nerve is responsible for producing the facial weakness itself?

A 35-year-old man wakes with sudden unilateral facial droop. He cannot wrinkle his forehead on the affected side or fully close that eye, and there is no limb weakness or other deficit. What is the diagnosis and key treatment?
UN6634.correct_answer: Bell's palsy — give oral corticosteroids and protect the eye

UN6634.presentation: Contralateral Upper Motor Neurone Facial Palsy (Stroke)
UN6634.stem: A 66-year-old man wakes with the right corner of his mouth drooping. When asked, he can wrinkle both sides of his forehead and close both eyes tightly. His right hand is clumsy and grip on that side is weak. Hearing and facial sensation are normal. Where is the lesion most likely to be?

UN6634.presentation: Mixed Upper And Lower Motor Neurone Signs
UN6634.stem: Visible wasting, fasciculations and brisk reflexes accompany progressively worsening weakness in both legs of a 64-year-old woman. Which diagnosis is most likely?

UN6634.presentation: Unilateral Facial Weakness Including the Forehead
UN6634.stem: A patient wakes with weakness of the left side of the face, unable to raise the left eyebrow or fully close the left eye, while the rest of their neurological examination is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A 60-year-old man has confirmed motor neurone disease with mixed upper and lower motor neuron signs and no sensory loss. Which drug is most likely to modestly prolong survival?

UN6696.stem: A 38-year-old woman with known myasthenia gravis develops increasing breathlessness and difficulty swallowing over 24 hours following a chest infection. Her forced vital capacity is falling on serial measurement. What is the most important immediate assessment?
UN6696.correct_answer: Serial FVC with airway and ventilation support on standby

UN6696.presentation: Deep Neck-Space Infection With Airway Risk
UN6696.stem: A patient being treated for acute tonsillitis develops worsening neck swelling over 24 hours, along with increasing difficulty swallowing and a new stridor. What is the most important immediate concern?
UN6696.correct_answer: Airway compromise from deep neck infection

UN6696.stem: A 14-year-old boy was pulled out of a river by friends after going under for a short time. He seemed fine at first, but a few hours later in the emergency department he has a persistent cough, increasing shortness of breath and crackles at both lung bases. Which complication is the main immediate concern?
UN6696.correct_answer: Respiratory compromise from aspiration-related lung injury

UN6696.stem: A patient with a known dental infection develops rapidly worsening swelling under the chin and tongue, increasing difficulty swallowing saliva and a change in his voice. What should be prioritised immediately?
UN6696.correct_answer: Assessment and protection of the airway

UN6696.stem: A 45-year-old woman with myasthenia gravis has a sudden deterioration with difficulty swallowing and shortness of breath. She cannot sustain a head-lift, and her forced vital capacity has fallen from 30 to 18 mL/kg over 6 hours, and she has a weak cough with pooled secretions. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

UN6696.presentation: Newly diagnosed myasthenia gravis — thymus imaging
UN6696.stem: A 34-year-old woman is newly diagnosed with generalised myasthenia gravis. Her acetylcholine receptor antibodies are positive and she has started pyridostigmine in the neurology clinic. Which imaging should be arranged next?

A 47-year-old woman with generalised myasthenia gravis, controlled on pyridostigmine, is admitted with acute pyelonephritis. She has no drug allergies and her kidney function is normal. Before choosing an intravenous antibiotic, the FY1 doctor checks for interactions with her myasthenia. Which antibiotic is contraindicated in her?
A patient admitted with severe community-acquired pneumonia has an arterial blood gas showing marked hypoxaemia with a PaCO2 that is normal. What type of respiratory failure does this represent?

UN6881.stem: A patient has pain over the outer aspect of the elbow that is reproduced by resisted wrist extension and by gripping. There is point tenderness over the lateral epicondyle. What is the most likely diagnosis and management?
UN6881.correct_answer: Lateral epicondylitis — activity modification and analgesia

UN6881.stem: A 69-year-old woman, on alendronic acid for osteoporosis for seven years, attends the surgery. She tells her GP that for six weeks she has had a dull ache in both thighs, worse on walking and now present at night. She has not fallen. She has no morning stiffness of the shoulders or back pain. There is tenderness over the outer aspect of the right mid-thigh, and hip movements are full. What is the most important diagnosis to consider?
Tingling and weakness develop in a 47-year-old woman's hand, worse overnight, involving her thumb and the next two fingers. Which nerve compression is responsible?

After undergoing pelvic surgery, a 61-year-old woman notices weakness when trying to straighten her knee and reduced sensation over the inner part of her lower leg. Which nerve is most likely affected?

A cyclist falls onto the handlebars and CT shows a fracture through the floor of the right orbit. He has numbness of the lower eyelid, the side of the nose and the upper lip on that side.

Which nerve is most likely to have been injured?
A 45-year-old office worker wakes most nights with tingling and numbness in her thumb, index and middle fingers, which she relieves by shaking her hand. Which nerve is most likely compressed?

A 66-year-old man who has smoked for 45 years attends the practice nurse with a painful ulcer over the outer aspect of his right ankle that has not healed for six weeks. For years he has had calf cramps after walking a short distance. The pain is worst at night and eases if he hangs his leg over the side of the bed. The ulcer is small, deep and punched-out with a pale base. The skin of the foot is shiny and hairless, and foot pulses are very weak. What type of ulcer is most likely?

A 49-year-old painter and decorator sees his GP with several months of pain over the outer aspect of his right shoulder, worse when working with his arm overhead. On examination, pain occurs as he actively lifts the arm out to the side through the middle part of its range, then eases as the arm goes higher. When the doctor moves the arm for him, the range is full, including external rotation. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN6882.stem: A 45-year-old woman has tingling and numbness in the thumb, index and middle fingers, worse at night, relieved by shaking the hand. Tapping over the wrist reproduces the symptoms. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 33-year-old woman at 30 weeks of pregnancy mentions at her antenatal appointment that she is woken most nights by pins and needles in her right hand. She finds relief by flicking her wrist. The tingling affects her thumb and the next two fingers, but her little finger is unaffected. Tapping over the front of her wrist reproduces the symptoms. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 31-year-old woman who is 29 weeks pregnant has a 4-week history of tingling and numbness in her right thumb, index and middle fingers. The symptoms wake her at night and ease when she shakes her hand. She has no neck pain. Examination shows normal bulk and power of the thenar muscles and normal upper limb reflexes, and Phalen's test reproduces her symptoms. What is the most appropriate initial management?
UN6882.correct_answer: Night-time wrist splint in neutral position

UN6882.stem: Tingling and weakness develop in a 47-year-old woman's hand, worse overnight, involving her thumb and the next two fingers. Which nerve compression is responsible?

A 67-year-old man is referred to the renal clinic with marked ankle oedema and heavy proteinuria. He also reports breathlessness on exertion, and an echocardiogram shows thickened ventricular walls with a restrictive filling pattern. He has burning, numb feet and carpal tunnel symptoms in both hands, and his tongue looks enlarged. His HbA1c is normal.

Which systemic condition best explains these findings?
A 66-year-old woman suddenly cannot find her words and develops weakness of her right arm, though she remains alert. Which cerebral hemisphere is most likely affected?

A 63-year-old woman who is a keen gardener has 8 months of aching at the base of her right thumb, worse when using secateurs, turning keys and opening jars. Examination shows squaring of the thumb base with tenderness at the radial edge of the thenar eminence. Pressing the thumb metacarpal towards the wrist while rotating it reproduces her pain with crepitus. Finkelstein test is negative and sensation in the hand is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A patient has slowly progressive limb weakness, visible muscle wasting and spontaneous twitching of the affected muscles, with reduced reflexes in those muscle groups. What type of lesion best fits these findings?

UN7031.stem: A 69-year-old woman, on alendronic acid for osteoporosis for seven years, attends the surgery. She tells her GP that for six weeks she has had a dull ache in both thighs, worse on walking and now present at night. She has not fallen. She has no morning stiffness of the shoulders or back pain. There is tenderness over the outer aspect of the right mid-thigh, and hip movements are full. What is the most important diagnosis to consider?

UN7031.correct_answer: Lateral epicondylitis — activity modification and analgesia

The ulcer is small, deep and punched-out with a pale base. The skin of the foot is shiny and hairless, and foot pulses are very weak. What type of ulcer is most likely?
