On examination, pain occurs as he actively lifts the arm out to the side through the middle part of its range, then eases as the arm goes higher. When the doctor moves the arm for him, the range is full, including external rotation. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A patient has burning, shooting pain with tingling in a distribution consistent with nerve damage (for example, painful diabetic neuropathy). Standard analgesics have not helped. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

UN7031.presentation: Rash Limited to a Dressing Site
UN7031.stem: A 36-year-old man develops an itchy, erythematous rash exactly in the shape of a plaster he applied two days earlier. The rash does not extend beyond the area of contact. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN7031.presentation: Traumatic Knee Pain with Bony Tenderness
UN7031.stem: A 49-year-old man falls directly onto his knee and now has pain and swelling. He can still fully extend the knee but has marked tenderness directly over the patella. Which investigation should be arranged first?

A 52-year-old woman is seen at her GP surgery. Three weeks ago she went hill walking in the Scottish Highlands and afterwards removed a small tick from her thigh. Over the past week a red patch has slowly spread outwards from the bite site to about the size of her palm, with a paler centre. She feels a little tired but has no neurological or cardiac symptoms. She is not pregnant and has no allergies. What is the most appropriate management?

UN7158.stem: A 69-year-old man suddenly cannot get his words out and has weakness in his right arm, with a normal blood glucose. Which finding most strongly points to a cortical rather than peripheral lesion?
Sudden weakness and numbness affecting the right arm and leg, with right facial droop, develop in a 69-year-old woman. Which side of the brain is most likely affected?
Which of these symptoms most specifically points to involvement of the dominant cerebral hemisphere, in a patient with sudden facial weakness, arm weakness and difficulty speaking?

UN7158.presentation: Crossed Cranial Nerve And Limb Signs
UN7158.stem: A 59-year-old woman suddenly develops double vision, difficulty swallowing and weakness of her right arm and leg together. Which anatomical site could explain this combination of cranial nerve and limb findings?
A 66-year-old woman suddenly cannot find her words and develops weakness of her right arm, though she remains alert. Which cerebral hemisphere is most likely affected?

A 31-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes is 11 weeks pregnant and has been tightening her glucose control on advice from the joint diabetes antenatal clinic. Her partner says she has had several episodes recently, mostly in the late morning. She wants to know which feature would most strongly suggest an episode is due to low blood glucose rather than something else. Which feature is most characteristic of hypoglycaemia?

UN7158.presentation: Facial Weakness Affecting the Whole Side of the Face
UN7158.stem: A patient develops sudden weakness of the entire left side of the face, including the inability to raise the left eyebrow or fully close the left eye. What type of facial nerve lesion does this represent?
UN7158.correct_answer: Lower motor neurone facial nerve palsy

UN7158.stem: A 71-year-old woman has sudden left-sided weakness together with an upper motor neurone pattern of facial weakness on the right. Which cranial nerve is responsible for producing the facial weakness itself?

UN7586.stem: A 9-year-old boy has recurrent episodes of severe central abdominal pain lasting one to several hours, associated with facial pallor and loss of appetite; he occasionally vomits but not always. He is completely well between attacks, and his mother has a history of migraine. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 26-year-old man attends his GP with throbbing headaches on the left side of his head two or three times a month. Each one starts with zigzag shimmering lines in his vision for about twenty minutes, followed by a headache lasting most of the day. During an attack he feels sick and cannot tolerate light or noise. He is completely well between attacks, and neurological examination including fundoscopy is normal. What is the most likely cause of his headaches?

A 16-year-old girl attends the GP surgery with her mother because of recurrent headaches over the past year. Each attack builds over an hour into a throbbing pain over one temple, makes her feel sick and lasts most of the day, and she has missed school several times. Between attacks she is well and examination is normal. Which additional feature would most support a diagnosis of migraine?

A 9-year-old girl of Turkish heritage is reviewed in the paediatric outpatient clinic. Since the age of four she has had attacks every few weeks of high fever with sharp pain in one side of her chest or across her abdomen, each settling on its own within two to three days. Between attacks she is completely well and her inflammatory markers return to normal. Her parents are related, and her older brother has had similar attacks. Which inherited condition is most likely?

A 19-year-old student presents to the GP surgery with a 5-hour history of fever, severe headache, photophobia and neck stiffness, and now a non-blanching petechial rash. She is alert with a blood pressure of 112/70. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
UN7586.correct_answer: Immediate IV (or IM) benzylpenicillin/ceftriaxone and urgent transfer

UN7586.stem: A 52-year-old woman develops an extremely sudden, severe headache that she describes as the worst she has ever experienced, accompanied by vomiting and sensitivity to light. Which diagnosis must be urgently considered?

A 19-year-old student presents with a 12-hour history of fever, severe headache, neck stiffness and a non-blanching petechial rash. He is drowsy with a blood pressure of 100/60. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

UN7586.presentation: Sudden Severe Testicular Pain in a Teenager
UN7586.stem: A 15-year-old boy develops sudden, severe pain in his right testicle with associated nausea and vomiting. Why is this presentation treated as a surgical emergency requiring immediate exploration?
UN7586.correct_answer: Testicular viability can be lost if torsion persists

UN7595.stem: A 50-year-old woman has several months of progressive symmetrical proximal muscle weakness (struggling to climb stairs and lift her arms), a heliotrope rash on the eyelids and scaly papules over the knuckles. What is the most appropriate next step after confirming the diagnosis?

A 55-year-old woman has bone pain and proximal muscle weakness, with difficulty climbing stairs and a waddling gait. Investigations show a low vitamin D, a low-normal calcium and phosphate, and a raised ALP and PTH. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 52-year-old man has noticed over four months that he struggles to lift his arms to shave and to get up from a low sofa. His thigh and upper arm muscles ache slightly. There is no rash, double vision or drooping of the eyelids, and sensation and reflexes are normal. He takes no regular medicines. His creatine kinase is markedly raised. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN7595.presentation: Suspected inflammatory myopathy — first blood test
UN7595.stem: A 52-year-old woman has 3 months of progressive difficulty rising from a chair, climbing stairs and lifting her arms above her head. Examination shows symmetrical weakness of the shoulder and hip girdle muscles. Sensation and reflexes are normal and there is no rash. An inflammatory myopathy is suspected. Which blood test is the most useful first investigation?

A 61-year-old woman who has taken atorvastatin for a year was prescribed clarithromycin for a chest infection eight days ago. She now has aching and weakness in both thighs and upper arms and struggles to climb stairs. Her urine is normal in colour. She has no skin rash. Her creatine kinase is markedly raised, her thyroid function is normal and her ESR is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 55-year-old woman with limited sun exposure and a poor diet has diffuse bone pain and proximal muscle weakness (difficulty climbing stairs and rising from a chair). Bloods show low calcium, low phosphate and a RAISED alkaline phosphatase, with a low vitamin D level. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 36-year-old man attends the emergency department because over five days he has found it increasingly difficult to climb stairs, and now his grip is weak too. He has tingling in both feet. Three weeks ago he had a bout of food poisoning after a barbecue. His knee and ankle reflexes cannot be elicited, and there is no sensory level on the trunk. What is the likeliest diagnosis?

A 45-year-old woman has central obesity, a rounded ‘moon’ face, purple abdominal striae, proximal muscle weakness, hypertension, new-onset diabetes and easy bruising. What is the most appropriate first-line investigation?

UN8160.stem: An elderly man has a triad of gait disturbance (a broad-based, shuffling 'magnetic' gait), urinary incontinence and cognitive decline. Imaging shows enlarged ventricles out of proportion to any atrophy. What is the diagnosis, and why does it matter?
UN8160.correct_answer: Normal pressure hydrocephalus — potentially reversible with shunting

UN8160.stem: A 74-year-old man has a several-month history of a broad-based, shuffling, 'magnetic' gait, worsening urinary incontinence and mild cognitive decline. Neuroimaging shows enlarged ventricles out of proportion to any cerebral atrophy. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 75-year-old man has a several-month history of a broad-based, shuffling, “magnetic” gait (his feet seem stuck to the floor), urinary incontinence, and mild cognitive slowing. CT of the head shows ventricular enlargement out of proportion to the degree of cortical atrophy. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 69-year-old retired teacher is brought to the memory clinic by his wife. Over eight months his steps have become short and wide-based, he struggles to start walking, he has begun wetting himself before he can reach the toilet, and he has become slow in his thinking and apathetic. A CT scan of the head shows dilated ventricles that are disproportionate to any sulcal widening. Which diagnosis is most likely?

A 26-year-old woman develops progressive difficulty walking upstairs over several days, two weeks after an episode of diarrhoea. On examination she has symmetrical weakness in both legs with absent reflexes. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 69-year-old retired teacher reports increasing forgetfulness over the past year. Cognitive testing shows mild impairment. She remains fully independent with shopping, finances, medication management and personal care. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 27-year-old man is seen in the neurology clinic with 5 days of numbness spreading up from his feet to his waist and new urinary urgency. Last year he had 3 weeks of double vision that recovered completely without treatment. Examination shows brisk reflexes in the legs and upgoing plantars. MRI shows several periventricular and juxtacortical white matter lesions and a short lesion in the cervical spinal cord. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Solid foods first, and now liquids too, have become progressively harder for a 58-year-old man to swallow. Which diagnosis should be suspected?

UN8290.stem: Following a stroke, a 68-year-old man can follow commands and clearly understands what is said to him, but his own speech is slow, laboured and reduced to short, fragmented phrases. What type of language disorder does this represent?
A 69-year-old man develops sudden left-sided weakness and appears completely unaware of objects placed on his left side. Which cerebral hemisphere is most likely involved?

Hearing tests are normal for a 3-year-old girl, and she clearly follows instructions and responds appropriately to what people say to her, yet strangers can barely make out a word when she talks. Which area of her development is mainly affected?

A 63-year-old right-handed man is brought to the emergency department by his wife, who noticed at breakfast that the right side of his face had dropped. He understands what is said to him but his speech is halting and effortful, and he cannot find the words he wants. His right arm is markedly weak, while his right leg is only mildly affected. He has no double vision, vertigo or difficulty swallowing. Which arterial territory is most likely to be involved?
A 69-year-old man suddenly cannot get his words out and has weakness in his right arm, with a normal blood glucose. Which finding most strongly points to a cortical rather than peripheral lesion?
Which of these symptoms most specifically points to involvement of the dominant cerebral hemisphere, in a patient with sudden facial weakness, arm weakness and difficulty speaking?
A 69-year-old develops gradually worsening painless jaundice along with weight loss. What diagnosis needs to be excluded?
A 3-year-9-month-old girl cannot yet combine more than two words together and strangers struggle to understand what she is saying, despite a normal hearing test. What should happen next?
UN8290.correct_answer: Arrange formal assessment of her speech and language development

UN8555.presentation: Acute Confusion in Sickle Cell Disease
UN8555.stem: A 9-year-old boy with known sickle cell disease becomes suddenly confused and develops weakness down one side of his body. What complication should be urgently considered?

UN8555.presentation: Migraine With Aura on Combined Hormonal Contraception
UN8555.stem: A woman taking the combined oral contraceptive pill develops new migraine with visual aura and asks whether she can continue taking it. Which concern is particularly relevant?
A woman taking the combined oral contraceptive pill realises she missed ONE pill and is now less than 48 hours late. She has had no other missed pills this cycle. What is the most appropriate advice?
UN8555.correct_answer: Take the missed pill now and continue; no extra precautions

UN8555.stem: A woman taking the combined oral contraceptive pill is started on carbamazepine for epilepsy. Why might her contraception become less reliable?
UN8555.correct_answer: Carbamazepine is an enzyme INDUCER that increases metabolism of the contraceptive hormones, reducing their levels

UN8555.presentation: After cerebral venous sinus thrombosis — safest future contraception
UN8555.stem: A 29-year-old woman is recovering from cerebral venous sinus thrombosis that developed while she was taking the combined oral contraceptive pill. The pill has been stopped and she is on oral anticoagulation. She wants reliable contraception and asks which method carries the least risk for her. According to UK medical eligibility criteria, which method is safest for her?

A 24-year-old woman attends the emergency department with sudden left-sided pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness. She is tachycardic. A CT pulmonary angiogram shows a pulmonary embolus. She does not smoke and has not travelled or had surgery recently. She runs three times a week, takes cetirizine for hay fever, a vitamin D supplement and a combined oral contraceptive pill, and uses an emollient for eczema. Which factor in her history is most relevant to this event?

UN8555.presentation: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis with haemorrhage — anticoagulation
UN8555.stem: A 31-year-old woman taking the combined oral contraceptive pill presents with 4 days of worsening headache and a focal seizure. MR venography confirms thrombosis of the superior sagittal sinus, and there is a small haemorrhagic venous infarct in the left parietal lobe. She is alert with mild right arm weakness. Her platelet count and clotting screen are normal. Which treatment should be started?

UN8555.presentation: Migraine with Aura and Combined Contraception
UN8555.stem: A 28-year-old woman who takes the combined oral contraceptive pill develops migraines preceded by visual zig-zag aura. What is the most appropriate advice regarding her contraception?
UN8555.correct_answer: Stop the combined pill and switch to a progestogen-only method

UN8556.stem: A 35-year-old man wakes with sudden unilateral facial droop. He cannot wrinkle his forehead on the affected side or fully close that eye, and there is no limb weakness or other deficit. What is the diagnosis and key treatment?
UN8556.correct_answer: Bell's palsy — give oral corticosteroids and protect the eye

UN8556.stem:
A 38-year-old man develops sudden severe spinning vertigo with nausea after a recent cold. It has lasted two days. He also reports muffled hearing and ringing in his left ear since the onset, and has never had a similar episode. He has no vascular risk factors, limb weakness, speech disturbance or double vision, and examination shows horizontal nystagmus.

Which diagnosis is most likely?

A 67-year-old man develops sudden left-sided facial droop. On examination he can wrinkle his forehead symmetrically, but the lower half of the left face is weak. He also has mild left arm weakness. What is the most appropriate immediate action?

A 36-year-old woman who smokes and uses a combined hormonal pill for contraception is brought to the emergency department an hour after she suddenly dropped her cup and could not stand. She has weakness of the left arm and leg, a left facial droop and slurred speech. She has no history of migraine, and her capillary blood glucose is normal. What diagnosis must be urgently considered?
A 70-year-old man develops sudden left arm weakness and slurred speech, which completely resolve within 30 minutes. CT brain shows no evidence of infarction. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 63-year-old man develops worsening swallowing difficulty, nasal-sounding speech and proximal limb weakness, with notably reduced tendon reflexes that increase slightly after sustained muscle contraction. Which condition should be considered, particularly given its association with small-cell lung cancer?

UN8556.presentation: Sudden hearing loss with facial droop
UN8556.stem:
A 61-year-old man woke this morning with muffled hearing in his right ear and has noticed that the right corner of his mouth droops when he smiles. He has no ear pain or discharge.

What is the most appropriate action?
UN8556.correct_answer: Immediate ENT assessment, or the stroke pathway if a stroke is suspected

UN8556.stem: A 69-year-old man who smokes and has type 2 diabetes describes an episode this morning in which the vision in his right eye went black, as if a blind had been pulled down, for about ten minutes. His vision then returned to normal. He had no headache, limb weakness or speech disturbance. On examination, visual acuity is 6/6 in both eyes, pupils are normal and fundoscopy is unremarkable. There is a bruit over the right carotid artery. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN8560.stem: Sudden weakness and numbness affecting the right arm and leg, with right facial droop, develop in a 69-year-old woman. Which side of the brain is most likely affected?

A 29-year-old woman with no past medical history comes in febrile, with a pounding headache, increasingly muddled, and has had several fits affecting one side of her body. Which diagnosis needs to be high on the list?

UN8560.presentation: Acute Confusion in Sickle Cell Disease
UN8560.stem: A 9-year-old boy with known sickle cell disease becomes suddenly confused and develops weakness down one side of his body. What complication should be urgently considered?

UN8560.presentation: Bilateral Leg Weakness With Urinary Symptoms
UN8560.stem: New urinary difficulty, numbness around the perineum and worsening weakness and numbness in both legs develop in a 36-year-old woman. What is the most important diagnosis to consider?
A 70-year-old man develops sudden left arm weakness and slurred speech, which completely resolve within 30 minutes. CT brain shows no evidence of infarction. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 7-year-old girl is brought to her GP because her teacher has noticed that she switches off many times a day, sometimes in the middle of a sentence, with her eyelids fluttering. Each episode lasts only seconds, she does not fall, and she carries on with her task straight afterwards with no drowsiness. An episode is triggered in clinic when she is asked to breathe deeply and quickly for a few minutes. What kind of seizure is she most likely having?

A 19-year-old man of Armenian descent has had episodes of fever up to 39.5°C with severe abdominal pain since childhood. Each episode lasts 1 to 3 days and settles without treatment. During one attack he had a laparoscopy, which was normal apart from a small amount of sterile peritoneal fluid. Between attacks he is entirely well and his CRP returns to normal. His parents are first cousins and his younger sister has similar episodes, sometimes with a hot, swollen ankle. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN8560.presentation: Features Of An Upper Motor Neurone Lesion
UN8560.stem: A patient suddenly becomes weak down one side of the body. Of the options given, which examination sign best fits an upper motor neurone cause?

UN8585.stem: A 58-year-old woman develops a tremor, generalised slowness of movement and difficulty starting to walk; her symptoms began predominantly on one side. Which feature is most characteristic of Parkinson's disease?

A 72-year-old man reports progressive slowness of movement over a year. He has an asymmetric resting tremor of the right hand and increasing stiffness, and his handwriting has become smaller. On examination there is cogwheel rigidity, bradykinesia, and a resting tremor that decreases when he reaches for an object. What is the most likely diagnosis?

An older man has a slowly progressive, asymmetrical resting tremor ('pill-rolling'), rigidity (cogwheel) and bradykinesia, with a shuffling gait. He has no early falls and no eye-movement abnormality. What is the most likely diagnosis and most effective symptomatic treatment?
UN8585.correct_answer: Idiopathic Parkinson's disease — levodopa (with a dopa-decarboxylase inhibitor)

UN8585.stem: A 70-year-old man with known Parkinson's disease struggles to start walking and repeatedly freezes when approaching doorways. What term describes this symptom?
A 75-year-old man is found to have a tremor at rest, slowness of movement and increased muscle tone. Which diagnosis is most likely?
A 72-year-old woman with Parkinson's disease has had several unexplained falls because she cannot correct her balance quickly enough when she is pushed off-centre. Which feature best explains this?

A 68-year-old man with known Parkinson's disease finds it hard to get going when he starts walking, and his stride length shortens progressively as he continues. Which cardinal motor sign does this describe?

UN8585.presentation: New Unilateral Tremor in an Older Man
UN8585.stem: A 68-year-old man presents with a new tremor affecting one hand at rest, slowness of movement and reduced arm swing while walking. Which diagnosis best fits this presentation?

UN8586.stem: A young adult has a movement disorder (tremor and dystonia), personality change and deranged liver function. Slit-lamp examination shows brown rings at the corneal margin. What is the most appropriate diagnostic test?

A 70-year-old man who still volunteers at a charity shop has, over three years, become unable to remember the names of new colleagues or what he did the day before, and he now gets muddled when giving change at the till. Neurological examination shows no tremor, rigidity, involuntary movements or focal deficit. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
A young man started on an antipsychotic a day ago develops a sustained involuntary upward deviation of the eyes and neck spasm. He is distressed but alert. What is the most appropriate treatment?
On examination, a patient is noted to have involuntary, rhythmic back-and-forth movement of both eyes. What is this finding called?

UN8586.presentation: Tingling and Spasms After Neck Surgery
UN8586.stem: A day after undergoing a total thyroidectomy for a large multinodular goitre, a patient develops tingling around her mouth and fingers along with involuntary muscle spasms. Blood tests show a low serum calcium. What is the most likely cause?

A young man started on an antipsychotic (or an antiemetic such as metoclopramide) a day ago develops a sustained, distressing upward deviation of the eyes and abnormal neck posturing. He is alert. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
UN8586.correct_answer: An anticholinergic such as IV or IM procyclidine

UN8586.stem: A 75-year-old man is found to have a tremor at rest, slowness of movement and increased muscle tone. Which diagnosis is most likely?
A woman at 39 weeks' gestation describes a sudden gush of clear watery fluid from the vagina, with no contractions yet. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN8587.presentation: Essential tremor refractory to first-line drugs — next step
UN8587.stem: A 66-year-old woman has had essential tremor for ten years. Despite propranolol at the highest dose she tolerates, and a trial of primidone that did not help, her tremor now stops her writing, using a cup or feeding herself. She has no rigidity, bradykinesia or rest tremor. She is seen by her GP. What is the most appropriate next step?
UN8587.correct_answer: Refer to neurology for specialist options

UN8587.presentation: Essential tremor — first investigation in primary care
UN8587.stem: A 45-year-old man sees his GP with a 6-month history of a bilateral tremor of the hands that is worse when holding a cup or writing. His father had a similar tremor. He has no rigidity or bradykinesia and no other neurological signs. He drinks within recommended limits and takes no regular medicines. Which investigation is most appropriate to request first?

A patient has a bilateral, symmetrical tremor of the hands that is present on maintaining a posture and on action (e.g. holding a cup or writing), improves after a small amount of alcohol, and there is a family history. There is no bradykinesia or rigidity. What is the most likely diagnosis and first-line treatment?

UN8587.presentation: Tremor That Appears Only With Action
UN8587.stem: A 60-year-old retired teacher notices both her hands shake noticeably when she holds a cup of tea or tries to write, but the shaking disappears completely when her hands are resting in her lap. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN8587.presentation: Tremor not clinically separable from parkinsonism — imaging
UN8587.stem: A 68-year-old man is seen in the neurology clinic with a two-year history of tremor in both hands when holding objects. On examination there is also a slight tremor of the right hand at rest, and arm swing may be mildly reduced on the right, but there is no clear bradykinesia or rigidity. The neurologist cannot confidently distinguish essential tremor from early parkinsonism on clinical grounds. Which investigation should be considered?
Writing or holding a cup of tea makes a 49-year-old man's tremor most apparent, and the rest of his neurological exam is unremarkable. Which diagnosis is most likely?

UN8587.presentation: Essential tremor — drug choice when propranolol is contraindicated
UN8587.stem: A 52-year-old woman has essential tremor diagnosed by her GP. The tremor now makes it hard for her to write and drink from a cup, and she would like medication. She has asthma treated with an inhaled corticosteroid and a reliever inhaler, and has needed oral steroids for an exacerbation in the last year. Thyroid function is normal. Which drug is most appropriate to offer?

A 72-year-old man reports progressive slowness of movement over a year. He has an asymmetric resting tremor of the right hand and increasing stiffness, and his handwriting has become smaller. On examination there is cogwheel rigidity, bradykinesia, and a resting tremor that decreases when he reaches for an object. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN8588.presentation: Intention Tremor and an Unsteady Gait
UN8588.stem: A patient has a tremor that worsens as the hand approaches a target, overshoots when reaching for objects, and a wide-based, unsteady gait. Which neurological structure is most likely affected?

A 35-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by a friend, who found an empty strip of his prescribed diazepam tablets beside him an hour ago. No alcohol or other drugs are thought to be involved.

Which combination of findings is he most likely to show?
UN8588.correct_answer: Drowsiness, slurred speech and unsteady gait

UN8588.stem: A 55-year-old man presents with an unsteady, broad-based gait and a tremor that worsens as his finger approaches his nose on examination. Which part of the nervous system is most likely affected?

A 45-year-old woman with bipolar disorder, stable on lithium for several years, attends the emergency department after four days of vomiting and watery diarrhoea. She now has a coarse tremor, slurred speech and an unsteady gait. Which mechanism best explains her current presentation?
UN8588.correct_answer: Fluid and sodium loss have reduced renal lithium clearance, raising the level

UN8588.presentation: Sudden Vertigo With Inability to Stand
UN8588.stem: A 59-year-old man develops sudden severe vertigo, is unable to stand or walk unsupported, and is found to have limb incoordination and nystagmus on examination. Which neurological structure should be particularly suspected?

A patient has an unsteady, broad-based gait with slurred ('scanning') speech, nystagmus, an intention tremor, past-pointing and difficulty with rapid alternating movements (dysdiadochokinesia). Where does this localise?

A 50-year-old man with chronic alcohol dependence is brought in confused, with unsteady gait and abnormal eye movements (ophthalmoplegia and nystagmus). What is the most appropriate immediate management?

A 79-year-old woman living alone is admitted after a fall at home. She takes several regular medicines and has noticeably unsteady gait. Which intervention is most likely to reduce her future risk of falls?
UN8588.correct_answer: Multifactorial falls assessment with medication review

UN8595.presentation: Myasthenia gravis — next test when acetylcholine receptor antibodies are negative
UN8595.stem: A 34-year-old woman is seen in the neurology clinic with a 3-month history of drooping eyelids, double vision and difficulty swallowing, all worse towards the end of the day. She also has fatigable neck weakness. Pupils, reflexes and sensation are normal. Serum acetylcholine receptor antibodies are negative. Which blood test should be requested next?

A 47-year-old woman with generalised myasthenia gravis, controlled on pyridostigmine, is admitted with acute pyelonephritis. She has no drug allergies and her kidney function is normal. Before choosing an intravenous antibiotic, the FY1 doctor checks for interactions with her myasthenia. Which antibiotic is contraindicated in her?

UN8595.presentation: Newly diagnosed myasthenia gravis — thymus imaging
UN8595.stem: A 34-year-old woman is newly diagnosed with generalised myasthenia gravis. Her acetylcholine receptor antibodies are positive and she has started pyridostigmine in the neurology clinic. Which imaging should be arranged next?

UN8595.presentation: Crossed Cranial Nerve And Limb Signs
UN8595.stem: A 59-year-old woman suddenly develops double vision, difficulty swallowing and weakness of her right arm and leg together. Which anatomical site could explain this combination of cranial nerve and limb findings?

A 35-year-old woman has intermittent drooping of the left eyelid that worsens through the day and with sustained upgaze, along with intermittent double vision. Her symptoms improve after a period of rest. The pupils are normal and the rest of the neurological examination is unremarkable. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A patient has slowly progressive limb weakness, visible muscle wasting and spontaneous twitching of the affected muscles, with reduced reflexes in those muscle groups. What type of lesion best fits these findings?
A 66-year-old woman suddenly cannot find her words and develops weakness of her right arm, though she remains alert. Which cerebral hemisphere is most likely affected?

A 31-year-old man is referred to the emergency department by his optometrist. For a month his eyelids have drooped more as each day goes on, and by the evening he sees double while watching television. His jaw tires when he chews tough food. He feels much better on waking. His pupils are normal and his tendon reflexes are preserved. What is the likeliest diagnosis?

UN8596.stem: A 64-year-old man has slowly worsening numbness and tingling that began in his feet and has spread upward, with diminished ankle reflexes. Which pattern is most consistent with a peripheral neuropathy?

A 55-year-old woman with pernicious anaemia stopped attending for her vitamin B12 injections two years ago. She now reports tingling in both feet and feeling unsteady when walking in the dark. On examination, vibration sense and joint position sense are reduced in both feet, ankle reflexes are absent and both plantar responses are extensor. Romberg's test is positive. Which condition is most likely?
UN8596.correct_answer: Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord

UN8596.presentation: Vitamin B12 Deficiency — Reversible Cognitive Impairment
UN8596.stem: A 78-year-old vegetarian woman has a few months of worsening memory, low mood and unsteadiness. Examination shows reduced vibration and proprioception in the feet with absent ankle reflexes. Blood tests show a macrocytic anaemia. Which reversible cause should be excluded?

UN8596.presentation: Subacute combined degeneration of the cord
UN8596.stem: A 58-year-old woman with vitiligo and hypothyroidism has had numb feet for several months and now falls when walking in the dark. She has reduced vibration and joint position sense in the feet, a positive Romberg test, absent ankle reflexes and extensor plantar responses. Her full blood count shows a macrocytic anaemia, her serum B12 is low and her folate is also low. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
UN8596.correct_answer: Intramuscular hydroxocobalamin first, adding folic acid once B12 replacement has started

UN8596.stem: A 59-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes for 15 years attends her annual diabetes foot check. She says both feet tingle and feel numb, as though she is walking on cotton wool, and are worse at night. Ankle reflexes are absent on both sides and she cannot feel the monofilament on either sole. Muscle power in her legs is normal. Which pattern of nerve damage best fits?

A patient with type 2 diabetes has painful, burning, symmetrical numbness and tingling in both feet (a glove-and-stocking distribution) that disturbs sleep. Glycaemic control has been optimised. He also has coexisting low mood. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment for the neuropathic pain?

A 45-year-old woman with vitiligo and hypothyroidism tells her GP she has had pins and needles in both feet and hands for several months, along with tiredness and a sore, smooth red tongue. Her blood count shows a raised mean cell volume and her vitamin B12 level is low. Which examination finding is most likely?
UN8596.correct_answer: Reduced vibration sense in the feet with absent ankle jerks

UN8596.stem: A 36-year-old man attends the emergency department because over five days he has found it increasingly difficult to climb stairs, and now his grip is weak too. He has tingling in both feet. Three weeks ago he had a bout of food poisoning after a barbecue. His knee and ankle reflexes cannot be elicited, and there is no sensory level on the trunk. What is the likeliest diagnosis?

UN8801.stem: Following a stroke, a 68-year-old man can follow commands and clearly understands what is said to him, but his own speech is slow, laboured and reduced to short, fragmented phrases. What type of language disorder does this represent?

A 72-year-old right-handed woman is admitted to the stroke unit. Her speech is slow, halting and effortful, with only a few words in each sentence, and she is visibly frustrated by it. She correctly follows instructions such as 'point to the window, then touch your nose'. Her right face and right arm are weak. Where is the lesion most likely to be?
Which of these symptoms most specifically points to involvement of the dominant cerebral hemisphere, in a patient with sudden facial weakness, arm weakness and difficulty speaking?

A 68-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 90 minutes after sudden onset right-sided weakness and facial droop. Examination confirms dense right hemiparesis and expressive aphasia. A CT head scan shows no evidence of intracranial haemorrhage. What is the most appropriate next step?
A 66-year-old woman suddenly cannot find her words and develops weakness of her right arm, though she remains alert. Which cerebral hemisphere is most likely affected?

A 63-year-old right-handed man is brought to the emergency department by his wife, who noticed at breakfast that the right side of his face had dropped. He understands what is said to him but his speech is halting and effortful, and he cannot find the words he wants. His right arm is markedly weak, while his right leg is only mildly affected. He has no double vision, vertigo or difficulty swallowing. Which arterial territory is most likely to be involved?
A 69-year-old man suddenly cannot get his words out and has weakness in his right arm, with a normal blood glucose. Which finding most strongly points to a cortical rather than peripheral lesion?

Hearing tests are normal for a 3-year-old girl, and she clearly follows instructions and responds appropriately to what people say to her, yet strangers can barely make out a word when she talks. Which area of her development is mainly affected?

UN8815.presentation: Red-Flag Feature of a Parotid Lump
UN8815.stem: A 63-year-old man has a slowly enlarging, painless lump in his parotid gland that he has noticed for several months. Which associated feature would be particularly concerning for malignancy?
UN8815.correct_answer: New weakness of the muscles on that side of the face

UN8815.stem: A 45-year-old office worker has recurrent headaches most afternoons, described as a dull, band-like pressure across both sides of her head. She has no vomiting, no visual disturbance and no focal weakness. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 45-year-old woman presents to ED with a sudden-onset, severe "thunderclap" headache that reached maximum intensity within seconds. She vomited once. She is now pain-free but feels tired. CT head is performed 8 hours after the onset and is reported as normal. What is the most appropriate next step to exclude subarachnoid haemorrhage?
UN8815.correct_answer: Perform a lumbar puncture (LP) 12 hours after headache onset

UN8815.stem: A 45-year-old man suddenly develops the worst headache of his life, reaching maximum intensity within seconds, followed by neck stiffness and photophobia. Which feature most strongly supports a diagnosis of subarachnoid haemorrhage?
UN8815.correct_answer: Meningism developing after a thunderclap-onset headache

UN8815.stem: A 48-year-old woman presents with a sudden, severe occipital headache that reached maximum intensity within seconds while exercising, with neck stiffness and vomiting. A CT head performed 3 hours after onset is reported as normal. What is the most appropriate next step?
UN8815.correct_answer: Lumbar puncture at least 12 hours after headache onset

UN8815.stem: A 26-year-old man has recurrent, sudden episodes of intense fear with palpitations, sweating, trembling and a sense of impending doom, each peaking within a few minutes. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN8815.presentation: Transient visual obscurations — symptom of papilloedema
UN8815.stem:
A 19-year-old university student who is overweight has had headaches most days for two months. When she bends to pick up books from the floor and then straightens up, the sight in both eyes goes dark for a couple of seconds and then comes back completely. She sees no zigzag lines or flashing lights and has no floaters. Her blood pressure does not fall when she stands, and her visual acuity is normal.

What is the most likely explanation for these episodes?
Watering of the eye and nasal blockage on the same side accompany repeated attacks of intense one-sided eye pain in a 41-year-old man. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN8818.stem: A 19-year-old woman collapses in a shopping centre. Her friend says she suddenly went stiff and cried out, then all four limbs jerked for about two minutes. She bit the side of her tongue and was incontinent of urine. Paramedics find her drowsy and disorientated for around twenty minutes before she gradually returns to normal. Her capillary glucose is normal. Which diagnosis best explains this event?

UN8818.presentation: Prolonged convulsive seizure in a child
UN8818.stem:
A 7-year-old boy with epilepsy is brought into the emergency department by ambulance. His teacher saw him collapse with stiffening and rhythmic jerking of all four limbs about 15 minutes ago, and he has been jerking continuously since then without waking. No individual emergency care plan is available. High-flow oxygen is being given and intravenous access has just been obtained.

What is the most appropriate immediate management?
UN8818.correct_answer: IV lorazepam, following the status epilepticus pathway

UN8818.stem: A 25-year-old woman has a first generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting about 90 seconds, witnessed by her partner, with full recovery afterwards. She has a family history of epilepsy. Neurological examination and capillary glucose are normal, and there is no head injury. What is the most appropriate next step?

UN8818.presentation: Seizure with fever in a toddler
UN8818.stem:
An 18-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department after her mother saw her go stiff and then shake all four limbs while unresponsive for about two minutes. She has had ear pain and a high temperature since yesterday. Thirty minutes later she is playing, alert and has a normal neurological examination with no rash or neck stiffness.

Which diagnosis is most likely?

A 26-year-old man with known epilepsy has a generalised tonic–clonic seizure in the emergency department waiting room. The jerking stops briefly, but before he opens his eyes or responds to voice, a second convulsion begins. Staff place him on his side and give oxygen, and his capillary glucose is normal.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
A 28-year-old man has his first generalised tonic-clonic seizure. He holds an ordinary (Group 1) driving licence. What is the correct advice regarding driving?
UN8818.correct_answer: He must stop driving and notify the DVLA, with a minimum 6-month ban

UN8818.stem: A patient in the emergency department has been having a generalised tonic-clonic seizure continuously for 6 minutes. Intravenous access is in place, airway is being supported and oxygen given, and a capillary glucose is normal. What is the most appropriate first-line drug?
A patient has been having a continuous generalised tonic-clonic seizure for 6 minutes. Airway and oxygen are being managed and glucose is normal. What is the most appropriate first-line drug?
UN8818.correct_answer: IV lorazepam (or buccal midazolam/rectal diazepam if no access)

UN8820.stem: A 25-year-old woman has a first generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting about 90 seconds, witnessed by her partner, with full recovery afterwards. She has a family history of epilepsy. Neurological examination and capillary glucose are normal, and there is no head injury. What is the most appropriate next step?

A 2-year-6-month-old boy is brought to the paediatric emergency department after a generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting 3 minutes during a febrile illness. He had one similar brief febrile seizure at 20 months and has no other neurological history. He recovered fully within 10 minutes. His temperature is 38.9°C and the left tympanic membrane is red and bulging. On review by the paediatric registrar he is alert and playing, with no signs of meningitis and a normal neurological examination. His parents feel confident to care for him at home. What is the most appropriate management?
UN8820.correct_answer: Observe for 1–2 hours and discharge with safety-netting

UN8820.stem: A 37-year-old electrician collapsed at work, and colleagues describe about a minute of rhythmic jerking of all his limbs followed by a period of confusion. He had slept normally, drinks little alcohol and takes no regular medicines. At the first seizure clinic his examination is normal, and both his brain MRI and EEG show no abnormality. There is no family history of epilepsy. Which management is best?
UN8820.correct_answer: Give safety and driving advice without starting antiseizure medication

UN8820.stem: A 70-year-old man had a 20-minute episode of right arm weakness and slurred speech yesterday, now fully resolved. He is not already on an anticoagulant. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
UN8820.correct_answer: Give aspirin and refer for specialist assessment within 24 hours

UN8820.stem:
An 18-month-old boy is found by his father shaking all four limbs and unresponsive while unwell with a high temperature and a runny nose. The shaking was still going on when the ambulance crew arrived about twenty minutes later, and it stopped only after the crew gave buccal midazolam. He is now drowsy but rousable, his temperature is 39°C and there is no neck stiffness or rash. This was his first seizure.

What is the most appropriate next step?
UN8820.correct_answer: Admit to hospital for immediate assessment by a paediatrician

UN8820.stem: A 35-year-old lorry driver is diagnosed with epilepsy following a first seizure. He states he will not inform the DVLA and will continue driving. The doctor is concerned about public safety. What is the most appropriate action?
UN8820.correct_answer: Explain his legal duty to tell the DVLA; if he continues to drive, inform the DVLA

UN8820.stem: A 47-year-old taxi driver was seen in the first seizure clinic last month after an unprovoked generalised seizure. He was told not to drive and to inform the DVLA. At a follow-up appointment he admits he is still working shifts in his taxi and says he will not tell the DVLA because he would lose his income. You have explained the risks to him again but he will not change his mind. What is the most appropriate action?
UN8820.correct_answer: Tell him you will inform the DVLA, then disclose the relevant information to them

UN8820.stem: A 28-year-old man has his first generalised tonic-clonic seizure. He holds an ordinary (Group 1) driving licence. What is the correct advice regarding driving?
UN8820.correct_answer: He must stop driving and notify the DVLA, with a minimum 6-month ban

UN8821.stem: A 34-year-old man's wife describes episodes that occur a few times a month. He first says he has a strange rising feeling in his stomach, then stares blankly, does not respond to her, chews repeatedly and fiddles with his shirt buttons. Each episode lasts around ninety seconds, after which he is muddled for a short time and cannot remember what happened. He has never fallen or jerked. Which seizure type best describes these episodes?

UN8821.presentation: Epilepsy — Drug Choice by Seizure Type
UN8821.stem: A 30-year-old man with newly diagnosed focal epilepsy needs a first-line antiepileptic. He has no contraindications. Which is an appropriate first-line choice for focal seizures?

A 23-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after her flatmate found her beside several empty boxes of amitriptyline. She is drowsy and agitated, with dry flushed skin and dilated pupils. Her pulse is 128/min and her blood pressure is low. Her ECG shows a sinus tachycardia with a broad QRS complex, and shortly after arrival she has a brief generalised seizure. Her airway is being managed. What is the most appropriate specific treatment?

UN8821.presentation: New Fluctuating Confusion After a Medication Change
UN8821.stem: A 75-year-old man becomes agitated and confused shortly after starting a new medication. He has no focal neurological signs, and his level of confusion seems to come and go throughout the day. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 35-year-old man started on an antipsychotic two weeks ago complains of an unbearable inner restlessness and a compulsion to keep moving. He paces constantly and cannot sit still, and finds it deeply distressing. There are no abnormal involuntary movements at rest. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 30-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of sudden breathlessness with audible inspiratory noise from the throat. Episodes start and stop abruptly, her oxygen saturations stay normal throughout, and trials of high-dose inhaled and oral steroids have not helped. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 70-year-old man who still volunteers at a charity shop has, over three years, become unable to remember the names of new colleagues or what he did the day before, and he now gets muddled when giving change at the till. Neurological examination shows no tremor, rigidity, involuntary movements or focal deficit. Which is the most likely diagnosis?

UN8821.presentation: Huntington disease — drug for troublesome chorea
UN8821.stem: A 46-year-old man with genetically confirmed Huntington disease is seen in the neurology clinic. Over the past year his involuntary movements have become worse, and he now spills drinks and has fallen twice. His mood is good, he has no history of depression and he has no suicidal thoughts. Liver function is normal. The team decides to start medication for his chorea. Which drug is most appropriate?

UN8823.presentation: Acute Confusion in Sickle Cell Disease
UN8823.stem: A 9-year-old boy with known sickle cell disease becomes suddenly confused and develops weakness down one side of his body. What complication should be urgently considered?

A patient treated for anaphylaxis after a wasp sting appears to recover fully, but several hours later develops recurrent wheeze and hypotension without any further sting or allergen exposure. What is this phenomenon called?

A 29-year-old woman with no past medical history comes in febrile, with a pounding headache, increasingly muddled, and has had several fits affecting one side of her body. Which diagnosis needs to be high on the list?

A 38-year-old woman develops weakness affecting the entire left side of her face, including being unable to close her left eye and losing movement of her forehead on that side. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A patient has an acute facial (lower motor neurone) weakness on one side, together with a painful vesicular rash in and around the ear and ear canal on the same side, with some altered taste and hearing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
UN8823.correct_answer: Ramsay Hunt syndrome (geniculate ganglion herpes zoster)

UN8823.presentation: Features Of An Upper Motor Neurone Lesion
UN8823.stem: A patient suddenly becomes weak down one side of the body. Of the options given, which examination sign best fits an upper motor neurone cause?

A 26-year-old woman develops progressive difficulty walking upstairs over several days, two weeks after an episode of diarrhoea. On examination she has symmetrical weakness in both legs with absent reflexes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A 47-year-old man with chronic alcohol dependence has ongoing memory gaps that he unknowingly fills with invented stories, without any intention to deceive. What is this phenomenon called?

UN8824.presentation: Fluent Speech That Makes No Sense
UN8824.stem: A patient speaks in long, grammatically fluent sentences after a stroke, but the content is largely nonsensical, and he appears not to understand simple instructions given to him. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Which of these symptoms most specifically points to involvement of the dominant cerebral hemisphere, in a patient with sudden facial weakness, arm weakness and difficulty speaking?

A 66-year-old right-handed woman is brought to the emergency department 40 minutes after her husband noticed her face drooping on the left and that she could not lift her left arm. She also reports reduced feeling in the left hand. She speaks fluently and follows commands correctly. Where is the lesion most likely to be?

Following a stroke, a 68-year-old man can follow commands and clearly understands what is said to him, but his own speech is slow, laboured and reduced to short, fragmented phrases. What type of language disorder does this represent?
A 3-year-9-month-old girl cannot yet combine more than two words together and strangers struggle to understand what she is saying, despite a normal hearing test. What should happen next?
UN8824.correct_answer: Arrange formal assessment of her speech and language development

UN8824.stem: A 66-year-old woman suddenly cannot find her words and develops weakness of her right arm, though she remains alert. Which cerebral hemisphere is most likely affected?
A 69-year-old man suddenly cannot get his words out and has weakness in his right arm, with a normal blood glucose. Which finding most strongly points to a cortical rather than peripheral lesion?

UN8824.presentation: New behaviour that challenges in a non-speaking autistic child — first step
UN8824.stem: A 9-year-old autistic boy who does not use spoken language is brought to his GP by his mother. Over the past 2 weeks he has started hitting the right side of his face and banging his head. He is eating less and is waking at night. There have been no changes at home or school. What is the most appropriate next step?
UN8824.correct_answer: Look for a physical cause such as dental pain

UN8825.presentation: Coughing on Swallowing After a Stroke
UN8825.stem: Two days after an ischaemic stroke, a patient coughs repeatedly every time they are given water to drink. What complication should be suspected?

Care home staff ask the visiting GP about an 82-year-old woman with advanced Alzheimer's disease. At mealtimes she holds food in her mouth for long periods, coughs while eating and drinking, and her voice sounds wet afterwards. Her weight is stable and she is not currently unwell. Which complication is she most at risk of?

A patient with a recent stroke and impaired swallowing develops a pneumonia, with consolidation seen in the right lower lobe. What is the most likely type of pneumonia and an important management consideration?
UN8825.correct_answer: Aspiration pneumonia — antibiotics and a swallow assessment

UN8825.stem: A 69-year-old man with motor neurone disease attends the neurology clinic with his wife. She says that over recent weeks he splutters when drinking tea and that his voice becomes gurgly afterwards. His speech has also become slurred. He has no limb swelling, ear pain, loin pain or headache. Which complication is he most at risk of?

UN8825.presentation: Progressive Swallowing Difficulty in an Older Smoker
UN8825.stem: A 68-year-old man with a 40-pack-year smoking history and regular heavy alcohol intake reports three months of worsening difficulty swallowing solid food and unintentional weight loss of 6 kg. What serious diagnosis must be excluded?

A 70-year-old man reports gradually worsening difficulty swallowing solids over two months and is found on blood tests to have unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia. Endoscopy identifies an irregular, ulcerated lesion in the mid-oesophagus. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A man with untreated HIV (CD4 count 90 cells/µL) has progressive pain on swallowing (odynophagia) and difficulty swallowing. Examination shows white plaques on the oral mucosa that scrape off. What is the most likely cause of his swallowing symptoms?

UN8825.presentation: Migraine With Aura on Combined Hormonal Contraception
UN8825.stem: A woman taking the combined oral contraceptive pill develops new migraine with visual aura and asks whether she can continue taking it. Which concern is particularly relevant?

UN8826.stem: A 55-year-old man presents with an unsteady, broad-based gait and a tremor that worsens as his finger approaches his nose on examination. Which part of the nervous system is most likely affected?
A 70-year-old man develops sudden left arm weakness and slurred speech, which completely resolve within 30 minutes. CT brain shows no evidence of infarction. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN8826.presentation: Sudden Vertigo With Inability to Stand
UN8826.stem: A 59-year-old man develops sudden severe vertigo, is unable to stand or walk unsupported, and is found to have limb incoordination and nystagmus on examination. Which neurological structure should be particularly suspected?

A 52-year-old woman with bipolar disorder on long-term lithium develops a diarrhoeal illness. Over two days she becomes drowsy with a coarse tremor, slurred speech and unsteadiness. She was recently started on a thiazide diuretic for hypertension. Her lithium level is 2.1 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate management?
UN8826.correct_answer: Stop lithium, give IV fluids and check renal function and lithium level

UN8826.stem: A 69-year-old man develops sudden left-sided weakness and appears completely unaware of objects placed on his left side. Which cerebral hemisphere is most likely involved?
Out of nowhere, a 73-year-old man becomes severely dizzy, starts vomiting, loses his coordination and his speech turns slurred. What is the critical diagnosis that must not be missed?

Friends bring a 24-year-old man to the emergency department after he took several alprazolam tablets bought online. He is slumped in a wheelchair and slurring his words. Which pattern is most typical of this type of drug toxicity?
UN8826.correct_answer: Sedation with slurred speech and unsteadiness, often with near-normal vital signs

UN8826.presentation: Hearing and Balance Problems on an Antibiotic
UN8826.stem: A patient receiving intravenous gentamicin for a severe infection develops tinnitus, reduced hearing and unsteadiness while walking. Which adverse effect of this drug class is responsible?

UN8839.stem: A patient with known metastatic prostate cancer develops progressively worsening back pain (worse on lying flat and coughing), then bilateral leg weakness, a sensory level on the trunk, and difficulty passing urine. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

A 61-year-old man with prostate cancer that has spread to bone phones the acute oncology service. For two days he has had a band-like pain around his chest, his legs feel heavy and unsteady, and he is struggling to pass urine. On arrival at hospital he has brisk knee reflexes and reduced sensation below the level of his umbilicus. Which diagnosis must be urgently considered?

UN8839.presentation: Metastatic spinal cord compression — co-prescribing with dexamethasone
UN8839.stem: A 66-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer attends the emergency department with severe thoracic back pain and new weakness of both legs. Metastatic spinal cord compression is suspected, the oncology team's MSCC coordinator has been contacted and an MRI scan of the whole spine is booked. High-dose oral dexamethasone is prescribed. He has no history of diabetes or peptic ulcer disease. Which medicine should be co-prescribed with the dexamethasone?

UN8839.presentation: Bilateral Leg Weakness With Urinary Symptoms
UN8839.stem: New urinary difficulty, numbness around the perineum and worsening weakness and numbness in both legs develop in a 36-year-old woman. What is the most important diagnosis to consider?

UN8839.presentation: Metastatic spinal cord compression — immobilisation while awaiting MRI
UN8839.stem: A 58-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer is assessed in the emergency department. She has severe mid-thoracic back pain that is much worse when she moves or coughs, and new weakness of both legs with brisk reflexes. Metastatic spinal cord compression is suspected. Dexamethasone has been given, the MSCC coordinator has been contacted and an MRI scan of the whole spine is planned for later today. How should she be positioned while awaiting the MRI scan?
UN8839.correct_answer: Nurse lying flat or with partial elevation

UN8839.stem: A 69-year-old ex-smoker with lung cancer is admitted to a hospice for symptom control. The nursing team report that his upper back pain has become much more severe over a few days and he now needs help to stand because his legs have become weak. What diagnosis must be considered urgently?

UN8839.presentation: Pressure ulcer prevention in spinal cord injury
UN8839.stem: A 58-year-old man with a complete thoracic spinal cord injury is admitted to a rehabilitation ward. He has no sensation below the level of his umbilicus and is intermittently incontinent of urine and faeces. Which plan best protects his skin?
UN8839.correct_answer: Frequent skin inspection, scheduled repositioning and a high-specification pressure-redistributing mattress

UN8839.stem: A 66-year-old woman with known metastatic breast cancer rings the acute oncology helpline. For a week she has had worsening pain in the middle of her back that wakes her at night and wraps around her chest like a band. Since yesterday her legs have felt heavy and she has stumbled twice at home. Which diagnosis must be urgently excluded?

UN8846.stem: A 26-year-old woman develops progressive difficulty walking upstairs over several days, two weeks after an episode of diarrhoea. On examination she has symmetrical weakness in both legs with absent reflexes. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 30-year-old man develops progressive, symmetrical ascending leg weakness over 5 days, 2 weeks after a diarrhoeal illness. Reflexes are absent. CSF shows raised protein with a normal cell count. What is the most appropriate treatment, alongside monitoring of respiratory function?

A 45-year-old man presents with progressive ascending weakness of both legs over 4 days, now reaching the lower trunk. There is areflexia, and he had a diarrhoeal illness 2 weeks ago. Sensation is intact. Which investigation will best confirm the diagnosis?
A 52-year-old man with Guillain-Barré syndrome has weakness that is now extending to his arms. He is admitted for close monitoring. Which parameter best predicts impending respiratory failure?

A 45-year-old woman presents with a 3-day history of ascending symmetrical weakness starting in her feet. She now has difficulty standing and has mild facial weakness. Her deep tendon reflexes are absent. She has no respiratory distress, but you perform spirometry. The forced vital capacity (FVC) is 1.2 L (predicted normal 3.2 L). What is the single most appropriate immediate next step?
UN8846.correct_answer: Urgent ITU/HDU referral for monitoring and preparation for potential ventilatory support

UN8846.stem: A 25-year-old man develops ascending weakness over a week, starting in his legs, with loss of reflexes and mild distal numbness. He had diarrhoea three weeks ago. What is the most important investigation to monitor in the acute phase?

UN8846.presentation: Bilateral Leg Weakness With Urinary Symptoms
UN8846.stem: New urinary difficulty, numbness around the perineum and worsening weakness and numbness in both legs develop in a 36-year-old woman. What is the most important diagnosis to consider?

A 46-year-old woman is admitted with 5 days of tingling in her feet and increasing weakness, first in her legs and now in her arms. She had a flu-like illness 10 days ago. She now needs a walking frame. Reflexes are absent in all four limbs and she has mild bilateral facial weakness. Forced vital capacity is being monitored and is currently stable. Lumbar puncture shows a raised protein with a normal white cell count. What is the most appropriate treatment?

UN8875.stem: Which of these symptoms most specifically points to involvement of the dominant cerebral hemisphere, in a patient with sudden facial weakness, arm weakness and difficulty speaking?

On examination he has a right hemiparesis and dysarthria. Blood pressure is 180/95 mmHg and capillary glucose is normal. He takes no anticoagulants. What is the most appropriate immediate next step?

A 36-year-old woman who smokes and uses a combined hormonal pill for contraception is brought to the emergency department an hour after she suddenly dropped her cup and could not stand. She has weakness of the left arm and leg, a left facial droop and slurred speech. She has no history of migraine, and her capillary blood glucose is normal. What diagnosis must be urgently considered?

A 73-year-old man develops sudden severe dyspnoea and chest pain three days after a myocardial infarction. Examination reveals a new pansystolic murmur loudest at the apex and widespread pulmonary crackles. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 67-year-old man develops sudden left-sided facial droop. On examination he can wrinkle his forehead symmetrically, but the lower half of the left face is weak. He also has mild left arm weakness. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
Sudden weakness and numbness affecting the right arm and leg, with right facial droop, develop in a 69-year-old woman. Which side of the brain is most likely affected?

A 68-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 90 minutes after sudden onset right-sided weakness and facial droop. Examination confirms dense right hemiparesis and expressive aphasia. A CT head scan shows no evidence of intracranial haemorrhage. What is the most appropriate next step?

A 58-year-old woman develops sudden severe breathlessness, pleuritic chest pain, a rapid heart rate and a low blood pressure shortly after a long-haul flight. Which complication of pulmonary embolism is particularly concerning in this presentation?

UN8879.stem: Sudden weakness and numbness affecting the right arm and leg, with right facial droop, develop in a 69-year-old woman. Which side of the brain is most likely affected?

UN8879.presentation: Facial Weakness Affecting the Whole Side of the Face
UN8879.stem: A patient develops sudden weakness of the entire left side of the face, including the inability to raise the left eyebrow or fully close the left eye. What type of facial nerve lesion does this represent?
UN8879.correct_answer: Lower motor neurone facial nerve palsy

A 23-year-old woman develops sudden weakness of her right leg the day after a distressing argument. Examination shows give-way weakness, a positive Hoover's sign, and normal reflexes and tone. MRI of the brain and spine is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

On examination she has weakness of the left face and arm, ignores objects on her left side, and has a slightly drooping right upper eyelid with a smaller right pupil. His temperature is 38.4°C, Glasgow Coma Scale score is 14 and there is mild right arm and leg weakness. A brain abscess is suspected and blood cultures have been taken. Which investigation should be performed next?
UN8968.correct_answer: Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI of the brain

UN8968.correct_answer: Arrange an immediate non-contrast CT head as part of urgent stroke team assessment

UN8969.presentation: Acute ischaemic stroke within the thrombolysis window
UN8969.stem: A 66-year-old woman suddenly develops left facial droop, left arm weakness and slurred speech while shopping at 10:15. She arrives in the emergency department at 11:30. She ignores her left side and has a moderately severe deficit on stroke scoring. She takes no anticoagulants. Blood glucose is normal and blood pressure is 172/94 mmHg. Non-contrast CT head shows no haemorrhage. What is the most appropriate management?
UN8969.correct_answer: IV thrombolysis and CT angiography to assess for thrombectomy

Paramedics attend a 66-year-old woman with long-standing poorly controlled hypertension who felt a sudden tearing pain between her shoulder blades. Paramedics bring a 79-year-old man with type 2 diabetes treated with gliclazide into the emergency department after his daughter found him with left-sided weakness and slurred speech. He has been off his food with a chest infection. On arrival his capillary glucose is very low. Within ten minutes of intravenous glucose, his speech and arm strength return completely to normal. What is the most likely explanation?
UN8969.correct_answer: Focal neurological deficit due to hypoglycaemia

UN9089.correct_answer: Idiopathic Parkinson's disease — levodopa (with a dopa-decarboxylase inhibitor)

UN9089.stem: A 58-year-old woman develops a tremor, generalised slowness of movement and difficulty starting to walk; her symptoms began predominantly on one side. Which feature is most characteristic of Parkinson's disease?

A 75-year-old man is found to have a tremor at rest, slowness of movement and increased muscle tone. Which diagnosis is most likely?

UN9089.presentation: New Unilateral Tremor in an Older Man

The neurologist cannot confidently distinguish essential tremor from early parkinsonism on clinical grounds. Which investigation should be considered?
