A 35-year-old woman with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis develops acute weakness and numbness of both legs over 2 days, impairing her walking. MRI shows a new gadolinium-enhancing lesion in the spinal cord. She is afebrile with no evidence of infection. What is the most appropriate treatment for this relapse?

A 28-year-old woman presents with subacute painful loss of vision in one eye (optic neuritis). She recalls a separate episode of numbness and weakness in one leg, lasting two weeks, that fully resolved 18 months ago. MRI of the brain shows several scattered white-matter lesions. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 27-year-old man is seen in the neurology clinic with 5 days of numbness spreading up from his feet to his waist and new urinary urgency. Last year he had 3 weeks of double vision that recovered completely without treatment. Examination shows brisk reflexes in the legs and upgoing plantars. MRI shows several periventricular and juxtacortical white matter lesions and a short lesion in the cervical spinal cord. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN9332.presentation: Neurological Episodes Separated in Time and Location
UN9332.stem: A 27-year-old woman had an episode of blurred vision in one eye six months ago that fully resolved, and now presents with new tingling and weakness in her right leg. Which diagnosis is most consistent?
A patient with Wilson disease develops worsening neurological symptoms after starting penicillamine. What is the most appropriate alternative treatment?

A 29-year-old woman presents with a 4-day history of painful loss of vision in the left eye with reduced colour vision and a relative afferent pupillary defect. She had a previous episode of limb numbness that resolved. MRI shows periventricular and optic nerve lesions. What is the most appropriate management of this acute episode?

UN9391.stem: A 48-year-old woman presents with a sudden, severe occipital headache that reached maximum intensity within seconds while exercising, with neck stiffness and vomiting. A CT head performed 3 hours after onset is reported as normal. What is the most appropriate next step?
UN9391.correct_answer: Lumbar puncture at least 12 hours after headache onset

UN9391.stem: A 45-year-old woman has a sudden, severe occipital headache that reached maximum intensity within seconds ('the worst of my life'), with vomiting and neck stiffness. What is the most appropriate first investigation?

A 45-year-old woman presents to ED with a sudden-onset, severe "thunderclap" headache that reached maximum intensity within seconds. She vomited once. She is now pain-free but feels tired. CT head is performed 8 hours after the onset and is reported as normal. What is the most appropriate next step to exclude subarachnoid haemorrhage?
UN9391.correct_answer: Perform a lumbar puncture (LP) 12 hours after headache onset

UN9391.stem: A 45-year-old man suddenly develops the worst headache of his life, reaching maximum intensity within seconds, followed by neck stiffness and photophobia. Which feature most strongly supports a diagnosis of subarachnoid haemorrhage?
UN9391.correct_answer: Meningism developing after a thunderclap-onset headache

UN9391.stem: While lifting weights at the gym, a man develops an excruciating headache that reaches full intensity within seconds, followed by vomiting and neck stiffness. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN9391.presentation: Known migraine with a thunderclap headache — next step
UN9391.stem: A 34-year-old woman with a 10-year history of migraine without aura telephones her GP. Two hours ago, while lifting a heavy box, she developed a sudden, severe occipital headache that reached its worst within a minute. She says it is 'completely different' from her usual migraines and the worst headache she has ever had. She has vomited once. She is alert and has no weakness. What is the most appropriate next step?
UN9391.correct_answer: Send her to the emergency department immediately

UN9391.stem: A 52-year-old woman develops an extremely sudden, severe headache that she describes as the worst she has ever experienced, accompanied by vomiting and sensitivity to light. Which diagnosis must be urgently considered?

A 45-year-old woman presents with a sudden, severe “thunderclap” headache that peaked within seconds, associated with vomiting, neck stiffness and a brief collapse. A non-contrast CT head, performed 8 hours after onset, is reported as normal. She is now neurologically intact. What is the most appropriate next investigation?

UN9422.stem: A 67-year-old man develops sudden left-sided facial droop. On examination he can wrinkle his forehead symmetrically, but the lower half of the left face is weak. He also has mild left arm weakness. What is the most appropriate immediate action?

A 38-year-old man develops sudden severe spinning vertigo with nausea after a recent cold. It has lasted two days. He also reports muffled hearing and ringing in his left ear since the onset, and has never had a similar episode. He has no vascular risk factors, limb weakness, speech disturbance or double vision, and examination shows horizontal nystagmus.

Which diagnosis is most likely?

Paramedics bring a 79-year-old man with type 2 diabetes treated with gliclazide into the emergency department after his daughter found him with left-sided weakness and slurred speech. He has been off his food with a chest infection. On arrival his capillary glucose is very low. Within ten minutes of intravenous glucose, his speech and arm strength return completely to normal. What is the most likely explanation?
UN9422.correct_answer: Focal neurological deficit due to hypoglycaemia

UN9422.stem: In a patient thought to have IBS, which feature should prompt a search for an alternative diagnosis?

UN9422.presentation: Acute Focal Weakness With a Very Low Glucose
UN9422.stem: A man is brought into the emergency department with sudden right-sided weakness and slurred speech. A capillary glucose check shows a level of 1.8 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
A 70-year-old man develops sudden left arm weakness and slurred speech, which completely resolve within 30 minutes. CT brain shows no evidence of infarction. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 35-year-old man wakes with sudden unilateral facial droop. He cannot wrinkle his forehead on the affected side or fully close that eye, and there is no limb weakness or other deficit. What is the diagnosis and key treatment?
UN9422.correct_answer: Bell's palsy — give oral corticosteroids and protect the eye

UN9422.stem: A 36-year-old woman who smokes and uses a combined hormonal pill for contraception is brought to the emergency department an hour after she suddenly dropped her cup and could not stand. She has weakness of the left arm and leg, a left facial droop and slurred speech. She has no history of migraine, and her capillary blood glucose is normal. What diagnosis must be urgently considered?

UN9518.presentation: Acute ischaemic stroke within the thrombolysis window
UN9518.stem: A 66-year-old woman suddenly develops left facial droop, left arm weakness and slurred speech while shopping at 10:15. She arrives in the emergency department at 11:30. She ignores her left side and has a moderately severe deficit on stroke scoring. She takes no anticoagulants. Blood glucose is normal and blood pressure is 172/94 mmHg. Non-contrast CT head shows no haemorrhage. What is the most appropriate management?
UN9518.correct_answer: IV thrombolysis and CT angiography to assess for thrombectomy

UN9518.stem: A 68-year-old man presents with acute left-sided weakness and dysarthria. He was last known to be well 2 hours ago. A non-contrast CT head shows no haemorrhage and no established infarct. He has no contraindications to thrombolysis and his blood pressure is 165/90 mmHg. What is the most appropriate management?

A 72-year-old man suddenly develops right facial droop, right arm and leg weakness, and slurred speech while at home. His wife calls an ambulance and he arrives 70 minutes after symptom onset. On examination he has a right hemiparesis and dysarthria. Blood pressure is 180/95 mmHg and capillary glucose is normal. He takes no anticoagulants. What is the most appropriate immediate next step?

UN9518.presentation: Acute Confusion in Sickle Cell Disease
UN9518.stem: A 9-year-old boy with known sickle cell disease becomes suddenly confused and develops weakness down one side of his body. What complication should be urgently considered?

A 45-year-old woman presents with a sudden, severe “thunderclap” headache that peaked within seconds, associated with vomiting, neck stiffness and a brief collapse. A non-contrast CT head, performed 8 hours after onset, is reported as normal. She is now neurologically intact. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
A patient developed sudden right-sided weakness and aphasia 2 hours ago. A CT head shows no haemorrhage, and there are no contraindications. What is the most appropriate treatment?
UN9518.correct_answer: IV thrombolysis, considering thrombectomy if large-vessel occlusion

UN9518.stem: A 45-year-old woman has a sudden, severe occipital headache that reached maximum intensity within seconds ('the worst of my life'), with vomiting and neck stiffness. What is the most appropriate first investigation?

A 60-year-old man develops sudden right-sided weakness and expressive dysphasia. He was last seen well 2 hours ago. A CT head shows no haemorrhage and no established infarct. His blood pressure is 170/95 and glucose is normal. What is the most appropriate treatment?

UN9576.stem: Which of these symptoms most specifically points to involvement of the dominant cerebral hemisphere, in a patient with sudden facial weakness, arm weakness and difficulty speaking?

A 68-year-old man presents with acute left-sided weakness and dysarthria. He was last known to be well 2 hours ago. A non-contrast CT head shows no haemorrhage and no established infarct. He has no contraindications to thrombolysis and his blood pressure is 165/90 mmHg. What is the most appropriate management?

A 58-year-old woman develops a tremor, generalised slowness of movement and difficulty starting to walk; her symptoms began predominantly on one side. Which feature is most characteristic of Parkinson's disease?

A 70-year-old man with atrial fibrillation taking apixaban presents 90 minutes after sudden left-sided weakness. CT shows no haemorrhage. His last apixaban dose was this morning. What is the most appropriate management?
UN9576.correct_answer: Assess thrombectomy eligibility; thrombolysis is generally contraindicated on a therapeutic DOAC

UN9576.stem: A 60-year-old woman has sudden right hemiplegia, gaze deviation and global aphasia. She was last well 90 minutes ago. CT shows no haemorrhage; CT angiography confirms a proximal left middle cerebral artery occlusion. What is the most appropriate treatment?
UN9576.correct_answer: Mechanical thrombectomy, with IV thrombolysis if eligible

UN9576.stem: A 58-year-old woman develops sudden severe breathlessness, pleuritic chest pain, a rapid heart rate and a low blood pressure shortly after a long-haul flight. Which complication of pulmonary embolism is particularly concerning in this presentation?

A 58-year-old man has central crushing chest pain for 40 minutes. His ECG shows ST-segment elevation in leads V1 to V4. He presents to a hospital with a primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) centre, and PCI can be delivered within 90 minutes. What is the most appropriate immediate reperfusion strategy?

A 68-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 90 minutes after sudden onset right-sided weakness and facial droop. Examination confirms dense right hemiparesis and expressive aphasia. A CT head scan shows no evidence of intracranial haemorrhage. What is the most appropriate next step?

UN9665.stem: Watering of the eye and nasal blockage on the same side accompany repeated attacks of intense one-sided eye pain in a 41-year-old man. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN9665.presentation: Severe Unilateral Eye Pain With Autonomic Features
UN9665.stem: A 38-year-old man describes nightly episodes over the past two weeks of excruciating pain around his right eye lasting about an hour, with the right eye watering and the right nostril becoming blocked during each attack. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 9-year-old boy has recurrent episodes of severe central abdominal pain lasting one to several hours, associated with facial pallor and loss of appetite; he occasionally vomits but not always. He is completely well between attacks, and his mother has a history of migraine. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 65-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of severe, brief, electric shock-like pain over her right cheek and jaw, each lasting a few seconds. The pain is triggered by brushing her teeth, eating and cold air. Neurological examination is normal. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

A 30-year-old man has recurrent attacks of excruciating, strictly unilateral pain around one eye, lasting about an hour and recurring at the same times each day for several weeks. During attacks that eye waters and the nostril runs, and he is restless. What is the most appropriate acute treatment?
UN9665.correct_answer: High-flow oxygen and a subcutaneous triptan

UN9665.stem: A 40-year-old man has recurrent episodes of severe throbbing headache, palpitations, sweating and pallor. During an episode his blood pressure is 210/120 mmHg, returning to normal between episodes. He feels intensely anxious during the attacks. What is the most appropriate initial investigation?

A 46-year-old man has recurrent episodes of severe pain and swelling at the base of his big toe, often following heavy meals and alcohol intake. Which dietary factor is particularly associated with gout attacks?

A 26-year-old man sees his GP with 6 days of nasal congestion, purulent discharge and left-sided facial pain. Since this morning his left upper and lower eyelids have become red and swollen, and he has double vision when looking to the left. His temperature is 38.2°C. What is the most appropriate management?
UN9665.correct_answer: Refer to hospital for same-day assessment

UN9669.stem: A 72-year-old man suddenly develops right facial droop, right arm and leg weakness, and slurred speech while at home. His wife calls an ambulance and he arrives 70 minutes after symptom onset. On examination he has a right hemiparesis and dysarthria. Blood pressure is 180/95 mmHg and capillary glucose is normal. He takes no anticoagulants. What is the most appropriate immediate next step?

A 58-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by ambulance. Her husband found her at breakfast with a drooping face, slurred speech and a weak right arm; she had been seen well less than an hour earlier. Her capillary glucose is normal and she is haemodynamically stable. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
UN9669.correct_answer: Arrange an immediate non-contrast CT head as part of urgent stroke team assessment

UN9669.stem: Sudden weakness and numbness affecting the right arm and leg, with right facial droop, develop in a 69-year-old woman. Which side of the brain is most likely affected?

A 74-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by ambulance 40 minutes after her husband noticed her speech became slurred and her left arm fell limply off the arm of her chair while she was watching television. She takes no anticoagulants. Thrombolysis is being considered. Which investigation is needed first?
UN9669.correct_answer: Non-contrast CT scan of the head

UN9669.presentation: Brain abscess — first imaging and avoiding lumbar puncture
UN9669.stem: A 46-year-old man is admitted with 5 days of worsening headache, fever and new right-sided weakness. Two weeks ago he was treated for a dental abscess. His temperature is 38.4°C, Glasgow Coma Scale score is 14 and there is mild right arm and leg weakness. A brain abscess is suspected and blood cultures have been taken. Which investigation should be performed next?
UN9669.correct_answer: Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI of the brain

UN9669.stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with a sudden, severe “thunderclap” headache that peaked within seconds, associated with vomiting, neck stiffness and a brief collapse. A non-contrast CT head, performed 8 hours after onset, is reported as normal. She is now neurologically intact. What is the most appropriate next investigation?

A 68-year-old man presents with acute left-sided weakness and dysarthria. He was last known to be well 2 hours ago. A non-contrast CT head shows no haemorrhage and no established infarct. He has no contraindications to thrombolysis and his blood pressure is 165/90 mmHg. What is the most appropriate management?

A 45-year-old woman has a sudden, severe occipital headache that reached maximum intensity within seconds ('the worst of my life'), with vomiting and neck stiffness. What is the most appropriate first investigation?

UN9742.stem: A 68-year-old man with confirmed vitamin B12 deficiency reports tingling and numbness in both feet, along with difficulty with balance when walking. Which complication is particularly important to recognise here?
UN9742.correct_answer: Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord

UN9742.presentation: Deep Neck-Space Infection With Airway Risk
UN9742.stem: A patient being treated for acute tonsillitis develops worsening neck swelling over 24 hours, along with increasing difficulty swallowing and a new stridor. What is the most important immediate concern?
UN9742.correct_answer: Airway compromise from deep neck infection

UN9742.stem: A 68-year-old man develops a painful cluster of blistering lesions across the left side of his forehead and upper eyelid, sparing the tip of his nose. Which complication is particularly important to consider?

A patient with a known dental infection develops rapidly worsening swelling under the chin and tongue, increasing difficulty swallowing saliva and a change in his voice. What should be prioritised immediately?
UN9742.correct_answer: Assessment and protection of the airway

UN9742.stem: A 38-year-old woman with known myasthenia gravis develops increasing breathlessness and difficulty swallowing over 24 hours following a chest infection. Her forced vital capacity is falling on serial measurement. What is the most important immediate assessment?
UN9742.correct_answer: Serial FVC with airway and ventilation support on standby

UN9742.stem: An 81-year-old woman with long-standing Parkinson disease lives in a care home. She has been treated for three chest infections in four months, each affecting the right lower zone on chest X-ray. Carers say her eyes water and she splutters when drinking tea, she takes a long time to finish meals, and food stays in her mouth. She has never smoked. What is the most likely underlying cause of her recurrent infections?

A 58-year-old woman develops a tremor, generalised slowness of movement and difficulty starting to walk; her symptoms began predominantly on one side. Which feature is most characteristic of Parkinson's disease?

UN9742.presentation: Influenza Complication in an Older Adult
UN9742.stem: During a winter flu outbreak in her area, the family of an 81-year-old woman bring her in because she has suddenly spiked a temperature, developed a cough, and become muddled, which is completely out of character for her. Which complication is particularly important to consider in an older adult?

UN9746.stem: A 36-year-old woman who smokes and uses a combined hormonal pill for contraception is brought to the emergency department an hour after she suddenly dropped her cup and could not stand. She has weakness of the left arm and leg, a left facial droop and slurred speech. She has no history of migraine, and her capillary blood glucose is normal. What diagnosis must be urgently considered?

A 67-year-old man develops sudden left-sided facial droop. On examination he can wrinkle his forehead symmetrically, but the lower half of the left face is weak. He also has mild left arm weakness. What is the most appropriate immediate action?

A 66-year-old woman tells her optometrist that for 6 weeks she has been knocking cups off the left side of the table and catching her left shoulder on doorways. Her visual acuity is 6/9 in each eye, her pupils react normally and her fundi appear healthy. On confrontation she may be missing targets in the left half of the field of each eye, but her answers vary and the finding is uncertain. She is referred to the hospital eye service so that any field loss can be mapped precisely and monitored.

Which investigation will most accurately chart any loss of visual field?
A 70-year-old man suffers a stroke affecting the left occipital lobe. Afterwards, he has lost the same side of the visual field — the right side — in both eyes. What is this visual deficit called?

A 70-year-old woman with hypertension and hyperlipidaemia woke this morning unable to see the upper half of the visual field in her right eye. It is painless and has not improved. She has no headache, jaw claudication or scalp tenderness. Visual acuity is 6/9 in the right eye. Fundoscopy shows a pale, swollen inferior half of the retina with a bright yellow refractile plaque in the inferior branch retinal arteriole near the disc. The superior retina and the veins look normal. The optic disc is normal. A right carotid bruit is heard. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 72-year-old man suddenly develops right facial droop, right arm and leg weakness, and slurred speech while at home. His wife calls an ambulance and he arrives 70 minutes after symptom onset. On examination he has a right hemiparesis and dysarthria. Blood pressure is 180/95 mmHg and capillary glucose is normal. He takes no anticoagulants. What is the most appropriate immediate next step?

A 71-year-old woman with long-standing hypertension and type 2 diabetes wakes with weakness of the left side of her face, her left arm and her left leg, all affected to a similar degree. Her speech content and understanding are normal, her visual fields are full and she has no neglect of the left side. Sensation is intact. Which type of stroke is most likely?

UN9746.presentation: Neck pain, headache and focal deficit in a young adult — carotid dissection
UN9746.stem:
A 41-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after her left arm and the left side of her face suddenly became weak, and she started bumping into things on her left. For 3 days she has had a constant pain in the right side of her neck spreading to her right forehead, which began after a roller-coaster ride. She has never had migraines. On examination she has weakness of the left face and arm, ignores objects on her left side, and has a slightly drooping right upper eyelid with a smaller right pupil. She is afebrile, and her blood pressure and capillary glucose are normal.

Which diagnosis best explains her presentation?

UN10009.stem: A 72-year-old man reports progressive slowness of movement over a year. He has an asymmetric resting tremor of the right hand and increasing stiffness, and his handwriting has become smaller. On examination there is cogwheel rigidity, bradykinesia, and a resting tremor that decreases when he reaches for an object. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN10009.presentation: Asymmetric Resting Tremor With Slowness and Stiffness
UN10009.stem: A 70-year-old man's wife reports that his right hand shakes when it is resting in his lap but settles when he reaches for a cup. He has become noticeably slower getting out of a chair, and his right arm feels stiff on examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A 75-year-old man is found to have a tremor at rest, slowness of movement and increased muscle tone. Which diagnosis is most likely?

A 74-year-old woman has been diagnosed with Parkinson's disease by a specialist. Over the past year her handwriting has become small, she has a tremor of her left hand at rest, and she now takes a long time to dress and has difficulty turning over in bed. Examination shows asymmetrical rigidity and slow, small movements. She lives alone and wants treatment to stay independent. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
UN10009.correct_answer: Levodopa combined with a dopa-decarboxylase inhibitor

UN10009.stem: An older man has a slowly progressive, asymmetrical resting tremor ('pill-rolling'), rigidity (cogwheel) and bradykinesia, with a shuffling gait. He has no early falls and no eye-movement abnormality. What is the most likely diagnosis and most effective symptomatic treatment?
UN10009.correct_answer: Idiopathic Parkinson's disease — levodopa (with a dopa-decarboxylase inhibitor)

UN10009.stem: A 64-year-old woman has noticed over the past year that her handwriting has become smaller and she has become slower at everyday tasks. Her husband says she shuffles when she walks. On examination there is a pill-rolling tremor of her left hand at rest that improves when she reaches for an object, and cogwheel rigidity at the left wrist. Loss of which neurons underlies her condition?
UN10009.correct_answer: Dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra

UN10009.stem: A 58-year-old woman develops a tremor, generalised slowness of movement and difficulty starting to walk; her symptoms began predominantly on one side. Which feature is most characteristic of Parkinson's disease?

A 72-year-old retired teacher is brought to his GP by his wife, who says his handwriting has become tiny and he now takes a long time to get dressed. He takes no regular medication. On examination his right hand shakes while resting in his lap but settles when he reaches for a pen. He has a reduced arm swing on the right when walking, and there is cogwheel stiffness at the right wrist. What is the likeliest diagnosis?

UN10031.stem: Tingling and weakness develop in a 47-year-old woman's hand, worse overnight, involving her thumb and the next two fingers. Which nerve compression is responsible?

A patient has weakness of the small muscles of the hand with a 'claw' appearance of the ring and little fingers, weak finger abduction/adduction, and sensory loss over the little finger and medial half of the ring finger. There is a positive Froment's sign. Which nerve is affected?
UN10031.correct_answer: The ulnar nerve (commonly at the elbow)

UN10031.stem: A 40-year-old office worker who habitually rests his elbows on his desk reports tingling in his right hand for several weeks. Sensation is reduced over the fifth digit and the medial side of the fourth digit, and he has weakness when spreading his fingers apart. Sensation over the thumb and index finger is normal. Which nerve is the likely source of his symptoms?

A 64-year-old man with type 2 diabetes notices that he can no longer lay his right hand flat on a table. Over the past year his little finger has gradually bent at the knuckle. It is painless and does not catch or click. There is a firm nodule in the palm with a cord extending into the little finger, and a fixed flexion deformity at the MCP joint. Sensation is normal and there is no wasting of the small muscles of the hand. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A 45-year-old office worker wakes most nights with tingling and numbness in her thumb, index and middle fingers, which she relieves by shaking her hand. Which nerve is most likely compressed?

A 64-year-old man has slowly worsening numbness and tingling that began in his feet and has spread upward, with diminished ankle reflexes. Which pattern is most consistent with a peripheral neuropathy?

A paediatric registrar is called to the delivery suite to see a baby boy with a bilateral cleft of the lip and palate, an extra digit on the ulnar side of each hand and small, close-set eyes. There is also a sharply defined area of absent skin on the scalp. An echocardiogram shows a congenital heart defect. Which karyotype is most likely?

A patient with type 2 diabetes has painful, burning, symmetrical numbness and tingling in both feet (a glove-and-stocking distribution) that disturbs sleep. Glycaemic control has been optimised. He also has coexisting low mood. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment for the neuropathic pain?

UN10033.stem: A 71-year-old woman has sudden left-sided weakness together with an upper motor neurone pattern of facial weakness on the right. Which cranial nerve is responsible for producing the facial weakness itself?

A 67-year-old man develops sudden left-sided facial droop. On examination he can wrinkle his forehead symmetrically, but the lower half of the left face is weak. He also has mild left arm weakness. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
A 66-year-old woman suddenly cannot find her words and develops weakness of her right arm, though she remains alert. Which cerebral hemisphere is most likely affected?

UN10033.presentation: Facial Weakness Affecting the Whole Side of the Face
UN10033.stem: A patient develops sudden weakness of the entire left side of the face, including the inability to raise the left eyebrow or fully close the left eye. What type of facial nerve lesion does this represent?
UN10033.correct_answer: Lower motor neurone facial nerve palsy

UN10033.stem: A 38-year-old woman develops weakness affecting the entire left side of her face, including being unable to close her left eye and losing movement of her forehead on that side. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN10033.presentation: Facial Weakness That Spares the Forehead
UN10033.stem: A patient has weakness affecting only the lower part of the left side of the face, with normal, symmetrical forehead wrinkling on both sides. Which lesion best explains this finding?
Which of these symptoms most specifically points to involvement of the dominant cerebral hemisphere, in a patient with sudden facial weakness, arm weakness and difficulty speaking?
Sudden weakness and numbness affecting the right arm and leg, with right facial droop, develop in a 69-year-old woman. Which side of the brain is most likely affected?

UN10135.stem: A young adult has fever, headache, confusion and a witnessed seizure, with altered behaviour but no purpuric rash. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment while investigations proceed?

UN10135.presentation: Fever, Neck Stiffness and Non-Blanching Rash
UN10135.stem: A university student presents with fever, a severe headache, neck stiffness and a rash that does not fade under pressure. She is becoming increasingly drowsy. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN10135.presentation: Suspected viral encephalitis — key CSF test
UN10135.stem: A 46-year-old woman is admitted to the acute medical unit with 3 days of fever and headache. Today she has become confused, with odd behaviour and difficulty finding words. There is no rash and no neck stiffness. Intravenous aciclovir has been started. CT head is normal, there are no contraindications to lumbar puncture, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) has been obtained. Which CSF test is most important for identifying the cause of her illness?

A 19-year-old student presents with fever, confusion and hypotension. There is a rapidly spreading non-blanching purpuric rash. Neck stiffness is absent. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
UN10135.correct_answer: Immediate IV ceftriaxone (do not delay for investigations)

UN10135.stem: A 29-year-old woman with no past medical history comes in febrile, with a pounding headache, increasingly muddled, and has had several fits affecting one side of her body. Which diagnosis needs to be high on the list?
A 68-year-old woman presents with confusion, fever, and hypotension (BP 82/50 mmHg). She has a serum lactate of 4.8 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
UN10135.correct_answer: Implement the Sepsis Six bundle immediately

UN10135.stem: A 19-year-old woman has fever, severe headache, neck stiffness and photophobia, and is becoming drowsy. She has a non-blanching purpuric rash. Suspected meningococcal meningitis with septicaemia. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

UN10135.presentation: Blood cultures in suspected bacterial meningitis
UN10135.stem:
A 34-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department with a high fever, intense headache and neck stiffness that came on over the last 12 hours. Bacterial meningitis is suspected. She is conscious, her airway is safe and she has no rash.

Which investigation should be taken without delay as part of her first assessment?

UN10227.stem: A 38-year-old woman with known myasthenia gravis develops increasing breathlessness and difficulty swallowing over 24 hours following a chest infection. Her forced vital capacity is falling on serial measurement. What is the most important immediate assessment?
UN10227.correct_answer: Serial FVC with airway and ventilation support on standby

UN10227.stem: A patient with a known dental infection develops rapidly worsening swelling under the chin and tongue, increasing difficulty swallowing saliva and a change in his voice. What should be prioritised immediately?
UN10227.correct_answer: Assessment and protection of the airway

UN10227.presentation: Deep Neck-Space Infection With Airway Risk
UN10227.stem: A patient being treated for acute tonsillitis develops worsening neck swelling over 24 hours, along with increasing difficulty swallowing and a new stridor. What is the most important immediate concern?
UN10227.correct_answer: Airway compromise from deep neck infection

UN10227.stem: A 45-year-old woman with myasthenia gravis has a sudden deterioration with difficulty swallowing and shortness of breath. She cannot sustain a head-lift, and her forced vital capacity has fallen from 30 to 18 mL/kg over 6 hours, and she has a weak cough with pooled secretions. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

A 47-year-old woman with generalised myasthenia gravis, controlled on pyridostigmine, is admitted with acute pyelonephritis. She has no drug allergies and her kidney function is normal. Before choosing an intravenous antibiotic, the FY1 doctor checks for interactions with her myasthenia. Which antibiotic is contraindicated in her?

UN10227.presentation: Newly diagnosed myasthenia gravis — thymus imaging
UN10227.stem: A 34-year-old woman is newly diagnosed with generalised myasthenia gravis. Her acetylcholine receptor antibodies are positive and she has started pyridostigmine in the neurology clinic. Which imaging should be arranged next?

A 35-year-old woman has intermittent drooping of the left eyelid that worsens through the day and with sustained upgaze, along with intermittent double vision. Her symptoms improve after a period of rest. The pupils are normal and the rest of the neurological examination is unremarkable. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN10227.presentation: Myasthenia gravis — next test when acetylcholine receptor antibodies are negative

He has a reduced arm swing on the right when walking, and there is cogwheel stiffness at the right wrist. What is the likeliest diagnosis?

A 72-year-old man with Parkinson's disease has long-standing constipation, which is common in his condition. He takes senna tablets at night, and at a medication review with the practice pharmacist he asks how they actually work. What is the main action of this type of laxative?

UN10265.stem: A 68-year-old man with confirmed vitamin B12 deficiency reports tingling and numbness in both feet, along with difficulty with balance when walking. Which complication is particularly important to recognise here?
UN10265.correct_answer: Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord

UN10265.presentation: Nitrous oxide-related vitamin B12 deficiency — initial test
UN10265.stem: A 20-year-old student presents to his GP with 3 weeks of numbness in both feet and an unsteady gait. He says he has inhaled large amounts of nitrous oxide from canisters most weekends for the past year. Romberg test is positive and vibration sense is reduced at the ankles. Vitamin B12 deficiency caused by nitrous oxide use is suspected. Which test should be used as the initial test for vitamin B12 deficiency?

UN10265.presentation: Vitamin B12 Deficiency — Reversible Cognitive Impairment
UN10265.stem: A 78-year-old vegetarian woman has a few months of worsening memory, low mood and unsteadiness. Examination shows reduced vibration and proprioception in the feet with absent ankle reflexes. Blood tests show a macrocytic anaemia. Which reversible cause should be excluded?

A 66-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has taken metformin for 12 years. He has tingling in both feet. He eats a mixed diet including meat and dairy, has had no gastrointestinal surgery and has no other risk factors for vitamin B12 deficiency. Total vitamin B12 is low, haemoglobin is normal, and his GP judges metformin to be the cause. His diabetes is well controlled and metformin suits him. Which is the most appropriate treatment plan?
UN10265.correct_answer: Vitamin B12 replacement while continuing metformin

UN10265.presentation: Suspected B12 deficiency with neurological signs — timing of treatment
UN10265.stem: A 68-year-old man is seen on the acute medical unit with 2 months of numbness in both feet, unsteadiness in the dark and falls. Vibration and joint position sense are impaired in the feet and Romberg's test is positive. Haemoglobin is 92 g/L with mean cell volume 118 fL. Vitamin B12 deficiency with spinal cord involvement is suspected. What is the most appropriate management?
UN10265.correct_answer: Send a B12 level, then start intramuscular B12 now

UN10265.stem: A 41-year-old man reports tiredness, pins-and-needles in both feet, and soreness of his tongue. Full blood count reveals an elevated mean corpuscular volume. Which deficiency is most likely responsible?

A 27-year-old woman who has eaten a strict vegan diet for five years, without supplements, sees her GP with tiredness, a sore red smooth tongue and pins and needles in both feet. She looks pale with a slight lemon tinge. Blood tests show an anaemia with large red cells. She drinks no alcohol and her thyroid function is normal. Which deficiency is most likely?

UN10265.presentation: Vitamin B12 deficiency — negative anti-intrinsic factor antibody
UN10265.stem: A 55-year-old woman with vitiligo and hypothyroidism has confirmed vitamin B12 deficiency. She eats a mixed diet, takes no medicines linked to deficiency and has had no gastrointestinal surgery. Autoimmune gastritis (pernicious anaemia) is suspected, but her anti-intrinsic factor antibody test is negative. What is the most appropriate interpretation of this result?

UN10462.stem: A 23-year-old man describes recurrent episodes beginning with a rising sensation in the stomach and a feeling of déjà vu, followed by lip-smacking and plucking at his clothes, for which he is amnesic, lasting about a minute with brief postictal confusion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
UN10462.correct_answer: Focal seizures of temporal lobe origin

UN10462.stem: A 25-year-old woman has a first generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting about 90 seconds, witnessed by her partner, with full recovery afterwards. She has a family history of epilepsy. Neurological examination and capillary glucose are normal, and there is no head injury. What is the most appropriate next step?

A 31-year-old woman is on the postnatal ward 18 hours after an uncomplicated vaginal birth. During labour her blood pressure was raised and her urine dipstick showed protein. The midwife calls you because she has just had a generalised seizure lasting about a minute and is now drowsy. Her capillary glucose is normal and she has never had a seizure before. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 40-year-old man with known epilepsy is brought to the emergency department with continuous generalised tonic-clonic seizure activity. He has now been convulsing for 25 minutes and has not regained consciousness between seizures. Intravenous access is established and he has already received two doses of intravenous lorazepam 10 minutes apart, which have not terminated the seizure. What is the most appropriate next step?
A young adult has fever, headache, confusion and a witnessed seizure, with altered behaviour but no purpuric rash. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment while investigations proceed?

A 7-year-old girl is brought to her GP because her teacher has noticed that she switches off many times a day, sometimes in the middle of a sentence, with her eyelids fluttering. Each episode lasts only seconds, she does not fall, and she carries on with her task straight afterwards with no drowsiness. An episode is triggered in clinic when she is asked to breathe deeply and quickly for a few minutes. What kind of seizure is she most likely having?

An 82-year-old woman who recently started indapamide and sertraline is brought to the emergency department after a generalised seizure at home. The seizure has stopped, but she remains drowsy and is vomiting repeatedly. Her serum sodium is 116 mmol/L. Her airway is secure and her blood glucose is normal. Which treatment should be given now?
UN10462.correct_answer: Intravenous hypertonic (2.7% to 3%) sodium chloride bolus with close sodium monitoring

UN10462.stem: A 30-year-old woman attends after a night of heavy drinking and repeated retching, followed by several episodes of vomiting fresh red blood. In triage she feels dizzy, her systolic pressure is low and her heart rate is fast. What is the immediate priority?

UN10463.stem: A 73-year-old man has recently been diagnosed with dementia. He still drives regularly and asks what he should do next regarding his driving licence. What is the most appropriate advice?
UN10463.correct_answer: Inform the DVLA and follow advice regarding fitness to drive

UN10463.stem: A patient with epilepsy continues to drive against advice and has not informed the DVLA, despite you explaining the legal duty. What is the most appropriate action?
UN10463.correct_answer: Advise them again; if they still drive, inform the DVLA

UN10463.stem:
A 35-year-old man with a car driving licence has been treated on an acute psychiatric ward for his first manic episode. He is now settled, has insight and is due to be discharged next week. He tells you he plans to drive himself home.

What is the most appropriate advice about driving?
UN10463.correct_answer: He must not drive and must notify the DVLA himself

UN10463.stem: A 28-year-old man has his first generalised tonic-clonic seizure. He holds an ordinary (Group 1) driving licence. What is the correct advice regarding driving?
UN10463.correct_answer: He must stop driving and notify the DVLA, with a minimum 6-month ban

UN10463.stem: A 35-year-old lorry driver is diagnosed with epilepsy following a first seizure. He states he will not inform the DVLA and will continue driving. The doctor is concerned about public safety. What is the most appropriate action?
UN10463.correct_answer: Explain his legal duty to tell the DVLA; if he continues to drive, inform the DVLA

UN10463.stem: A 55-year-old bus driver has had two unprovoked generalised tonic-clonic seizures a month apart. A neurologist diagnoses epilepsy and starts lamotrigine. He asks what this means for his car and bus licences. What is the correct advice?
UN10463.correct_answer: He must tell the DVLA; he cannot drive a car until seizure-free for 1 year, and must be seizure-free for 10 years without medication before driving a bus

UN10463.presentation: Multiple sclerosis — driving and the DVLA
UN10463.stem: A 36-year-old man is diagnosed with relapsing–remitting multiple sclerosis in the neurology clinic. Since his latest relapse he has stiffness and weakness of his right leg that makes it hard to move his foot quickly between the pedals. He drives a car to work and has a standard car licence. He asks whether he needs to tell anyone about the diagnosis. What is the most appropriate advice about driving?
UN10463.correct_answer: He must tell the DVLA himself about his diagnosis

UN10463.presentation: Ménière disease — driving and the DVLA
UN10463.stem:
A 48-year-old woman who drives a car for work has Ménière disease confirmed by an ear, nose and throat (ENT) specialist. Over the past month she has had three sudden attacks of disabling rotational vertigo, each coming on without warning and lasting several hours. She asks her GP whether she can carry on driving.

What is the most appropriate advice?
UN10463.correct_answer: Stop driving and tell the DVLA about her condition

She returns to her GP with a painful, red, watering left eye, and her vision in that eye has become blurred. Fluorescein staining shows an area of corneal damage on the lower part of the cornea.

What is the most appropriate management?
UN10565.correct_answer: Same-day referral to the eye department

UN10565.stem: A 35-year-old man wakes with sudden unilateral facial droop. He cannot wrinkle his forehead on the affected side or fully close that eye, and there is no limb weakness or other deficit. What is the diagnosis and key treatment?
UN10565.correct_answer: Bell's palsy — give oral corticosteroids and protect the eye

UN10565.presentation: Unilateral Facial Weakness Including the Forehead
UN10565.stem: A patient wakes with weakness of the left side of the face, unable to raise the left eyebrow or fully close the left eye, while the rest of their neurological examination is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN10565.presentation: Facial nerve palsy — feature that needs urgent specialist referral
UN10565.stem:
A 52-year-old man sees his GP with weakness of the right side of his face, including his forehead. He cannot fully close his right eye. There are no limb symptoms, the ear canal and eardrum look normal, and there is no rash. The GP is considering a diagnosis of Bell palsy.

Which additional feature should most prompt specialist referral rather than treatment as Bell palsy in primary care?
UN10565.correct_answer: Weakness worsening slowly over three weeks

UN10565.stem: A 38-year-old woman develops weakness affecting the entire left side of her face, including being unable to close her left eye and losing movement of her forehead on that side. What is the most likely diagnosis?

There are no vesicles in or around the ear, and limb power, sensation and speech are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN10565.presentation: Facial Weakness Affecting the Whole Side of the Face
UN10565.stem: A patient develops sudden weakness of the entire left side of the face, including the inability to raise the left eyebrow or fully close the left eye. What type of facial nerve lesion does this represent?
UN10565.correct_answer: Lower motor neurone facial nerve palsy

UN10565.stem: A 52-year-old man sees his GP because he woke yesterday with the left side of his face drooping. He dribbles when drinking, cannot wrinkle his left forehead or fully close his left eye, and sounds seem uncomfortably loud in his left ear. There are no vesicles in the ear or mouth, the ear canal and drum look normal, and there is no limb weakness or other neurological sign. What is the most appropriate management?

He has a reduced arm swing on the right when walking, and there is cogwheel stiffness at the right wrist. What is the likeliest diagnosis?

A 64-year-old woman has noticed over the past year that her handwriting has become smaller and she has become slower at everyday tasks. Her husband says she shuffles when she walks. On examination there is a pill-rolling tremor of her left hand at rest that improves when she reaches for an object, and cogwheel rigidity at the left wrist. Loss of which neurons underlies her condition?
UN10566.correct_answer: Dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra

A 45-year-old man suddenly develops the worst headache of his life, reaching maximum intensity within seconds, followed by neck stiffness and photophobia. Which feature most strongly supports a diagnosis of subarachnoid haemorrhage?
UN10574.correct_answer: Meningism developing after a thunderclap-onset headache

UN10574.stem: While lifting weights at the gym, a man develops an excruciating headache that reaches full intensity within seconds, followed by vomiting and neck stiffness. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN10574.presentation: Fever, Neck Stiffness and Non-Blanching Rash
UN10574.stem: A university student presents with fever, a severe headache, neck stiffness and a rash that does not fade under pressure. She is becoming increasingly drowsy. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 38-year-old woman stops in the middle of a gym class, clutching the back of her head and saying it felt as if she had been hit with a bat. An hour later in the emergency department she is avoiding the lights, has vomited, and it hurts when her neck is bent forwards. Which feature of her presentation most supports subarachnoid haemorrhage?
UN10574.correct_answer: Neck stiffness developing after a headache that peaked instantly

UN10574.stem: A 45-year-old woman has a sudden, severe occipital headache that reached maximum intensity within seconds ('the worst of my life'), with vomiting and neck stiffness. What is the most appropriate first investigation?

A 48-year-old woman presents with a sudden, severe occipital headache that reached maximum intensity within seconds while exercising, with neck stiffness and vomiting. A CT head performed 3 hours after onset is reported as normal. What is the most appropriate next step?
UN10574.correct_answer: Lumbar puncture at least 12 hours after headache onset

UN10578.stem: Which of these symptoms most specifically points to involvement of the dominant cerebral hemisphere, in a patient with sudden facial weakness, arm weakness and difficulty speaking?

A 67-year-old man develops sudden left-sided facial droop. On examination he can wrinkle his forehead symmetrically, but the lower half of the left face is weak. He also has mild left arm weakness. What is the most appropriate immediate action?

A 71-year-old woman has sudden left-sided weakness together with an upper motor neurone pattern of facial weakness on the right. Which cranial nerve is responsible for producing the facial weakness itself?

A 36-year-old woman who smokes and uses a combined hormonal pill for contraception is brought to the emergency department an hour after she suddenly dropped her cup and could not stand. She has weakness of the left arm and leg, a left facial droop and slurred speech. She has no history of migraine, and her capillary blood glucose is normal. What diagnosis must be urgently considered?

A 72-year-old man suddenly develops right facial droop, right arm and leg weakness, and slurred speech while at home. His wife calls an ambulance and he arrives 70 minutes after symptom onset. On examination he has a right hemiparesis and dysarthria. Blood pressure is 180/95 mmHg and capillary glucose is normal. He takes no anticoagulants. What is the most appropriate immediate next step?

UN10578.presentation: Acute ischaemic stroke within the thrombolysis window
UN10578.stem: A 66-year-old woman suddenly develops left facial droop, left arm weakness and slurred speech while shopping at 10:15. She arrives in the emergency department at 11:30. She ignores her left side and has a moderately severe deficit on stroke scoring. She takes no anticoagulants. Blood glucose is normal and blood pressure is 172/94 mmHg. Non-contrast CT head shows no haemorrhage. What is the most appropriate management?
UN10578.correct_answer: IV thrombolysis and CT angiography to assess for thrombectomy

UN10578.stem: A 58-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by ambulance. Her husband found her at breakfast with a drooping face, slurred speech and a weak right arm; she had been seen well less than an hour earlier. Her capillary glucose is normal and she is haemodynamically stable. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
UN10578.correct_answer: Arrange an immediate non-contrast CT head as part of urgent stroke team assessment

UN10578.stem: A 66-year-old woman suddenly cannot find her words and develops weakness of her right arm, though she remains alert. Which cerebral hemisphere is most likely affected?

UN10581.stem: A 68-year-old man with known Parkinson's disease finds it hard to get going when he starts walking, and his stride length shortens progressively as he continues. Which cardinal motor sign does this describe?
A 60-year-old man has confirmed motor neurone disease with mixed upper and lower motor neuron signs and no sensory loss. Which drug is most likely to modestly prolong survival?

A 58-year-old woman develops a tremor, generalised slowness of movement and difficulty starting to walk; her symptoms began predominantly on one side. Which feature is most characteristic of Parkinson's disease?
A 70-year-old man with known Parkinson's disease struggles to start walking and repeatedly freezes when approaching doorways. What term describes this symptom?

A 60-year-old man has progressive weakness with a mix of wasting and fasciculations (lower motor neuron) alongside brisk reflexes and up-going plantars (upper motor neuron), with no sensory loss and no eye-movement or sphincter involvement. What is the most likely diagnosis?

UN10581.presentation: Mixed Upper And Lower Motor Neurone Signs
UN10581.stem: Visible wasting, fasciculations and brisk reflexes accompany progressively worsening weakness in both legs of a 64-year-old woman. Which diagnosis is most likely?

A 2-year-old born very prematurely has delayed motor milestones, stiff ('scissoring') legs with increased tone, brisk reflexes and persistent toe-walking. The motor problem is NON-progressive. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 72-year-old man reports progressive slowness of movement over a year. He has an asymmetric resting tremor of the right hand and increasing stiffness, and his handwriting has become smaller. On examination there is cogwheel rigidity, bradykinesia, and a resting tremor that decreases when he reaches for an object. What is the most likely diagnosis?
